The text used is (with a few unimportant modifications) that of Kühn (Volume II), as edited by Georg Helmreich; Teubner, Leipzig, 1893. <note>Karl Gottlob Kühn (1754–1840) produced the monumental twenty-volume edition of Galen's works which remains a standard reference for scholars.</note> The numbers of the pages of Kühn's edition are printed at the side of the Greek text <note>original: "Greek text"</note>, a parallel mark (||) in the line indicating the exact point of division between Kühn's pages.

Words in the English text which are enclosed in square brackets are supplementary or explanatory; practically all explanations, however, are relegated to the footnotes or introduction. In the footnotes, also, attention is drawn to words which are of particular <term>philological|The study of the history and development of languages</term> interest from the point of view of modern medicine.

# INTRODUCTION

<margin>Hippocrates and Galen.</margin>
If the work of Hippocrates <note>An ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) often called the "Father of Medicine," known for his ethical standards and clinical observations.</note> be taken as representing the foundation upon which the edifice of historical Greek medicine was reared, then the work of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician, surgeon, and philosopher (129 – c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medical science for over 1,300 years.</note>, who lived some six hundred years later, may be looked upon as the summit or apex of the same edifice. Galen’s merit is to have crystallised or brought to a focus all the best work of the Greek medical schools which had preceded his own time. It is essentially in the form of Galenism <note>The comprehensive medical system and philosophy developed by Galen.</note> that Greek medicine was transmitted to after ages.

<margin>The Beginnings of Medicine in Greece.</margin>
The ancient Greeks referred the origins of medicine to a god Asklepios <note>The Greek god of healing and medicine, son of Apollo.</note> (called in Latin Aesculapius <note>original: "Aesculapius"</note>), thereby testifying to their appreciation of the truly divine function of the healing art. The emblem of Aesculapius, familiar in medical symbolism at the present day, was a staff with a serpent coiled round it, the animal typifying wisdom in general, and more particularly the wisdom of the medicine-man, with his semi-miraculous powers over life and death.

> “Be ye therefore wise as serpents and harmless as doves.” <note>A biblical reference from Matthew 10:16, used here to illustrate the symbolic connection between serpents and wisdom.</note>

<summary>This introductory page establishes the historical relationship between Hippocrates and Galen, framing Galen as the pinnacle of Greek medical thought. It also explores the divine origins of medicine through the figure of Asklepios and the symbolism of the serpent staff.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION

<margin>The Asclepieia <note>Ancient Greek healing temples dedicated to the god Asclepius.</note> or Health-temples.</margin>
The temples of Aesculapius <note>The Latin name for the Greek god of healing, Asklepios.</note> were scattered over the ancient Hellenic world. To them the sick and ailing resorted in crowds. The treatment, which was in the hands of an hereditary priesthood, combined the best of the methods carried on at our present-day health-resorts, our hydropathics <note>Facilities providing water-based treatments or "water cures."</note>, sanatoriums, and nursing-homes. Fresh air, water-cures, massage, gymnastics, psychotherapy, and natural methods in general were chiefly relied on.

<margin>Hippocrates and the Unity of the Organism.</margin>
Hippocrates, the “ Father of Medicine ” (5th to 4th centuries, B.C.) was associated with the Asclepieum of Cos, an island off the south-west coast of Asia Minor, near Rhodes. He apparently revitalized the work of the health-temples, which had before his time been showing a certain decline in vigour, coupled with a corresponding excessive tendency towards sophistry <note>Deceptive or overly complex reasoning.</note> and priestcraft.

Celsus <note>A Roman medical writer of the 1st century AD.</note> says : “ Hippocrates of Cos was indeed the first of all those worthy of remembrance to separate this discipline from the pursuit of wisdom. ” <note>original: "Hippocrates Cous primus quidem ex omnibus memoria dignis ab studio sapientiae disciplinam hanc separavit." This refers to Hippocrates separating the practice of medicine from the abstract speculations of philosophy.</note> He means that Hippocrates first gave the physician an independent standing, separating him from the cosmological speculator <note>Philosophers who studied the origins and nature of the universe.</note>. Hippocrates confined the medical man to medicine. He did with medical thought what Socrates <note>The famous Athenian philosopher (c. 470–399 BC) known for shifting philosophy toward human ethics and behavior.</note> did with thought in general—he “ brought it down from heaven to earth. ” His watchword was “ Back to Nature ! ”

At the same time, while assigning the physician his post, Hippocrates would not let him regard that post as sacrosanct. He set his face against any

tendency to mystery-mongering, to exclusiveness, to sacerdotalism <note>A priest-like approach to medicine that relies on secret rituals or divine authority rather than transparent observation.</note>. He was, in fact, opposed to the spirit of trade-unionism in medicine. His concern was rather with the physician’s duties than his “rights.”

At the dawn of recorded medical history Hippocrates stands for the fundamental and primary importance of seeing clearly—that is of clinical *observation*. And what he observed was that the human organism, when exposed to certain abnormal conditions—certain stresses—tends to behave in a certain way : that in other words, each “disease” tends to run a certain definite course. To him a disease was essentially a process, one and indivisible, and thus his practical problem was essentially one of *prognosis* <term>prognosis: forecasting the likely course and outcome of an illness.</term>—“what will be the natural course of this disease, if left to itself?” Here he found himself to no small extent in opposition with the teaching of the neighbouring medical school of Cnidus <note>An ancient medical school that focused on categorizing diseases into many specific types rather than looking at the patient as a whole.</note>, where a more static view-point laid special emphasis upon the minutiae of diagnosis <term>diagnosis: the precise identification of a specific ailment.</term>

Observation taught Hippocrates to place unbounded faith in the recuperative powers of the living organism—in what we sometimes call nowadays the *healing power of Nature* <note>original: "vis medicatrix Naturae"</note>. His observation was that even with a very considerable “abnormality” of environmental stress the organism, in the large majority of cases, manages eventually by its own inherent powers to adjust itself to the new conditions. “Merely give Nature a chance,” said the father of medicine in effect, “and most

It contrasts the Hippocratic focus on the natural course of a disease (prognosis) with the rival school of Cnidus, which focused on specific classification (diagnosis).</summary>

His keen sense of the solidarity (or rather, of the constant interplay) between the organism and its environment (the "conditions" to which it is exposed) is instanced in his book, *Airs, Waters, and Places* <note>A foundational text in epidemiology and public health that examined how environment and climate affect human health.</note>. As we recognise, in our popular everyday psychology, that "it takes two to make a quarrel," so Hippocrates recognised that in <term>pathology: the study of the causes and effects of diseases</term>, it takes two (organism and environment) to make a disease.

As an outstanding example of his power of clinical observation we may recall the **Hippocratic face** <note>original: "facies Hippocratica"</note>, an accurate study of the countenance of a dying man.

His ideals for the profession are embodied in the "Hippocratic oath" <note>An ethical code for physicians, still influential today, which emphasizes patient confidentiality, non-maleficence, and professional integrity.</note>.

<margin>Anatomy</margin>
Impressed by this view of the organism as a unity, the Hippocratic school tended in some degree to overlook the importance of its constituent *parts*. The balance was re-adjusted later on by the labours of the anatomical school of Alexandria, which, under the sponsorship <note>original: "aegis"</note> of the enlightened Ptolemies <note>The Greek-speaking royal dynasty that ruled Egypt after the death of Alexander the Great.</note>, arose in the 3rd century B.C. Two prominent exponents of anatomy belonging to this school were Herophilus and Erasistratus, the latter of whom we shall frequently meet with in the following pages (see page 95 and following <note>original: "v. p. 95 et seq."</note>).

->INTRODUCTION<-

<margin>The Empirics.</margin>
After the death of the Master <note>Referring to Hippocrates, the "Father of Medicine."</note>, the Hippocratic school tended, as so often happens with the best of cultural movements, to show signs itself of diminishing vitality: the letter began to obscure and hamper the spirit. The comparatively small element of theory which existed in the Hippocratic physiology was made the groundwork of a somewhat over-elaborated "system." Against this tendency on the part of the "Dogmatic" or "Rationalist" school <note>The Dogmatists believed that hidden causes and theoretical systems were essential to medical practice.</note> there arose, also at Alexandria, the sect of the Empiricists. "It is not," they said, "the cause but the cure of diseases that concerns us; not how we digest, but what is digestible."

<margin>Greek Medicine in Rome.</margin>
Horace said "Captured Greece took captive her savage conqueror" <note>original: "Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit." - A famous line by the Roman poet Horace, reflecting how Greek culture, art, and science overwhelmed Roman life after Rome militarily conquered the Greek world.</note>. Political domination, the occupation of territory by armies, does not necessarily mean real conquest. Horace's statement applied to medicine as to other branches of culture.

The introducer of Greek medicine into Rome was Asclepiades (1st century <term>B.C.: Before the Common Era</term>). A man of forceful personality, and equipped with a fully developed philosophic system of health and disease which commended itself to the Roman <term>savants: learned scholars or experts</term> of the day, he soon attained to the pinnacle of professional success in the Latin capital: he is indeed to all time the type of the fashionable (and somewhat "faddy") West-end physician. His system was a purely mechanistic one, being based upon

This epic poem explained Epicurean philosophy—the idea that the world is made of atoms and void—to a Roman audience.</note>. The disbelief of Asclepiades in the self-maintaining powers of the living organism <note>Unlike Hippocrates, who believed the body had an innate power to heal itself (the "healing power of nature"), Asclepiades viewed the body as a machine governed by the movement of atoms.</note> are exposed and refuted at considerable length by Galen in the volume before us.

<margin>The Methodists.</margin>
Out of the teaching of Asclepiades that physiological processes depend upon "the particular way in which those first unaffected bodies [atoms] come together" <note>original: ἐν τῇ ποίᾳ συνόδῳ τῶν πρώτων ἐκείνων σωμάτων τῶν ἀπαθῶν. This refers to the arrangement and movement of indivisible particles within the body.</note> there was developed by his pupil, Themison of Laodicea, a system of medicine characterised by the most engaging simplicity both of diagnosis and treatment. This so-called “Methodic” system was intended to strike a balance between the excessive leaning to theoretical reasoning <note>The text uses "apriorism," referring to knowledge gained through deduction rather than observation.</note> shown by the Rationalist (Hippocratic) school and the opposite tendency of the Empiricists. “A pathological theory we must have,” said the Methodists in effect, “but let it be simple.” They held that the molecular groups constituting the tissues were traversed by minute channels (<term>pores<gloss>original: πόροι (póroi), "passages" or "pores"</gloss></term>); all diseases belonged to one or other of two classes; if the channels were constricted the disease was one of <term>stasis<gloss>original: στέγνωσις (stégnosis), meaning "constriction" or "tightness"</gloss></term>, and if they were dilated the disease was one of <term>flux<gloss>original: ῥύσις (rhýsis), meaning "flowing" or "discharge"</gloss></term>. Flux and stasis were indicated respectively by increase and diminution of the natural secretions;

<summary>This page describes how Asclepiades applied atomic theory to medicine, leading to the "Methodic" school which simplified all diseases into two states: the constriction (stasis) or dilation (flux) of bodily pores.</summary>

### INTRODUCTION

treatment was of opposites by opposites—of stagnation <note>The text uses the term "stasis," referring to a blockage or lack of movement in the body's hypothetical "pores."</note> by methods causing a widening <note>The text uses "dilatation," the process of opening or expanding the channels of the body.</note> of the channels, and conversely.

Wild as it may seem, this theory of disease held by the Methodists contained an element of truth; in various forms it has reappeared time and again at different points in medical history. Even today, there are specialists in disease who tend to describe certain conditions in terms of <term>vaso-constriction</term> <note>The narrowing or tightening of blood vessels.</note> and <term>vaso-dilatation</term> <note>The widening or relaxing of blood vessels.</note>. The flaw of the Methodist teaching was that it viewed a disease too much as something fixed and finished—an independent thing to be considered entirely apart from the specific patient or circumstances. The Methodists illustrate for us the "tyranny of names." In its failings, as in its strengths, this school has parallels in the modern day; we are all familiar with the doctor to whom a name—such as "tuberculosis," "gout," or "poisoning from the gut"—stands for a single, unchanging thing to be treated with a rigid and unvarying formula.

To such an individual, the old German saying, "In the end, everyone has a little bit of tuberculosis," <note>original: "Jedermann hat am Ende ein Bischen Tuberkulose." This proverb suggests that most people carry traces of infection or physical wear that do not necessarily constitute a "disease" requiring a rigid cure.</note> is simply incomprehensible.

All the medical schools which I have mentioned were still holding their ground in the 2nd century <term>A.D.</term>, with more or less popular support, when the great Galen made his entry into the world of Greek and Roman medicine.

# INTRODUCTION

<margin>His Nature and Nurture.</margin>
Claudius Galenus <note>Commonly known in English as Galen.</note> was born at Pergamos <note>An ancient Greek city in modern-day Turkey, famed for its culture and monumental architecture.</note> in Asia Minor in the year 131 A.D. His father was one Nicon, a well-to-do architect of that city. "I had the great good fortune," says Galen,¹ "to have as a father a highly amiable, just, good, and benevolent man. My mother, on the other hand, possessed a very bad temper; she used sometimes to bite her serving-maids, and she was perpetually shouting at my father and quarrelling with him—worse than Xanthippe with Socrates <note>Xanthippe was the wife of the philosopher Socrates, traditionally remembered as a shrewish and difficult woman.</note>. When, therefore, I compared the excellence of my father's disposition with the disgraceful passions of my mother, I resolved to embrace and love the former qualities, and to avoid and hate the latter."

Nicon called his son *Galenos* <note>original: "Γαληνός"</note>, which means *quiet, peaceable*, and although the physician eventually turned out to be a man of elevated character, it is possible that his somewhat excessive leaning towards controversy (exemplified in the following pages) may have resulted from the fact that he was never quite able to throw off the worst side of the maternal inheritance.

His father, a man well schooled in mathematics and philosophy, saw to it that his son should not lack a liberal education. Pergamos itself was an ancient centre of civilisation, containing, among other culture-institutions, a library only second in importance to that of Alexandria itself; it also contained an Asclepieium <note>A healing temple and medical complex dedicated to Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine.</note>.

¹ *On the Affections of the Mind*, p. 41 (Kühn's edition <note>Referring to the monumental 19th-century collection of Galen’s Greek texts and Latin translations by Karl Gottlob Kühn.</note>).

# INTRODUCTION

Galen’s training was essentially eclectic <note>An eclectic approach involves selecting what seems best from various different schools of thought rather than following a single dogma.</note>: he studied all the chief philosophical systems of the time—Platonic, Aristotelian, Stoic, and Epicurean—and then, at the age of seventeen, entered on a course of medical studies; these he pursued under the best teachers at his own city, and afterwards, during a period of *years of travel* <note>original: "Wanderjahre"—a German term for the years a journeyman or scholar spends traveling to gain experience from different masters.</note>, at Smyrna, Alexandria <note>Smyrna and Alexandria were two of the most significant cultural and scientific hubs of the ancient Mediterranean; Alexandria was particularly famous for its medical school.</note>, and other leading medical centres.

Returning to Pergamos, he received his first professional appointment—that of surgeon to the gladiators. After four years here he was drawn by ambition to Rome, being at that time about thirty-one years of age. At Rome the young Pergamene <note>A person from the city of Pergamos.</note> attained a brilliant reputation both as a practitioner and as a public demonstrator of anatomy; among his patients he finally numbered even the Emperor Marcus Aurelius himself. <gloss>3/</gloss>

Medical practice in Rome at this time was at a low ebb <note>In a state of decline, characterized by poor standards or lack of ethics.</note>, and Galen took no pains to conceal his contempt for the ignorance, charlatanism, and venality <note>The quality of being open to bribery or corruption.</note> of his fellow-practitioners. Eventually, in spite of his social popularity, he raised up such odium <note>General hatred or disgust directed toward someone as a result of their actions.</note> against himself in medical circles, that he was forced to flee the city. This he did hurriedly and secretly in the year 168 A.D., when thirty-six years of age. He betook himself to his old home at Pergamos, where he settled down once more to a literary life.

His respite was short, however, for within a year he was summoned back to Italy by imperial mandate <note>An official command issued by the Emperor.</note>. Marcus Aurelius was about to undertake an

<margin>Subsequent History of Galen's Works.</margin>
Galen wrote extensively, not only on *anatomy, physiology, and medicine in general, but also on logic*; his logical proclivities <note>Natural inclinations or tendencies.</note>, as will be shown later, are well exemplified in his medical writings. A considerable number of undoubtedly genuine works of his have come down to us. The full importance of his contributions to medicine does not appear to have been recognized till some time after his death, but eventually, as already pointed out, the terms <term>Galenism</term> <note>The medical system and philosophy based on Galen's works, which dominated Western and Islamic medicine for over 1,500 years.</note> and Greek medicine became practically synonymous.

A few words may be devoted to the subsequent history of his writings.

The Byzantine Empire, from the 4th century onwards, was the scene of much internal turmoil, in which the militant activities of the now State-established Christian church played a not inconsiderable part. The Byzantine medical scholars were at best compilers <note>A compiler in this context is a scholar who collects and organizes existing knowledge from earlier authorities—like Galen—rather than conducting new experiments or making original discoveries.</note>, and a typical compiler was Oribasius, body-physician to the Emperor Julian (4th century, A.D.); his excellent *Synopsis* was written in order to make the huge mass of the Galenic writings available for the ordinary practitioner.

<margin>Arabian Medicine.</margin>
Greek medicine spread, with general Greek culture, throughout Syria, and from thence was carried by the Nestorians <note>A sect of Christians who, after being declared heretics by the Church in the 5th century, fled to Persia and became vital intermediaries in translating Greek scientific texts into Syriac and Arabic.</note>, a persecuted heretical sect, into Persia; here it became implanted, and hence eventually spread to the Mohammedan world. Several of the Prophet’s successors (such as the Caliphs <note>A title for the civil and religious leaders of the Islamic world.</note> Harun-al-Rashid and Abdul-Rahman III) were great patrons of Greek learning, and especially of medicine. The Arabian scholars imbibed Aristotle and Galen with avidity. A partial assimilation, however, was the farthest stage to which they could attain; with the exception of pharmacology <note>The branch of medicine concerned with the uses, effects, and modes of action of drugs.</note>, the Arabians made practically no independent additions to medicine. They were essentially systematizers and commentators. “Averrhoës who made the great Commentary” <note>original: "Averrois che il gran comento feo"</note>¹

<margin>The Renaissance</margin>
The year 1453, when Constantinople <note>Now Istanbul; the fall of this city led many Greek scholars to flee to Italy, carrying ancient manuscripts with them.</note> fell into the hands of the Turks, is often taken as marking the commencement of the Renaissance. Among the many factors which tended to stimulate and awaken men’s minds during these spacious times was the re-discovery of the Greek classics, which were brought to Europe by, among others, the scholars who fled from Byzantium. The Arabo-Scholastic <note>Versions of Greek texts that had been translated into Arabic and then later into Latin for use in medieval universities.</note> versions of Aristotle and Galen were now confronted by their Greek originals. A passion for Greek learning was aroused. The freshness and truth of these old writings helped to awaken men to a renewed sense of their own dignity and worth, and to brace them in their own struggle for self-expression.

Prominent in this “Humanist” movement was the English physician, Thomas Linacre (*c.* 1460–1524) who, having gained in Italy an extraordinary zeal for the New Learning, devoted the rest of his life, after returning to England, to the promotion of the *humanistic studies* <note>original: "litterae humaniores"; This refers to the study of the classics—literature, history, and philosophy—intended to cultivate a more "human" and well-rounded intellect.</note>, and especially to making Galen accessible to readers of Latin. Paracelsus.

But the swing of the pendulum did not cease with the creation of the liberal “Greek” party; the dazzling vision of freedom was to drive some to a yet more anarchical position. Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who famously challenged traditional medical authority.</note>, who flourished in the first half of the 16th century, may be taken as typifying this extremist tendency. <margin>William Harvey (1578–1667)</margin>
William Harvey, the great Englishman who founded modern experimental physiology <note>The branch of biology dealing with how the internal parts of living organisms function.</note> and was the first to establish not only the fact of the circulation but also the physical laws governing it, is commonly reckoned the Father of Modern Medicine. He owed his interest in the movements of the blood to Fabricio of Acquapendente, his tutor at Padua, who drew his attention to the valves in the veins, thus suggesting the idea of a circular as opposed to a to-and-fro motion. Harvey’s great generalisation, based upon a long series of experiments performed on living subjects <note>original: "in vivo"</note>, was considered to have given the finishing blow <note>original: "coup de grâce"</note> to the Galenic physiology <note>The ancient medical system based on the theories of Galen, which had dominated medicine for over 1,000 years.</note>, and hence threw temporary discredit upon the whole system of medicine associated therewith.

<margin>
Back to Galen!
</margin>
While we cannot sufficiently praise the results of the long modern period of research—for which the work of the Renaissance anatomists from Vesalius to Harvey forms a perfect opening—we do not at all agree that Galen's general medical outlook was as completely proven wrong as many people imagine just because his anatomical errors were exposed. <note>The clause "Galen's general medical outlook was so entirely invalidated as many imagine by the conclusive demonstration of his anatomical errors" is marked with underlining and an overline in blue ink.</note> It is time for us now to turn to Galen again after three hundred years of virtual neglect. It may be that he will help us to see something fundamentally important for medical practice which is beyond the power even of our microscopes and X-rays to reveal. While the value of his work undoubtedly lies mainly in how it allows us to see one of the greatest early steps humans took in medical knowledge, it also has a very definite value of its own.

<margin>
Galen's Debt to his Precursors.
</margin>
We will not attempt here to determine how much of Galen's work is truly original and how much is taken from the efforts of those who came before him. In any case, there is no doubt that he was much more than a mere compiler and organizer of other men's work. He was great enough to not only collect, digest, and absorb all the best work done before his time, but also to add the results of his own observations, experiments, and reflections to it.

# INTRODUCTION

<margin>
Galen's "Physiology."
</margin>

<note>Blue ink underlining and a marginal bracket highlight the following section of text from "as a living thing" to "unity."</note>

What, now, is this “Nature” or biological principle upon which Galen, like Hippocrates, bases the whole of his medical teaching, and which, we may add, is constantly overlooked—if indeed ever properly apprehended—by many physiologists of the present day? By using this term Galen meant simply that, when we deal with a living thing, we are dealing primarily with a unity, which, as a living thing <note>original Latin: *quâ*; meaning 'in the capacity of' or 'as'</note>, is not further divisible; all its parts can only be understood and dealt with as being in relation to this principle of unity. Galen was thus led to criticise with considerable severity many of the medical and surgical specialists of his time, who acted on the assumption (implicit if not explicit) that the whole was merely the sum of its parts, and that if, in an ailing organism, these parts were treated each in and for itself, the health of the whole organism could in this way be eventually restored.

Galen expressed this idea of the unity of the organism by saying that it was governed by a *Physis* or Nature (the nature that governs the living creature <note>original Greek: ἡ φύσις ἤπερ διοικεῖ τὸ ζῷον</note>), with whose “faculties” or powers it was the province of <term>physiology: nature-lore <gloss>original Greek: φυσιολογία</gloss></term> to deal. It was because Hippocrates had a clear sense of this principle that Galen called him master. “Greatest,” say the Moslems, “is God <note>original: Allah</note>, and Mohammed is his prophet.” “Greatest,” said Galen, “is the Nature, and Hippocrates is its prophet.” Never did Mohammed more zealously maintain the unity of the Godhead than Hippocrates and Galen the unity of the organism.

<summary>This page defines Galen’s concept of "Nature" (Physis) as a principle of organic unity, arguing that a living being must be treated as a whole rather than a collection of parts. It establishes Galen's view of Hippocrates as the primary prophet of this holistic biological principle.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION

<margin>Galen's Physics.</margin>
But we shall not have read far before we discover that the term *Physiology*, as used by Galen, stands not merely for what we understand by it nowadays, but also for a large part of Physics as well. This is one of the chief sources of confusion in his writings. Having grasped, for example, the uniqueness of the process of <term>specific selection: the attraction of the kindred <gloss>original Greek: ὁλκὴ τοῦ οἰκείου</gloss></term>, by which the tissues nourish themselves, he proceeds to apply this principle in explanation of entirely different classes of phenomena; thus he mixes it up with the physical phenomenon of the attraction of the lode-stone <note>A naturally magnetized mineral; an early term for a magnet.</note> for iron, of dry grain for moisture, etc. It is noteworthy, however, in these latter instances, that he does not venture to follow out his comparison to its logical conclusion; he certainly stops short of hinting that the lodestone (like a living organ or tissue) *assimilates* <note>In this context, to digest or incorporate into itself.</note> the metal which it has attracted!

Setting aside, however, these occasional half-hearted attempts to apply his principle of a <term>Nature: Physis <gloss>original Greek: φύσις</gloss></term> in regions where it has no natural standing, we shall find that in the field of biology Galen moves with an assurance bred of first-hand experience.

<margin>
The Anatomists.
</margin>
In defense of the universal validity of his principle, Galen also tends to excessive disparagement of morphological factors <note>The physical shape and structure of organs.</note>; witness his objection to the view of the anatomist Erasistratus <note>An innovative Greek physician known for his mechanical descriptions of the body's functions.</note> that the calibre of vessels played a part in determining the secretion of fluids (p. 123), that digestion was caused by the mechanical action of the stomach walls (p. 243), and dropsy <note>An older medical term for edema, or the swelling caused by excess fluid in the body.</note> by induration <note>The hardening of an organ, such as the liver.</note> of the liver (p. 171).

<margin>
Characteristics of the Living Organism.
</margin>
While combating the atomic explanation of physical processes, Galen of course realized that there were many of these which could only be explained according to what we should now call “mechanical laws.” For example, non-living things could be subjected to <term>passive motion <gloss>original Greek: φορά</gloss></term>, they answered to the laws of gravity (<term>steered by the weight of their materials <gloss>original Greek: ταῖς τῶν ὑλῶν οἰακιζόμενα ῥοπαῖς</gloss></term>, p. 126). Furthermore, Galen did not fail to see that living things also were not entirely exempted from the operation of these laws; they too may be at least partly subject to gravity (*in the place cited*); a hollow organ exerts, by virtue of its cavity, an attraction similar to that of dilating bellows <note>A device that draws in air when its sides are pulled apart.</note>, as well as, by virtue of the living tissue of its walls, a specifically “vital” or selective kind of attraction (p. 325).

This active type of motion cannot be adequately stated in terms of the passive movements (groupings and re-groupings) of its constituent parts according to certain empirical “laws.” Alteration involves *self-movement*, a self-determination of the organism or organic part. Galen does not attempt to explain this fundamental characteristic of alteration any further; he contents himself with referring his opponents to Aristotle’s work on the “Complete Alteration of Substance” <note>Likely referring to Aristotle's "On Generation and Corruption," which discusses how substances change their fundamental nature.</note> (p. 9).

The most important characteristic of the <term>Nature <gloss>original Greek: Physis</gloss></term> is its <term>artistic skill <gloss>original Greek: technē</gloss></term>—its artistic creativeness. In other words, the living organism is a creative artist. This feature may be observed typically in its primary functions of growth and nutrition; these are dependent on the characteristic faculties or powers, by virtue of which each part draws to itself what is <note>original Greek: to oikeion</note> *proper or appropriate* to it and rejects what is <note>original Greek: to allotrion</note> *foreign*, thereafter appropriating or assimilating the attracted material; this assimilation is an example of the *alteration* (or qualitative change) already alluded to; thus the food eaten is “altered” into the various tissues of the body, each of these having been provided by “Nature” with its own specific faculties of attraction and repulsion.

->xxxi<-

# INTRODUCTION

<margin>
Galen's
Method.
</margin>
Like his master Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – 370 BCE) known as the "Father of Medicine," who emphasized clinical observation over superstition.</note>, Galen attached fundamental importance to clinical observation—to the evidence of the senses as the indispensable groundwork of all medical knowledge. He had also, however, a forte for rapid generalization from observations, and his logical proclivities disposed him [to structured systems, though his reliance on them was] limited. Galen and Bergson <note>Henri Bergson (1859–1941), a French philosopher who proposed that a "vital impulse" (élan vital) drives the evolution of living things.</note> agree in attaching most practical importance to the middle category—that of **Function**.

While it must be conceded that Galen, following Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher who believed that biological species were eternal and unchanging.</note>, had never seriously questioned the **fixity of species** <note>The historical belief that species do not change or evolve over time.</note>, the following quotation from his work *On Habits* <note>original Greek: Περὶ ἐθῶν (Peri ethōn)</note> (chapter 2) will show that he must have at least had occasional glimmerings of our modern point of view on the matter. Referring to **assimilation** <note>The process by which an organism absorbs nutrients and turns them into part of its own body; original Greek: ἐξομοίωσις (exomoiōsis).</note>, he says:

> “Just as everything we eat or drink becomes altered in quality, so of course also does the altering factor itself become altered. . . . A clear proof of the **assimilation** of things which are being nourished to that which is nourishing them is the change which occurs in plants and seeds; this often goes so far that what is highly noxious in one soil becomes, when transplanted into another soil, not merely harmless, but actually useful. This has been largely put to the test by those who compose memoirs on farming and on plants, as also by zoological authors who have written on the changes which occur according to the countries in which animals live. Since, therefore, not only is the nourishment altered by the creature nourished, but the latter itself also undergoes some slight alteration, *this slight alteration must necessarily become considerable in the course of time, and thus properties resulting from prolonged habit must come to be on a par with natural properties.*”

Galen fails to see the possibility that the “natural” properties themselves originated in this way, as activities which gradually became habitual—that is to say, that the effects of nurture may become a “second nature,” and so eventually nature itself.

The whole passage, however, may be commended to modern biologists—particularly, might one say, to those bacteriologists who have not yet realized how extraordinarily relative is the term **specificity** <note>In biology, the tendency of a process, such as an immune response, to act only on a specific target; the author suggests this "uniqueness" is more flexible than some scientists believe.</note> when applied to the subject-matter of their science.

<summary>This page discusses Galen's medical methodology, highlighting his balance between clinical observation and logical theory. It features an excerpt from his work "On Habits," where Galen touches on early evolutionary concepts by observing how environment and habit can alter the "natural" properties of plants and animals.</summary>

INTRODUCTION

particularly to deductive reasoning <note>A logical process where a conclusion is reached by starting with a general principle and applying it to a specific case.</note>. Examples of an almost Euclidean method <note>Referring to the style of the mathematician Euclid, who built complex proofs upon simple, self-evident axioms.</note> of argument may be found in the *On the Natural Faculties* (*e.g.* Book III. chap. i.). While this method undoubtedly gave him much help in his search for truth, it also not unfrequently led him astray. This is evidenced by his attempt, already noted, to apply the biological principle of **Nature** <note>original Greek: φύσις (physis); for Galen, this refers to the innate, creative power or "artistic" force that governs living organisms.</note> in physics. Characteristic examples of attempts to force facts to fit premises will be found in Book II. chap. ix., where our author demonstrates that yellow bile is “virtually” dry, and also, by a process of exclusion, assigns to the spleen the function of clearing away black bile. Strangest of all is his attempt to prove that the same principle of **specific attraction** by which the ultimate tissues nourish themselves (and the lodestone <note>A naturally magnetized mineral; Galen uses it as a physical analogy for how organs "pull" specific fluids to themselves.</note> attracts iron!) accounts for the reception of food into the stomach, of urine into the kidneys, of bile into the gall-bladder, and of semen into the uterus.

These instances are given, however, without prejudice to the system of generalisation and deduction which, in Galen’s hands, often proved exceedingly fruitful. He is said to have tried “to unite professional and scientific medicine with a philosophic link.” He objected, however, to such extreme attempts at simplification of medical science as that of the **Methodists** <note>A rival medical sect in Rome that rejected Galen's complex theories in favor of a very simple model of "constricted" or "relaxed" body channels.</note>, to whom diseases were isolated entities, without any relationships in time or space (*see page xv. above* <note>original Latin: *v. p. xv. supra*.</note>).

INTRODUCTION

...the “humoral theory” <note>A medical system originating with Hippocrates suggesting that human health is governed by the balance of four distinct bodily fluids, or “humors.”</note> of Hippocrates, according to which certain diseases were caused by one or more of the four humours (blood, phlegm, black and yellow bile) being in excess—that is, by various ***dyscrasiae*** <note>original: δυσκρασία (dyskrasia); literally a "bad mixture," referring to an imbalance of the humors.</note>. Our modern conception of “hormone” action shows certain resemblances with this theory.

Besides observation and reasoning, Galen took his stand on experiment; he was one of the first of experimental physiologists, as is illustrated in the present book by his researches into the function of the kidneys (p. 59 *and following*). He also conducted a long series of experiments into the physiology of the spinal cord, to determine what parts controlled movement and what sensibility.

As a practitioner he modelled his work largely on the broad and simple lines laid down by Hippocrates. He had also at his disposal all the acquisitions of biological science dating from the time of Aristotle five hundred years earlier, and reinforced by the discoveries in anatomy made by the Alexandrian school <note>A renowned center of learning in Egypt where, centuries before Galen, physicians like Herophilus and Erasistratus conducted the first systematic human dissections.</note>. To these he added a large series of researches of his own.

Galen never confined himself to what one might call the academic or strictly orthodox sources of information; he roamed the world over for answers to his queries. For example, we find him on his journeys between Pergamos <note>Galen’s home city in modern-day Turkey, famous for its great library and temple of Asclepius.</note> and Rome twice visiting the island of Lemnos in order to procure some of the ***terra sigillata*** <note>original Latin: "sealed earth"; a medicinal clay pressed into tablets and stamped with an official seal, highly valued in antiquity as an antidote for poisons and stings.</note>, a kind of earth which had a reputation for healing the bites of serpents and...

By inclination and training Galen was the reverse of a "party-man" <note>A physician who blindly followed the rigid dogmas of a specific medical school or "sect" rather than observing nature directly.</note>. In the *Natural Faculties* (p. 55) he speaks of the bane of sectarian partizanship, "harder to heal than any itch." He pours scorn upon the ignorant "Erasistrateans" <note>Followers of Erasistratus (3rd century BC), who viewed the body as a machine and often ignored the "vital forces" Galen championed.</note> and "Asclepiadeans" <note>Followers of Asclepiades (1st century BC), who believed the body was composed of disconnected atoms and pores, rejecting the idea of nature’s purposeful design.</note>, who attempted to hide their own incompetence under the shield of some great man's name (*cf.* p. 141).

Of the two chief objects of his censure in the *Natural Faculties*, Galen deals perhaps less rigorously with Erasistratus than with Asclepiades. Erasistratus did at least recognize the existence of a vital principle in the organism, albeit, with his eye on the structures which the scalpel displayed he tended frequently to forget it. The researches of the anatomical school of Alexandria <note>The premier center of Greek science in Egypt, famous for being the first place where systematic human dissection was permitted.</note> had been naturally of the greatest service to surgery, but in medicine they sometimes had a tendency to check progress by diverting attention from the whole to the part.

(2) A vital principle, conceived as being made up of matter in the most subtle imaginable state (i.e. air). This vital principle became resolved into three kinds: (a) **natural spirit** <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα φυσικόν (*pneuma physikon*); Latin: *spiritus naturalis*</note>, carried by the veins, and presiding over the subconscious vegetative life; this "natural spirit" is therefore practically equivalent to the **nature** <note>original Greek: φύσις (*physis*)</note> itself. (b) The **vital spirit** <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα ζωτικόν (*pneuma zōtikon*); Latin: *spiritus vitalis*</note>; here particularly is a source of error, since the air already alluded to as being carried by the arteries tends to be confused with this principle of "individuality" or relative autonomy in the circulatory (including, perhaps, the vasomotor) system. This view of a "vital principle" as necessarily consisting of matter in a finely divided, fluid, or "etheric" state is not unknown even in our day. Belief in the fundamental importance of the **Spirit** <note>original: "Pneuma"</note> formed the basis of the teaching of another vitalist school in ancient Greece, that of the Pneumatists <note>A medical sect that emerged in the 1st century BC, teaching that health and disease were determined by the state of the "pneuma" or breath of life.</note>.

In his opinion, the great bulk of the blood travelled with a to-and-fro motion in the veins, while a little of it, mixed with inspired air, moved in the same way along the arteries; whereas we now know that all the blood goes outward by the arteries and returns by the veins; in either case blood is carried to the tissues by blood-vessels, and Galen's ideas of tissue-nutrition were wonderfully sound. The ingenious method by which (in ignorance of the pulmonary circulation <note>The movement of blood from the heart to the lungs and back.</note>) he makes blood pass from the right to the left ventricle, may be read in the present work (p. 321) <note>Galen famously proposed that blood passed through invisible "pores" in the septum, the wall dividing the heart's chambers, a theory that persisted until the Renaissance.</note>. As will be seen, he was conversant with the <term>anastomoses</term> <note>anastomoses: natural connections or openings between two blood vessels.</note> between the ultimate branches of arteries and veins, although he imagined that they were not used under "normal" conditions.

<margin>Galen's Character.</margin>
Galen was not only a man of great intellectual gifts, but one also of strong moral fibre. In his short treatise "**That the Best Physician is also a Philosopher**" <note>original Greek: *Ὅτι ὁ ἄριστος ἰατρὸς καὶ φιλόσοφος*</note> he outlines his professional ideals. It is necessary for the efficient healer to be versed in the three branches of "philosophy," viz.: (a) **logic**, the science of how to think; (b) **physics**, the science of what is—i.e. of "Nature" in the widest sense; (c) **ethics**, the science of what to do. The amount of toil which he who wishes to be a physician must undergo—firstly, in mastering the work of his predecessors and afterwards in studying disease at first hand—makes it absolutely necessary that he should

Readers of the following pages will notice that Galen uses what we should call distinctly immoderate language towards those who ventured to differ from the views of his master Hippocrates (which were also his own). The employment of such language was one of the few weaknesses of his age which he did not transcend. Possibly also his mother’s choleric <note>choleric: easily angered. In Galen's medical theory, this was caused by an excess of yellow bile.</note> temper may have predisposed him to it.

The fact, too, that his vivisection <note>vivisection: the practice of performing operations on live animals for the purpose of experimentation or scientific research.</note> experiments (for example, pages 59 and 273) were carried out apparently without any kind of anesthesia being even thought of is abhorrent to the feelings of today, but must be excused also on the ground that callousness towards animals was then customary, men having probably never thought much about the subject.

<margin>Galen's Greek Style</margin>
Galen is a master of language, using a highly polished variety of Attic prose <note>Attic prose: the refined literary style of ancient Athens, which was the scholarly standard in Galen's time.</note> with a precision which can be only very imperfectly reproduced in another tongue. Every word he uses has an exact and definite meaning attached to it. Translation is particularly difficult when a word stands for a physiological conception which is not now held; instances are the words <term>distribution</term> <note>original: *anadosis* (ἀνάδοσις). In Galen’s system, this refers to the delivery of nutrients from the digestive tract to the various parts of the body.</note>, <term>addition</term> <note>original: *prosthesis* (πρόσθεσις). This refers to the stage where the distributed nutrients are applied to the tissues they will soon nourish.</note>, and <term>attachment</term> <note>original: *prosphysis* (πρόσφυσις). This is the final stage of nutrition, where the nutrient becomes fully assimilated into and "grown together" with the tissue.</note>, indicating certain steps in the process by which nutriment is conveyed from the alimentary canal to the tissues.

### INTRODUCTION

Readers will be surprised to find how many words are used by Galen which they would have thought had been expressly coined to fit modern conceptions; thus our author employs not merely such terms as **physiology** <note>physiology: the study of how living organisms and their parts function.</note>, **phthisis** <note>phthisis: a historical term for a wasting disease, typically pulmonary tuberculosis.</note>, **atrophy** <note>atrophy: the wasting away of body tissue or organs due to degeneration of cells.</note>, **anastomosis** <note>anastomosis: a connection made between adjacent blood vessels or other tubular structures.</note>, but also **haematopoietic** <note>haematopoietic: relating to the formation and development of blood cells.</note>, **anaesthesia**, and even **aseptic** ! It is only fair, however, to remark that these terms, particularly the last, were not used by Galen in quite their modern significance. <note>In Galen's time, "aseptic" referred to a state where wounds did not putrefy or rot, rather than the modern germ-free surgical environment.</note>

<margin>Summary.</margin>
To resume, then: What contribution can Galen bring to the art of healing at the present day? It was not, surely, for nothing that the great **Pergamene** <note>Pergamene: a native of Pergamon, the ancient Greek city where Galen was born and practiced medicine at the sanctuary of Asclepius.</note> gave laws to the medical world for over a thousand years!

Let us draw attention once more to:

(1) The high ideal which he set before the profession.

(2) His insistence on immediate contact with nature as the primary condition for arriving at an understanding of disease; on the need for due consideration of previous authorities; on the need also for reflection—for employment of the mind's eye (logical contemplation <note>original: "ἡ λογικὴ θεωρία" (hē logikē theōria) — refers to rational or systematic observation as opposed to mere sensory experience.</note>) as an aid to the physical eye.

(3) His essentially broad outlook, which often helped him in the comprehension of a phenomenon through his knowledge of an analogous phenomenon in another field of nature.

### INTRODUCTION

(4) His keen appreciation of the unity of the organism, and of the interdependence of its parts; his realization that the vital phenomena (**physiological** and **pathological**) <note>Physiology refers to normal bodily functions, while pathology refers to the study of disease.</note> in a living organism can only be understood when considered in relation to the environment of that organism or part. This is the foundation for the war that Galen waged **to the bitter end** <note>original French: "à outrance"</note> on the **Methodists** <note>The Methodists were a school of ancient physicians who believed that medical knowledge could be reduced to a few simple rules or "methods," often ignoring the specific needs or environment of the individual patient.</note>, to whom diseases were things without relation to anything. This dispute is, unfortunately, not touched upon in the present volume. What Galen combated was the tendency, familiar enough in our own day, to reduce medicine to the science of finding a label for each patient, and then treating not the patient, but the label. (This tendency, we may remark in parenthesis, is one which is obviously well suited for the standardizing purposes of a State medical service, and is therefore one which all who have the welfare of the profession at heart must most jealously watch in the difficult days that lie ahead.)

(5) His realization of the inappropriateness and inadequacy of physical formulae in explaining physiological activities. # SYNOPSIS OF CHAPTERS

## BOOK I

### CHAPTER I
Distinction between the effects of (a) the organism’s soul <note>original Greek: *psyche*. In ancient medicine, the "soul" was often viewed as the source of movement and sensation.</note> or (b) its nature <note>original Greek: *physis*. This refers to the innate biological force that governs the unconscious functions of the body.</note>. The author proposes to confine himself to a consideration of the latter—the vegetative <note>The "vegetative aspect" refers to biological processes shared with plants, such as growth, nutrition, and reproduction, which happen without conscious thought.</note>—aspect of life.

### CHAPTER II
Definition of terms. Different kinds of motion. *Alteration* or qualitative change. Refutation of the Sophists' <note>The Sophists were ancient Greek intellectuals and teachers; Galen often critiqued them for prioritizing clever rhetoric over scientific truth.</note> objection that such change is only apparent, not real. The four fundamental qualities <note>Galen follows the tradition that all matter is composed of combinations of the Hot, the Cold, the Dry, and the Moist.</note> of Hippocrates (later adopted by Aristotle). Distinction between *faculty* <note>The "faculty" is the power or potential an organ has to do something.</note>, *activity* (function), and *effect* (the work or product produced).

### CHAPTER III
It is by virtue of the *four qualities* that each part of the body functions. Some authorities believe the dry and the moist principles are secondary to the hot and the cold. Galen notes that Aristotle is inconsistent on this point.

### CHAPTER IV
We must suppose that there are biological faculties corresponding in number to the visible *effects* (or products) with which we are familiar. <note>In other words, if the body produces a specific substance or result, there must be a specific "power" or faculty within the body dedicated to making it happen.</note>

### CHAPTER V
*Genesis, growth, and nutrition.* *Genesis* <note>Embryogeny; the process of an organism coming into being.</note> is sub-divided into tissue-formation <note>original: histogenesis</note> and organ-formation <note>original: organogenesis</note>. *Growth* is a three-dimensional expansion of the solid parts formed during genesis. *Nutrition.*

# SYNOPSIS OF CHAPTERS

### CHAPTER VI

The process of <term>genesis (embryogeny, or the formation of the fetus)</term> from the moment of insemination onward. Each of the simple, elementary, and homogeneous parts—what we would today call tissues—is produced by a specific mixture of the four primary "altering" powers. These secondary powers include the <term>ostopoietic (bone-forming)</term> and <term>neuropoietic (nerve-forming)</term> faculties. Every tissue is assigned a specific function and purpose. The organization of these tissues into complex organs and their proper placement is managed by another power called the <term>diaplastic (moulding or formative faculty)</term>.

### CHAPTER VII

The text shifts from the creation of the body to its **growth**. Growth is defined as a process occurring primarily after birth; it consists of two factors: expansion and nutrition. Galen explains this using an analogy of a common game played by children.

### CHAPTER VIII

A detailed look at **nutrition**.

### CHAPTER IX

An explanation of how the three primary biological powers—genesis, growth, and nutrition—rely on several other subservient or "helper" powers to function correctly.

### CHAPTER X

Nutrition is revealed as a complex, multi-stage process:
1. The necessity of specialized organs for the various stages of "alteration" <note>Galen views digestion as a series of changes where food is "altered" until it matches the substance of the body.</note>, such as the transformation of bread into blood, and blood into bone.
2. The necessity of organs designed to excrete portions of food that cannot be used, such as the indigestible parts of plants.
3. The necessity of a third type of organ intended to distribute the <term>pabulum (nutritive fuel)</term> throughout the entire body.

### CHAPTER XI

An analysis of nutrition into three distinct stages: <term>prosthesis (application)</term>, <term>prosphysis (adhesion)</term>, and finally, assimilation. These stages are further explained by looking at certain "pathological" <note>Refers to states of disease or physical abnormality.</note> conditions. The chapter concludes by clarifying the various nuances of the term *nutriment*.

# SYNOPSIS OF CHAPTERS

### CHAPTER XII

A comparison of the two primary schools of medical philosophy: the **Atomists** (who believe life is a result of random particle collisions) and the **Vitalists** (who believe life is directed by a purposeful force). Galen identifies Hippocrates as a follower of the Vitalist school. Hippocrates argues that every living being is governed by an internal "nature" or original principle, which ensures the organism functions as a unified whole.

### CHAPTER XIII

A critique of the physician Asclepiades <note>Asclepiades of Bithynia was a popular physician in Rome who rejected the Hippocratic idea of "Nature" in favor of a mechanical, atomic view of the body.</note> and his failure to understand the kidneys and ureters. His theory that fluids are transformed into vapor within the body is refuted here. Galen describes a physical demonstration showing how urine is secreted in a living animal, which proves that Nature operates with foresight and "artistic" skill. The chapter also defends the idea that purgative drugs have a special, selective ability to draw out specific humors.

### CHAPTER XIV

While Asclepiades completely denies the existence of "attraction" (the power of one thing to pull another toward it), the philosopher Epicurus <note>Epicurus was the founder of the Epicurean school of philosophy; he believed the universe was composed of atoms and void.</note> acknowledges that it happens. However, Galen argues that Epicurus's attempt to explain attraction using atoms is a failure. Galen refutes Epicurus’s theory on why magnets attract iron and provides other examples of "specific attraction," such as how certain medicines draw out thorns or poisons, and how grain absorbs moisture.

### CHAPTER XV

Having established that urine is indeed secreted by the kidneys, Galen investigates the "logic" behind this process. He argues that the kidneys are not merely mechanical filters or sieves; instead, they possess a natural, specific <term>faculty of attraction</term>—a biological power that allows them to "pull" the urine from the blood.

### CHAPTER XVI

A critique of Erasistratus <note>A famous Greek anatomist and royal physician known for his mechanical descriptions of the body.</note>, who relied on the principle of <term>*horror vacui* (the belief that nature fills any empty space immediately)</term>. Galen argues that this mechanical principle can never explain how the kidneys secrete urine. While Erasistratus admitted that the kidneys perform this task, he never explained *how*. He chose to ignore the Hippocratic theory of "specific attraction" rather than attempting to disprove it. Galen labels the refusal of Asclepiades and Erasistratus to acknowledge these natural powers as a "servile" or narrow-minded approach to science.

<summary>This page summarizes Galen's arguments against mechanical views of the body, specifically defending the idea that the kidneys use a natural "attractive power" to produce urine. He contrasts the Hippocratic "Vitalist" view with the "Atomist" theories of Asclepiades, Epicurus, and Erasistratus.</summary>

<keywords>vitalism, atomism, Hippocrates, Asclepiades, Epicurus, Erasistratus, kidneys, urinary secretion, attraction, horror vacui, natural faculties</keywords>

## CHAPTER XVII

<margin>|</margin>Three other attempts—made by followers of the school of Erasistratus <note>Erasistratus was a 3rd-century BCE Greek anatomist who often sought mechanical explanations for bodily functions, which Galen frequently disputes.</note> and by Lycus of Macedonia—to explain how the kidneys manage to separate urine from the blood. All these theories fail because they ignore the obvious principle of **attraction** <note>Galen defines "attraction" as the innate power of an organ to pull specific fluids toward itself.</note>.

# BOOK II

## CHAPTER I

<margin>|</margin>In order to explain the <term>dispersal of food</term> <note>original: "anadosis"</note> from the digestive tract into the veins, there is no need to rely on the <term>abhorrence of a vacuum</term> <note>original: "horror vacui"</note> as Erasistratus did. Instead, the principle of specific attraction is at work here; furthermore, blood is pushed forward by the compression of the stomach and the contraction of the veins. It is possible, however, that Erasistratus’s theory of vacuum-filling plays a minor, secondary role.

## CHAPTER II

<margin>|</margin>The idea proposed by Erasistratus that bile is separated from the blood in the liver simply because it is a thinner fluid. He argues that bile alone can enter the narrow <term>stomata</term> <note>Small, mouth-like openings in the vessels.</note> of the bile-ducts, while the thicker blood can only enter the wider openings of the liver’s small veins.

## CHAPTER III

<margin>[</margin>The structural factors suggested by Erasistratus are completely inadequate to explain biological processes. Erasistratus is shown to be inconsistent with his own previous statements. This chapter discusses the immanence of <term>Nature</term> <note>original: "physis"</note>; her ability to shape the body is not merely superficial like that of a sculptor, but involves the transformation of the entire substance. In <term>embryogeny</term> <note>The formation and development of an embryo.</note>, the semen is the active principle, while the menstrual blood is the passive principle. The semen possesses **attractive**, **alterative**, and **formative** powers. The formation of the embryo is naturally followed by growth; these two distinct functions are explained here.

### CHAPTER IV

<margin>|</margin>The unjustified claim made by the followers of **Erasistratus** <note>A 3rd-century BCE Greek physician known for his mechanical descriptions of the body, often viewed as a rival to Galen’s theories.</note> that their founder had ties to the **Peripatetic** school <note>The philosophical school of Aristotle and his followers, known for their focus on biology and natural observation.</note>. In reality, the fundamental physiological principles of that school—which were all first established by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous 5th-century BCE "Father of Medicine."</note>—do not align with the theories of Erasistratus. The only point they share is the belief that Nature acts with purpose; however, in his practical applications, Erasistratus assumed there were many exceptions to this rule. It remains difficult to understand why he rejected the biological principle of **attraction** <note>The innate power of an organ to pull specific fluids or nutrients toward itself.</note> in favor of purely anatomical explanations.

### CHAPTER V

<margin>|</margin>A further difficulty raised by the statements of Erasistratus concerning how **bile** is separated and secreted within the liver.

### CHAPTER VI

<margin>|</margin>The same issues arise regarding **nutrition**. Even if we allow that veins might receive nutrient-rich blood through the principle of the <term>abhorrence of a vacuum</term> <note>original: "horror vacui"; the physical theory that nature immediately fills empty space with matter to prevent a void.</note>, how could this possibly explain the nutrition of the nerves? Erasistratus’s hypothesis—that visible nerves are composed of tiny, elementary nerves and vessels—merely moves the problem to a smaller scale without solving it. Furthermore, is Erasistratus’s "simple" nerve capable of being divided even further, as the **Atomists** <note>Philosophers who believed that the world is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms.</note> would suggest? If so, this contradicts the concept of a "constructive and artistic Nature" <note>The idea that Nature acts like a skilled craftsman, an idea Galen shares with Hippocrates.</note>. If his "simple" nerve is truly elementary and indivisible, it cannot contain a hollow space, meaning the vacuum principle cannot apply to it. Finally, how could this theory explain how a body part thinned by disease regains its original size, a process requiring more matter to be added than is lost? A quotation from Erasistratus shows that he did eventually acknowledge a form of "**attraction**," though not in the specific sense used by Hippocrates.

<summary>This page summarizes Galen's critique of Erasistratus, specifically arguing that mechanical theories like the "horror vacui" cannot explain complex biological processes like the nutrition of nerves or the purposeful growth of the body.</summary>

### CHAPTER VII

In the final analysis, the most basic living structures—what **Erasistratus** <note>A famous 3rd-century BCE physician and anatomist who often sought mechanical explanations for biological processes.</note> called "simple vessels"—must pull in their nourishment using an inherent power of **attraction**. This is similar to how a **lodestone** <note>A naturally magnetized mineral; an early term for a magnet.</note> pulls on iron. By accepting this power, the entire process of <term>nutrient distribution</term> <note>original: "anadosis"; the movement of nutrients from the digestive tract into the veins and throughout the body.</note> can be explained from start to finish without needing to rely on the theory of the <term>abhorrence of a vacuum</term> <note>original: "horror vacui"; the mechanical idea that nature pulls fluid into a space simply to prevent it from being empty.</note>.

### CHAPTER VIII

This chapter examines the disregard Erasistratus had for the **humors** <note>The four vital fluids of ancient medicine: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>. Regarding the excessive production of **bile**, Galen argues that preventing its buildup is better than treating it later; therefore, we must understand its underlying causes. The central question is: does blood already exist within our food, or is it created inside the body? 

Galen critiques Erasistratus’s purely mechanical and anatomical explanation of <term>dropsy</term> <note>A condition involving the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the body; modern medicine calls this edema.</note>. Erasistratus completely ignores the role of the **four qualities** (such as the importance of **innate heat** <note>The vital, life-sustaining warmth that ancient physicians believed was central to digestion and life itself.</note>) in how the humors are generated. Yet, the mystery of how the body produces blood is just as vital as understanding how the stomach digests food.

Galen provides proof that bile does not exist in food before we eat it. He relies on the **four fundamental qualities** established by **Hippocrates** and **Aristotle**—heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. He explains how the humors are formed from food once it enters the veins:
*   When **heat** is perfectly balanced, blood is produced.
*   When there is too much heat, **bile** is produced.
*   When heat is lacking, **phlegm** is produced.

Various conditions determine whether a person has a "cold" or "warm" **temperament** <note>The specific "mixture" of qualities that defines an individual's unique physical makeup.</note>. The four primary categories of disease each result from an excess of one of these four qualities. Erasistratus unintentionally admits this when he blames indigestion during a fever on the <term>impaired function</term> <note>original: "functio laesa"; a medical term for an organ or part of the body that can no longer perform its job.</note> of the stomach. Galen asks: what causes this impairment? The proof shows it is the fever itself—an excess of innate heat.

If heat is so influential in causing sickness, it must be equally important in maintaining health. This is because the causes of <term>perfect health</term> <note>original: "eucrasia"; the ideal balance of the bodily humors and qualities.</note> are directly related to the causes of <term>imbalance</term> <note>original: "dyscrasia"; an unhealthy or disordered mixture of the bodily qualities.</note>. This same logic explains the **origin of the humors**. Adding heat to something already warm makes it bitter; for example, honey turns into bile in people who are already "warm" in temperament. However, in elderly people, whose heat is fading, it turns into healthy blood. This proves that bile is not "pre-existing" in food, but is a product of the body's own internal processing.

<summary>This page outlines Galen’s argument that biological processes like nutrition and humor production depend on innate powers and qualities—specifically heat—rather than the purely mechanical "plumbing" theories proposed by Erasistratus.</summary>

## CHAPTER IX

The way organs perform their duties depends on how the four primary qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—are blended. For example, the stomach's ability to contract relies on this balance. Proper medical treatment is only possible when a physician understands what causes these functions to fail. In this regard, the followers of **Erasistratus** <note>A 3rd-century BCE physician who often favored mechanical explanations over the traditional "qualities" of the body.</note> act essentially as **Empiricists** <note>A medical sect that relied purely on observation and experience, often ignoring the underlying "hidden causes" of disease.</note>.

Once a doctor understands the meaning of a <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>original: "dyskrasia"; literally a "bad mixture" or imbalance of the four bodily humors.</note>, they naturally follow the **Hippocratic principle** of treating opposites with opposites—such as cooling a stomach that has overheated or warming one that has become chilled. It is useless to simply know what an organ does; one must understand the *bodily condition* that disrupts that function.

The composition of the four **humors** <note>The vital fluids that the ancients believed regulated health: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> is explained as follows:
*   **Blood** is warm and moist.
*   **Yellow bile** is warm and dry (essentially, even if it appears otherwise).
*   **Phlegm** is cold and moist.
*   **Black bile** represents the fourth combination: cold and dry.

To filter this black bile from the blood, Nature provided the **spleen**—an organ that Erasistratus claimed had no purpose at all. The proof of the spleen's vital importance is seen in the **jaundice**, **toxemia** <note>The buildup of harmful substances in the blood.</note>, and other illnesses that occur when it is diseased. Erasistratus’s failure to address the views of the leading medical authorities on the spleen shows how weak his arguments are.

The **Hippocratic** view has now been proven through both deduction and observation. This chapter also explains the traditional view on how humors are generated, the normal and diseased forms of yellow and black bile, and the role played by the <term>innate heat</term> <note>The vital internal fire that ancient physicians believed was the source of life and the driver of digestion.</note> in producing them. Other types of bile are merely transition stages between these types. Abnormal forms of bile are removed by the **liver** and the **spleen**. However, **phlegm** does not require a specific organ to filter it out, as the body is capable of fully processing it through <term>metabolism</term> <note>The internal process of converting substances for the body's use or energy.</note>.

Finally, there is a great need to study the works of the **Ancients** <note>Referring to the classical Greek medical authorities, particularly Hippocrates.</note> with care to truly master this subject.

# SYNOPSIS OF CHAPTERS

## BOOK III

### CHAPTER I

**A summary of certain points previously demonstrated.**
Every part of a living creature has an attractive faculty <note>The natural power to pull in necessary nutrients.</note> and an alterative faculty <note>The power to change or "assimilate" nutrients into the substance of the body.</note>; it draws in the nutritional juice that is proper to it. This process of assimilation is preceded by **adhesion** <note>original: "prosphysis"; the stage where nutrients stick to the tissue.</note> and, before that, by **application** <note>original: "prosthesis"; the initial placement of nutrients against the body's tissues.</note>. Application is the ultimate goal of the attractive power. However, adhesion and assimilation would not follow if each part did not also possess a faculty for holding the nutrients in position once they have been applied. **There is a logical necessity, based on first principles, for this retentive faculty.** <note>original: "a priori".</note>

### CHAPTER II

The existence of this same faculty is to be proven **through observation of its effects.** <note>original: "a posteriori".</note> Its corresponding **function** (which is the active expression of this faculty or potential) is **clearly seen in the large hollow organs, notably the womb and the stomach.**

### CHAPTER III

**the exercise of the retentive faculty is particularly well seen in the womb.** Its purpose is to allow the embryo to reach full development; once this growth is complete, a new power—the **expulsive faculty**—which has been inactive until this point, comes into play. These are the characteristic signs and symptoms of pregnancy: the tight grip of the womb on the growing embryo, and the precise closure of the **opening of the womb** <note>original: "os uteri".</note> while the retentive faculty is at work. The opening then widens and the womb begins its expulsive activities at full term, or if the fetus dies. A prolapse <note>The slipping of the organ out of its proper place.</note> can occur from the over-exertion of this faculty. **The role of the midwife. The supporting muscles used during childbirth.** <note>original: "parturition".</note>

### CHAPTER IV

The same two faculties are seen in the stomach. **Gurgling or rumbling noises** <note>original: "borborygmi".</note> show that this organ is weak and is not gripping its contents tightly enough. An undue delay of food in a weak

...as a transition-stage between food and blood; the appearance of waste in the intestine is another proof of the great transformation effected in the stomach. The denial by Asclepiades <note>A Greek physician who practiced in Rome and argued that the body was composed of "unconnected elements," denying the existence of biological "faculties."</note> of any real change in the quality of food in the stomach is proven false. Similarly, the denial by Erasistratus <note>A famous Alexandrian anatomist often criticized by Galen for his purely mechanical view of the body.</note> that digestion resembles a boiling process <note>original: "pepsis"; the Greek word for digestion also implies "cooking" or "ripening" through heat.</note> arises from his taking the terminology too literally.

### CHAPTER VIII

Erasistratus denies that the stomach exerts any pull during the act of swallowing. That he is wrong, however, is proved by the anatomical structure of the stomach—its inner coat, with its vertical fibers, obviously acts as a **pulling force from the front** <note>original: "vis a fronte"; an attractive force pulling from the destination.</note>, while its outer coat exercises a **pushing force from behind** <note>original: "vis a tergo"; a propulsive force pushing from the source.</note> through the contraction of its circular fibers; this latter force also comes into play during vomiting. The stomach uses the **gullet** <term>oesophagus</term> as a kind of hand to draw its food in with. The functions of these two coats are also proved by **live dissection** <term>vivisection</term>. Swallowing cannot be attributed merely to the force of gravity.

### CHAPTER IX

These four faculties <note>The powers of attraction, alteration, retention, and expulsion.</note> which support nutrition are thus clearly visible in many different parts of the body.

### CHAPTER X

There is a need for expanding upon the statements of the ancient physicians. The Ancients are superior to the Moderns. This decline in medical knowledge can only be corrected by a truly efficient education of the youth. The author outlines the chief requirements for such an education.

### CHAPTER XI

For the sake of the few who truly seek the truth, the argument will be continued. A third kind of fiber—the **oblique** or slanted fiber—assists in the **power of holding** <term>retention</term>; the author describes the way in which this fiber is arranged in different layers of the organ walls.
