### CHAPTER XII

The factor which brings the **expulsive faculty** <note>original: "apokritike dynamis"; the natural power an organ has to rid itself of waste, foreign material, or substances causing it distress.</note> into action is essentially a condition of the organ or its contents which is the reverse of that which determined **attraction**. There is a clear analogy between **abortion** and **normal childbirth** <term>parturition</term>. Whatever produces discomfort must be expelled. That this same discomfort also determines the expulsion of contents from the **gall-bladder** is not as immediately evident as it is in the case of the stomach, uterus, or urinary bladder, but it can be logically demonstrated.

### CHAPTER XIII

Expulsion takes place through the same channel as attraction (**for example**, in the stomach, gall-bladder, and uterus). Similarly, the **delivery** <term>anadosis</term> of nutriment to the liver from the food-canal via the **mesenteric veins** <note>The veins that carry blood and nutrients from the intestines directly to the liver for processing.</note> may have its direction reversed. There is a continuous "give-and-take" between different parts of the body; the superior strength of certain parts is natural, while in others it is acquired. When the liver contains abundant food and the stomach is depleted, the latter may draw nutrients back from the former; this occurs when an animal can get nothing to eat, and so prevents starvation. 

Similarly, when one part becomes over-distended, it tends to deposit its excess in some weaker part near it; this part then passes it on to some still weaker part, which cannot get rid of it; hence the formation of deposits <note>Galen is referring here to the localized accumulation of waste or "humors" that lead to disease or swelling.</note> of various kinds. Further instances are provided of the reversal of the normal direction of **delivery** from the food canal through the veins. Such a reversal of functions would, in any case, be expected **from theoretical deduction** <note>original: "a priori"</note>. In the vomiting associated with **intestinal obstruction**, matter may be carried backwards all the way from the intestine to the mouth; it is not surprising, therefore, that, under certain circumstances, food-material might be driven right back from the skin-surface to the alimentary canal (**for instance**, in cases of excessive chilling of the body's surface); not much is needed to determine this reversal of direction. The action of **purgative drugs** upon the terminals of the veins is also explored; one part draws from another until the whole body participates; similarly, in intestinal obstruction, each part passes on the irritating substance to its weaker neighbor...

## CHAPTER XIV

The superficial arteries, when they dilate <note>expand</note>, draw in air from the atmosphere, while the deeper arteries draw in a fine, vaporous blood from the veins and heart. Lighter matter, such as air, will always be drawn in preferentially over heavier matter; this is why the arteries in the food-canal draw in practically none of the nutrient matter contained within it.

## CHAPTER XV

There are two kinds of attraction: the **mechanical attraction** of dilating bellows and the **"physical" (vital) attraction** by living tissue of nutrient matter which is specifically "allied" or appropriate to it. The former kind—resulting from the **nature's abhorrence of a vacuum** <term>horror vacui</term> <note>The physical principle that empty space must be instantly filled by surrounding matter.</note>—acts primarily on light matter, whereas vital attraction has no essential concern with such mechanical factors. 

A hollow organ exercises the former kind of attraction by virtue of its cavity, and the second kind by virtue of the living tissue of its walls. This principle is applied to the question of what the arteries contain. The text discusses the **connections** <term>anastomoses</term> <note>Small junctions or openings where the venous and arterial systems meet.</note> of arteries and veins. It also describes **small openings** <term>Foramina</term> in the **dividing wall** <term>septum</term> of the heart, which allow some blood to pass from the right to the left ventricle. The large size of the **aorta** <note>The main artery of the body.</note> is likely due to the fact that it carries not only the **vital spirit** <term>pneuma</term> <note>original: "pneuma"; the life-force or "breath" believed to be refined in the heart and lungs.</note> received from the lungs, but also some of the blood which percolates through the dividing wall from the right ventricle. Thus, arteries carry not merely the vital spirit, but also some light vaporous blood, which certain parts of the body require more than others.

## ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES
### BOOK I
### CHAPTER I

<margin>Kühn Edition Vol. II. p. 1</margin> Since sensation and voluntary movement <note>original: "κινεῖσθαι κατὰ προαίρεσιν" (kineisthai kata proairesin)—literally movement according to choice or will.</note> are the particular characteristics of animals, while growth and nutrition are shared also by plants, the former would be the works of the **soul**, and the latter the works of **nature**. <note>original: "ψυχῆς" (psyches) and "φύσεως" (physeos). To a Greek physician, "Nature" (Physis) is the subconscious vital force that manages the body's internal chemistry, while "Soul" (Psyche) manages awareness and movement.</note> If someone were to grant a "soul" to plants as well, and by making a distinction were to call this one "vegetative" and the other "sensitive," such a person would not be saying anything different, but he would be using a term that is not at all customary. 

But for our part, being convinced that **clarity** is the greatest virtue of language, <margin>2</margin> and knowing that clarity is ruined || by nothing so much as by unusual names, we follow the custom of the majority in our naming. We say that animals are governed by both soul and nature together, but plants by nature alone; and growth and nutrition, we say, are the works of **nature**, not of the soul.

<margin>Kühn Edition Vol. II, p. 1</margin> Since feeling and voluntary motion are peculiar to animals, while growth and nutrition are common to plants as well, we may look on the former as the effects <note>original: "Ergon" (έργον)—literally a completed "work" or "deed." To Galen, "Nature" is the subconscious vital force that manages the body's internal chemistry and physical maintenance.</note> And if there is anyone who allows a share in soul to plants as well, and separates the two kinds of soul by naming the kind in question *vegetative* and the other *sensory*, this person is not saying anything different, although his language is somewhat unusual. 

We, however, for our part, are convinced that the chief merit of language is **clarity**, and we know that nothing detracts so much from this as do unfamiliar terms; accordingly, we employ those terms which the bulk of people are accustomed to use. We say that animals are governed at once by their soul and by their nature, and plants by their nature alone, and that growth and nutrition are the effects of **nature**, not of soul.

# GALEN
## ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES
### II

In this discourse, we shall investigate the **powers** <note>original: "dynameis" (δυνάμεις). In ancient medicine, these are the innate abilities or "faculties" that allow an organism to perform functions like digestion or growth.</note> from which these effects originate, as well as any other works of **Nature** <note>original: "Physis" (φύσις). For Galen, Nature is an active, artisan-like force that governs the body.</note> that may exist.

First, however, we must distinguish and clearly define the various terms we intend to use in this treatise, and to what specific things we apply them. This process will prove to be not merely an explanation of names, but a demonstration of the very works of Nature.

When a body undergoes no change from its current state, we say that it is **at rest**. If, however, it departs from this state in any respect, we then say that it undergoes **motion** <note>original: "kinesis" (κίνησις). In this context, motion refers to any kind of change or transformation, not just moving from one place to another.</note> in that respect. Accordingly, when a body departs in various ways from its pre-existing state, it is said to undergo various kinds of motion. 

For instance, if that which is white becomes black, or what is black becomes white, it undergoes motion in respect to **color**. Or, if what was previously sweet now becomes <margin>3</margin> bitter—or, conversely, if the bitter becomes sweet—it will be said to undergo motion in respect to **flavor**. <note>original: "chumos" (χυμός). While this can mean "humor" (like blood or bile), here it refers to the quality of taste.</note> <note>original: "austēron" (αὐστηρὸν). This describes a harsh, dry, or astringent bitter taste.</note> To both of these instances, as well as to those previously mentioned, we shall apply the term **qualitative motion**. 

Furthermore, it is not only things that are altered in regard to color and flavor that we say undergo motion; when a warm thing becomes cold, or a cold thing becomes warm, we also speak of it undergoing motion. Similarly, when any...

...from moist, or moist from dry. The common name we give to all these changes is **alteration** <note>original: "alloiosis" (ἀλλοίωσιν). This refers to qualitative change, where the essence of a thing remains the same but its attributes—like color or temperature—change.</note>.

This is one kind of motion. Another kind belongs to those bodies that change their positions and are said to move from place to place; the name for this is **local motion** <note>original: "phora" (φορά). Often translated as "conveyance" or "translation," this is simple movement through space.</note>.

These two motions are simple and primary. Composite motions arising from them are **growth** and **decay** <note>original: "auxēsis" (αὔξησίς) and "phthisis" (φθίσις). These refer to the creation of a new substance or the total destruction of an old one—for example, when wood turns to ash.</note>. Coming-to-be is the process of leading into **substance** <note>original: "ousia" (οὐσία). The fundamental reality or "being" of a thing.</note>, while passing-away is the opposite.

Common to all these motions is the **change** <margin>4</margin> of that which previously existed, just as common to states of rest is the preservation of what previously existed. Now, that the food is changed into blood—as perceived by sight, taste, and touch—is a fact that even the **sophists** <note>Galen often uses "sophist" as a derogatory term for rival theorists who use clever but (in his view) logically flawed arguments to deny the evidence of the senses.</note> admit. However, they no longer agree that this change is true in reality. For some of them believe all such perceptions are merely deceptions and misdirections of our senses, which are affected differently at different times, while the underlying substance receives none of these qualities for which it is named. Others allow that the **qualities** exist within the substance, but claim they are unchangeable and immutable...

# GALEN

...from age to age; they claim that these apparent alterations happen through **separation and aggregation** <note>original: "diakrisin te kai synkrisin" (διακρίσει τε καὶ συγκρίσει). This is the theory that things don't "change" their nature, they just get shuffled around like bricks in a wall.</note>, as Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was a pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that "everything is in everything" and change is just the rearranging of pre-existing "seeds."</note> asserts.

<margin>5</margin>
If I were to turn aside from my path to refute these men, my sidebar would become larger than the main work itself. For if they are ignorant of all that has been written concerning **alteration involving the whole substance** <note>original: "kat’ holēn tēn ousian alloiōseōs." This is the core Aristotelian idea that a thing can change its very nature, not just its position.</note>¹ by Aristotle and, after him, by Chrysippus <note>original: Footnote 2. If, however, they are aware of these works but nonetheless choose the worse path over the better, then they will surely consider my own words to be useless as well.³ That Hippocrates also held this view—though he lived even earlier than Aristotle—I have demonstrated in other writings. Galen believes these are the primary forces that drive all biological processes.</note> in total which act upon one another, and by which everything that is subject to **generation and destruction** <note>The cycle of coming-into-being and passing away.</note> is produced and destroyed.

Furthermore, Hippocrates was the first of all to recognize that these qualities are **blended through and through** <note>original: "kerannysthai... hola di’ holōn." In these cases, I call the motion of the vein and of the muscle an **activity**, and that of the food and the bones a **symptom** or **affection** <note>original: *symptoma* or *pathos*—these terms describe a secondary state or something that "happens to" an object because of an outside force, rather than something the object does itself.</note>, since the first group undergoes **alteration** and the second group is merely **transported**. One might, therefore, also speak of the activity as an effect of **Nature** <term>Nature<gloss>Greek: *physis*; for Galen, this is the internal "craftsman" or creative principle within every living thing that governs growth and health.</gloss></term>—for example, digestion, absorption <note>original: *anadosis*—literally a "yielding-up" or "delivery." One could not, however, in every case call the effect an activity; thus flesh is an effect of Nature, but it is, of course, not an activity. It is, therefore, clear that one of these terms is used in two senses, but not the other.

Why, then, does he use all four in his work *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: *Peri geneseōs kai phthoras*—Aristotle’s treatise on how things come into being and pass away.</note>, but in his *Meteorology*, his *Problems*, and many other places, does he use only two? ### IV

The faculty in the veins, then, which is called the **blood-making** faculty <note>original: *haimatopoietikē*—the power of the body to transform nutrients into blood.</note>, and indeed every other faculty, is understood as being relative to something. For it is primarily the cause of the **activity** <note>original: *energeia*; in Galen’s philosophy, this refers to the active functioning or "working" of an organ.</note>, and secondarily, by consequence, the cause of the **product** <note>original: *ergon*; the final result or "work" of an organ, such as the blood produced by the veins.</note>. But if the cause is relative to something—namely, to that which is produced by it, and to nothing else—it is clear that the faculty is also a relative term. 

As long as we remain ignorant of the true essence of the cause that is acting, we call it a "faculty," saying that there is a certain **blood-making** faculty in the veins, and likewise a **digestive** faculty in the stomach, a **pulsative** faculty in the heart, and for each of the other parts, a <margin>10</margin> specific faculty for the || activity belonging to that part. If, then, we intend to discover by systematic method how many and what kind of faculties there are, we must begin from the products themselves. For each of these products is generated by a specific activity, and each of these activities is preceded by a specific cause.

### V

The products of **nature** <term>nature<gloss>Greek: *physis*; Galen views Nature as a creative, artistic force that shapes and maintains the body.</gloss></term>, then, while the animal is still being conceived and shaped in the womb, are all the various parts of the body. Once the animal has been born, however, the common product for all parts is the development to its perfect size, and after that, its preservation for as long as possible.

There are, of necessity, three activities for these three products mentioned, one for each: **generation**,

## IV

<margin>method</margin>
The so-called **blood-making** <note>original: *haematopoietic*; the internal power that transforms nutrients into blood.</note> faculty in the veins, then, as well as all the other faculties, falls within the category of relative concepts. This is primarily because the faculty is the cause of the **activity** <note>original: *energeia*; the actual functioning or "work" being done by an organ.</note>, but also, by consequence, because it is the cause of the **effect** <note>original: *ergon*; the finished product or result of the activity.</note>. But, if the cause is relative to something—for it is the cause of what results from it, and of nothing else—it is obvious that the faculty also falls into the category of the relative; and so long as we are ignorant of the true essence of the cause which is operating, we call it a "faculty." 

Thus we say that there exists in the veins a **blood-making** faculty, as also a **digestive** <note>original: *peptic*; from the Greek term for "cooking" or "ripening" food.</note> faculty in the stomach, a **pulsatile** <note>original: *sphygmic*; the power responsible for the rhythmic beating of the heart and arteries.</note> faculty in the heart, and in each of the other parts a special faculty corresponding to the function or activity of that part. <insert>[</insert>If, therefore, we are to investigate methodically the number and kinds of faculties, we must begin with the effects; for each of these effects comes from a certain activity, and each of these again is preceded by a cause.<insert>]</insert>

...**growth** and **nutrition**. But **genesis** <note>original: *genesis*; here referring to the beginning of life in the womb, or what we might call embryogeny.</note> is not a simple, single activity of nature; rather, it is a complex process made up of both **alteration** <note>original: *alloiosis*; the chemical-like change of one substance into another, such as food into blood or tissue (histogenesis).</note> and **shaping**. In order for bone, nerve, vein, and every other part to come into being, the underlying **substance** <note>original: *ousian*; the fundamental material or essence from which the animal is formed.</note> must be altered. Furthermore, so that the creature may acquire its proper shape, position, cavities, <margin>11</margin> outgrowths, attachments, and all such features, this altered substance must be **shaped** <note>original: *diaplasis*; the ordering of tissues into specific organs (organogenesis).</note>. You would not be wrong to call this substance the "matter" of the living creature, just as wood is the matter of a ship or wax is the matter of a statue.

**Growth** is the increase and expansion in length, breadth, and depth of those solid parts of the animal which have already been shaped. **Nutrition**, on the other hand, is the addition of nutrients to these same parts without that expansion.

### VI

Let us speak first, then, of **genesis**, which we said arises from both alteration and shaping occurring together.

When the **seed** <note>original: *spermatos*</note> has been cast into the womb—or into the earth, for in this regard there is no difference—over certain fixed periods of time, many different parts are constituted from the substance being generated. This happens through the qualities of moisture, dryness, cold, heat, and all the other properties.

<summary>Galen defines the three primary biological functions: genesis (creation via alteration and shaping), growth (expansion of solid parts), and nutrition (replenishment). He compares the development of an embryo from a seed to the growth of a plant from the soil.</summary>

### ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, BOOK I, CHAPTERS V–VI

...namely, **Genesis** <note>original: *genesis*; refers to the initial creation or formation of the embryo.</note>, **Growth**, and **Nutrition**. **Genesis**, however, is not a simple activity of Nature, but is compounded of **alteration** <note>original: *alloiosis*; the process by which the "material" changes its fundamental qualities.</note> and of **shaping** <note>original: *diaplasis*; the process of "molding" or "modeling" the transformed material into specific organs and structures.</note>. That is to say, in order that bone, nerve, veins, and all other tissues may come into existence, the underlying substance from which the animal springs must be **altered**; and in order that the substance so altered may acquire its appropriate shape and position, its cavities, outgrowths, attachments, and so forth, it has to undergo a **shaping** or formative process. One would be justified in calling this substance which undergoes alteration the **material** of the animal, just as wood is the material of a ship, and wax of an image.

**Growth** is an increase and expansion in length, breadth, and thickness of the solid parts of the animal—those parts which have already been subjected to the molding or shaping process. **Nutrition** is an addition of substance to these parts, but without that expansion in size.

## VI

Let us speak then, in the first place, of **Genesis**, which, as we have said, results from **alteration** together with **shaping**.

They do this many times until the bladder appears to them to have reached a sufficient degree of **growth** <note>original: "auxēseōs."</note>. But in these actions of the children, it is clearly evident that as much as the internal capacity of the bladder increases in size, the body of the bladder itself must necessarily be reduced in thickness. If the children were able to **nourish** <note>original: "anatrephein." To provide nutritional support to the tissue as it expands.</note> this thinness, they would be producing a large bladder from a small one in a manner similar to Nature. As it stands, however, they lack this capacity, and this process cannot be brought to imitation in any way—not only by <margin>18</margin> children, but by anyone else; for this is the unique property of **Nature** <note>original: "physis."</note> alone.

Thus it is now clear to you that **nutrition** <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "threpsis." The process of taking in and assimilating food into the substance of the body.</note> is necessary for things that are growing. For if a body were to be stretched without being nourished, it would acquire a false appearance rather than true growth. Moreover, even the act of stretching in every direction belongs only to those things grown by Nature. For when we stretch bodies, they undergo this in only one **dimension** <note>original: "diastasin."</note> and are diminished in the others; we cannot find anything that we can extend in all three dimensions while it remains continuous and unbroken. It is the work of Nature alone to expand a body in every direction while it remains continuous with itself and preserves its entire original **form** <note>original: "idean."</note>.

<summary>Galen uses the analogy of children inflating a bladder to demonstrate that true growth requires both expansion and nutrition. He concludes that only Nature can expand a body in all three dimensions simultaneously without thinning or breaking it.</summary>

game in the district of **Ionia** <note>original: "Iōnia." A region on the central coast of western Asia Minor, a major center of the Greek intellectual world.</note>, and among not a few other nations. As they rub, they sing songs, to a certain measure, time, and rhythm, and all their words are an exhortation to the **bladder** <note>original: "kystin." Likely the urinary bladder of a pig or ox, used by children as a toy similar to a modern balloon.</note> to increase in size. When it appears to them fairly well distended, they again blow air into it and expand it further; then they rub it again. This they do several times, until the bladder seems to them to have become large enough. Now, clearly, in these doings of the children, the more the interior cavity of the bladder increases in size, the thinner, necessarily, does its substance become. But, if the children were able to bring nourishment to this thin part, then they would make the bladder big in the same way that **Nature** <term>Nature<gloss>original: "physis." For Galen, this is the creative power that governs the growth and function of living organisms.</gloss></term> does. As it is, however, they cannot do what Nature does, for to imitate this is beyond the power not only of children, but of any one soever; it is a property of Nature alone.

It will now, therefore, be clear to you that **nutrition** <term>nutrition<gloss>original: "threpsis." The process of taking in food and transforming it into the actual substance of the body's organs.</gloss></term> is a necessity for growing things. For if such bodies were distended, but not at the same time nourished, they would take on a false appearance of **growth** <term>growth<gloss>original: "auxēsis." Specifically, the increase in size of the solid parts of an organism.</gloss></term>, not a true growth. And further, to be distended *in all directions* belongs only to bodies whose growth is directed by Nature; for those which are distended by us undergo this distension in one direction but grow less in the others; it is impossible to find a body which will remain entire and not be torn through whilst we stretch it in the three dimensions. Thus Nature alone has the power to expand a body in all directions so that it remains unruptured and preserves completely its previous form.

### VIII

Now, it seems our discussion has reached the subject of **nutrition** <term>nutrition<gloss>original: "threpsis." The biological process of taking in food and converting it into the living substance of the body.</gloss></term>, which is the final and third topic we proposed at the beginning. For when nourishment flows in and is added to every part of the nourished body, the active process is "nutrition," and the "nutritive faculty" is its cause. 

<margin>19</margin> 

Here too, the type of activity is **alteration** <note>original: "alloiōsis." A fundamental change in the quality or essence of a substance, rather than just its shape or location.</note>, but it is not the same kind as that found in **generation** <note>original: "genesis." The process of something coming into existence or being born.</note>. In that case, what did not exist before came into being later; but in nutrition, that which flows in is **made similar** <note>original: "synexomoioutai." The process of assimilation where food becomes identical to the body part it nourishes—for example, food becoming bone or muscle.</note> to that which already exists. For this reason, thinkers have reasonably called the first kind of alteration "generation" and this kind "**assimilation**" <note>original: "exomoiōsin," meaning "making like."</note>.

### IX

Since we have sufficiently discussed the three **faculties of Nature** <term>Nature<gloss>original: "physis." The internal force that governs the development and maintenance of living things.</gloss></term>, and it appears the animal needs nothing else—possessing as it does the means to grow, to reach its full development, and to be preserved for as long as possible—this account might perhaps seem sufficient already to explain all the faculties of nature. But if one should consider again that not—

Such then is ***growth*** <term>growth<gloss>original: "auxēsis." The biological process by which a living part expands in all directions, distinct from mere mechanical swelling.</gloss></term>, and it cannot occur without the nutriment which flows to the part and is worked up into it.

## VIII

WE have, then, it seems, arrived at the subject of **Nutrition**, which is the third and remaining consideration which we proposed at the outset. For, when the matter which flows to each part of the body in the form of nutriment is being worked up into it, this activity is ***nutrition***, and its cause is the ***nutritive faculty***. Of course, the kind of activity here involved is also an **alteration** <note>original: "alloiōsis." A fundamental change in the qualities of a substance, such as food turning into blood or flesh.</note>, but not an alteration like that occurring at the stage of ***genesis*** <note>original: "genesis." Refers to generation or coming-into-being; specifically, this refers to the initial formation of tissues, not the pre-natal development already described in Chapter 6.</note>. For in the latter case something comes into existence which did not exist previously, while in nutrition the inflowing material becomes **assimilated** <note>original: "exomoiōsis." Literally "making like" or "likening"; the process by which food is transformed to match the specific substance of the body part it is nourishing.</note> to that which has already come into existence. Therefore, the former kind of alteration has with reason been termed ***genesis***, and the latter, ***assimilation***.

## IX

Now, since the three **faculties of Nature** <term>faculties of Nature<gloss>The internal powers of a living organism: the generative, the growth-promoting, and the nutritive.</gloss></term> have been exhaustively dealt with, and the animal would appear not to need any others (being possessed of the means for growing, for attaining completion, and for maintaining itself as long a time as possible), this treatise might seem to be already complete, and to constitute an exposition of all the faculties of Nature. If, however, one considers that it has not...

While it literally means "necessity," in Galen's philosophy, it refers to a restrictive "law of Nature" that governs physical processes.</note> of several organs for the **alteration** <term>alteration<gloss>original: "alloiosis." A fundamental change in the qualities of a substance (like color or density) to make it like the body it nourishes.</gloss></term> of <margin>21</margin> food is something every || living creature requires. For instance, for yellow to become red, or red to become yellow, only a single and simple alteration is needed; but for white to become black, or black to become white, the substance must pass through all the intermediate stages. <note>Galen's central point here is that no great change—whether in color, texture, or smell—can occur in a single leap; nature requires gradual steps.</note> Therefore, the softest thing could not suddenly become the hardest, nor the hardest suddenly become the softest, just as the foulest-smelling thing could not suddenly become fragrant, nor the fragrant suddenly become foul.

How, then, could bone ever be produced from blood if the blood were not first greatly thickened and whitened? Or how could blood be produced from bread if the bread did not gradually lose its whiteness and gradually acquire redness? To be sure, it is very easy for flesh to be formed from blood; for if **Nature** <note>Galen treats "Nature" (Physis) as an active, intelligent force that "works" on the body's materials.</note> thickens the blood to the point that it gains a certain consistency and is no longer fluid, this would be the first stage of "newly-formed flesh." Moreover, it is quite obvious that bread—and even more so <margin>22</margin> lettuce, beetroots, || and the like—requires an immense amount of **alteration** to be turned into blood.

This, then, is one reason why there are so many organs involved in the transformation of food. The second reason is the nature of the **waste products** <term>waste products<gloss>original: "perittomata." ### XI

We must now recall the goal itself, for the sake of which Nature has fashioned so many and such various parts. Now, the name of this process, as has been said before, is **nutrition** <term>nutrition<gloss>original: "threpsis." For Galen, nutrition is not just eating, but the specific end-point where food turns into living flesh.</gloss></term>. The definition associated with this name is the **assimilation** <term>assimilation<gloss>original: "homoiōsis." Literally "making alike." Galen defines this as the "assimilation of the nourisher to the nourished," or making the food identical to the body part.</gloss></term> of that which nourishes to that which is being nourished. For this to occur, **adhesion** <term>adhesion<gloss>original: "prosphysis." The second-to-last stage of nutrition where the nutrient fluid becomes firmly "glued" to the tissue.</gloss></term> must first take place, and for that to happen, **addition** <term>addition<gloss>original: "prosthesis." The very first stage of local nutrition, where the nutrient fluid is simply applied or "placed next to" the tissue it will eventually become.</gloss></term> must occur. For once the **humor** <note>The liquid nourishment carried in the blood.</note> intended to nourish any part of the animal has leaked out of the vessels, it is first distributed through the whole part, then it is **added**, then it **adheres**, and finally, it is completely **assimilated**.

<summary>Galen concludes his survey of the body's functional systems and defines nutrition as a four-stage process: distribution, addition (prosthesis), adhesion (prosphysis), and finally assimilation (homoiosis).</summary>

## XI

Let us once more, then, recall the actual purpose for which Nature has constructed all these parts. Its name, as previously stated, is **nutrition**, and the definition corresponding to the name is: *an **assimilation** <term>assimilation<gloss>original: "homoiōsis," meaning "to make like." This is the final stage of nutrition where food is transformed into the exact same substance as the organ it is feeding.</gloss></term> of that which nourishes to that which receives nourishment.*

And in order that this may come about, we must assume a preliminary process of ***adhesion*** <term>adhesion<gloss>original: "prosphysis," literally "growing onto" or attachment. Galen uses this to describe the moment the nutrient fluid "sticks" to the tissue before being absorbed.</gloss></term>, and for that, again, one of ***presentation*** <term>presentation<gloss>original: "prosthesis," literally "placing next to" or apposition. This is the stage where the nutrient fluid is delivered and sits right against the tissue.</gloss></term>. For whenever the juice which is destined to nourish any of the parts of the animal is emitted from the vessels, it is in the first place dispersed all through this part, next it is **presented**, and next it **adheres**, and becomes completely **assimilated**.

<summary>Galen defines the physiological process of nutrition as a three-stage transformation where nutrients are presented to a tissue, adhere to it, and finally become identical to it through assimilation.</summary>

Furthermore, that which is still held within the veins, and even more so that which remains in the stomach, is called "**nutriment**" <note>original: "trophē." > "Nutriment is that which is currently nourishing, that which is almost nutriment, and that which is destined to be nutriment."

By "almost nutriment," he meant the material that has reached the body parts and is beginning to adhere or attach to them. Finally, by "destined to be nutriment," he meant everything else—that which is still contained within the stomach and the veins.

### XII

It is quite clear, therefore, that nutrition must necessarily be a process of **assimilation** between the source of nourishment and the body being nourished. 

However, there are those who argue that this assimilation does not actually happen in reality, but is merely an illusion. These are the people who believe that **Nature** <note>original: "Physis." In Galen’s view, Nature is a creative, purposeful force, almost like a divine craftsman.</note> is not **artistic** <term>artistic<gloss>original: "technikos." This refers to the "technē" or craftsmanship of Nature; the idea that biological processes are not random but are carried out with the skill and foresight of a master artisan.</gloss></term>. They claim she shows no forethought for the welfare of the animal and possesses no inherent powers to transform certain substances, attract what is needed, or expel what is waste.

Generally speaking, two main schools of thought <note>Galen is likely referring to the "Mechanists" (who saw the body as a machine governed by physical atoms) versus the "Vitalists" (like himself and Hippocrates, who saw the body as governed by purposeful biological forces).</note> have emerged in both medicine and philosophy regarding these matters:

### ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, BOOK I, CHAPTER XII

...what is foreign. Further, she <note>Nature is personified here as a female creative force.</note> skillfully moulds everything during the stage of genesis; and she also provides for the creatures after birth, employing here other faculties again, namely, one of affection and forethought for offspring, and one of sociability and friendship for kindred. 

According to the other school, none of these things exist in the **natures** <note>original: "physesin." Galen refers to the individual "nature" or biological blueprint inherent in every living thing.</note> of living things, nor is there in the soul any original innate idea, whether of agreement or difference, of separation or synthesis, of justice or injustice, of the beautiful or ugly; all such things, they say, arise in us *from sensation and through sensation*, and animals are steered by certain images and memories.

Some of these people have even expressly declared that the soul possesses no reasoning faculty, but that we are led like cattle by the impression of our senses, and are unable to refuse or dissent from anything. It is worth hearing how he explains the passage of urine into the bladder and marveling at the man’s "wisdom." He abandons these wide and clearly visible paths to hypothesize others that are invisible, <margin>32</margin> narrow, and entirely imperceptible ||. If we are to claim that vapors pass through these parts, why on earth do they not pass through the **peritoneum** <term>the thin, transparent membrane that lines the abdominal cavity</term> and the **diaphragm** <note>original: "phrenon," a term often used in antiquity to refer to the midriff or diaphragm.</note>, thereby filling the entire **epigastrium** <term>the upper part of the abdomen, located just above the stomach</term> and the chest with water?

<margin>33</margin>
But perhaps it is neither the thickness nor the thinness of the membranes, but rather the **position** of the bladder that causes the vapors to be carried into it. And yet, even if every other reason made it plausible for them to collect there, the matter of position alone would be enough to prevent it. For the bladder lies low down in the body, while vapors have a natural tendency to rise upward; thus, they would have filled everything in the region of the chest and the lungs long before they ever reached the bladder.

And yet, why do I mention the position of the bladder, the peritoneum, and the chest? # ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, BOOK I

### Chapter xiii (Continued)

->62<-

Nothing has any natural **sympathy** <term>the Stoic and Hippocratic idea that all parts of a living organism are interconnected and respond to one another</term> with anything else, since all substance is divided and broken up into **unconnected elements** <term>literally "unfitted" or "unjoined" elements; a reference to Asclepiades’ theory that the body is composed of fragmented particles or atoms</term> and nonsensical masses. Consequently, out of necessity, he [Asclepiades] made countless statements contrary to clearly visible facts and ignored **Nature's** power to attract what is appropriate and expel what is foreign.

Regarding **sanguification** <term>the process of turning food into blood</term> and **distribution** <note>original: "ἀναδόσεως" (anadosis); the dispersal of nutrients from the digestive tract to the rest of the body</note>, he invented some cold-hearted babble. But regarding the clearing away of waste products, having absolutely nothing to say, he did not hesitate to directly contradict the visible facts. In the case of the secretion of urine, he stripped the kidneys and ureters of their function and hypothesized certain invisible pores leading into the bladder. It was, I suppose, a great and dignified thing for him to distrust what is visible and trust in what is invisible!

<margin>40</margin> In the case of **yellow bile**, his audacity is even greater and more reckless; for he says it is generated in the bile-vessels, and not merely separated out from the blood.

How is it then that for those suffering from **jaundice** <note>original: "ἰκτερικοῖς" (ikterikois); a condition where the skin and eyes turn yellow due to bile buildup</note>, both things happen at once: their excrement contains no bile at all, while their whole body becomes full of it? Here again, he is forced to talk nonsense, much like what he said regarding urine. He talks no less nonsense about **black bile** and the **spleen**, neither understanding what **Hippocrates** said nor attempting to refute things he does not know, speaking with a frantic and insane mouth.

...naturally in **sympathy** <term>the Stoic and Hippocratic concept that all parts of a living organism are interconnected and respond to one another</term> with anything else, all substance being divided and broken up into inharmonious elements and absurd **molecules** <term>Galen uses the term 'onkoi' to mock Asclepiades’ version of atoms—fragmented particles that supposedly make up the body without any unifying biological force</term>. Being utterly unable to find anything to say regarding the **clearing-out** <note>original: "κάθαρσις" (catharsis); the process of purging or filtering waste products from the body</note> of superfluities, he did not hesitate to join issue with obvious facts. In this matter of **urinary secretion**, he deprived both the kidneys and the ureters of their activity by assuming that there were certain invisible channels opening into the bladder. It was, of course, a grand and impressive thing to do: to mistrust the obvious and to pin one's faith in things which could not be seen!

Also, in the matter of the **yellow bile**, he makes an even grander and more spirited venture; for he says this is actually generated in the bile-ducts, and not merely separated out <note>Galen's view, following Hippocrates, was that bile exists in the blood and is filtered out by the liver and gallbladder; Asclepiades argued the ducts created it themselves</note>.

How comes it, then, that in cases of **jaundice** <term>a yellowing of the skin and eyes caused by bile buildup</term> two things happen at the same time—that the dejections contain absolutely no bile, and that the whole body becomes full of it? He is forced here again to talk nonsense, just as he did in regard to the urine. He also talks no less nonsense about the **black bile** and the **spleen**, not understanding what was said by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous 5th-century BCE physician whom Galen considers the ultimate authority on medicine</note>; and he attempts in stupid—I might say insane—language to contradict what he knows nothing about.

What benefit, then, did he gain for his medical treatments from such doctrines? He is unable to cure a kidney disease, or **jaundice** <term>a yellowing of the skin traditionally attributed to a buildup of yellow bile</term>, or **melancholy** <term>literally "black-bile-ness," a condition thought to be caused by an excess of black bile</term>. Note 1 in the original text clarifies this refers to urine</note>. <margin>41</margin>
According to the "wonderful" **Asclepiades** <note>Galen is being sarcastic here, as Asclepiades was his chief intellectual rival</note>, it makes no difference whether one gives a **water-drawing** <term>hydragōgon</term> or a **bile-drawing** <term>cholagōgon</term> drug to patients with **dropsy** <term>the swelling of soft tissues due to the accumulation of excess water, known today as edema</term>. Must we not, therefore, consider him mad, or else entirely inexperienced in the practical works of the medical art? For who does not know that if a **phlegm-drawing** drug were given to those suffering from **jaundice**, they would not be purged even four **kyathoi** <term>a small Greek cup or measure, roughly equivalent to 1.5 fluid ounces</term>? Nor would they be purged if any of the **water-drawing** drugs were used. But when a **bile-drawing** drug is given, a vast amount of bile is evacuated, and the skin of those so purged immediately becomes clear. We ourselves, at any rate, after treating the underlying condition in the liver and purging the patient once, have frequently relieved them of their illness. However, if you were to attempt the purge with a phlegm-drawing drug, you would accomplish nothing further.

What benefit did he derive from these opinions in terms of medical treatment? He was unable to cure a **kidney ailment** <term>likely referring to kidney stones or chronic renal failure</term>, nor **jaundice** <term>a yellowing of the eyes and skin</term>, nor a disease of **black bile** <term>often called melancholy; believed to be caused by an excess of a dark, thick humor</term>. Furthermore, he refused to agree with the view held not only by **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BCE) whom Galen deeply admired</note> but by all men regarding drugs—that some of them **purge** <term>to physically clear out or empty</term> away **yellow bile**, others **black bile**, some **phlegm** <term>a cold, moist humor associated with the lungs and brain</term>, and others the thin and watery waste <note>original: "perittoma." The author's note indicates this refers specifically to urine</note>.

He maintained that all the substances **evacuated** <note>original: "kenoumenon," meaning emptied from the body. Note 2 in the source refers to a technical discussion on page 67</note> were *produced by the drugs themselves*, just as **yellow bile** is produced by the biliary passages! According to this extraordinary man <note>Galen is being highly sarcastic here</note>, it matters nothing whether we give a **water-drawing drug** <term>original: "hydragogue"; a medication intended to remove excess water from the body</term> or a **bile-drawing drug** <term>original: "cholagogue"; a medication intended to trigger the release of bile</term> in a case of **dropsy** <term>edema, or the swelling of the body due to trapped fluid</term>. He claims these all equally **purge** and dissolve the body, producing a liquid of a certain appearance that did not exist as such before! <note>Note 3 in the original text explains that Asclepiades rejected the idea of "offending matter" (original Latin: *materia peccans*). Instead, he believed diseases were caused by the disrupted movement of "molecules" or "masses" (original Greek: *onkoi*). Therefore, he believed drugs didn't find existing fluids but melted the body's tissues into new fluids.</note>

Must we not, therefore, suppose he was either mad, or entirely unacquainted with the practical side of medicine? For who does not know that if a drug for attracting **phlegm** be given in a case of **jaundice**, it will not even **evacuate** four **small cups** <term>original: "cyathi." A Greek measure of volume; four cyathi is approximately one-third of a pint or 120ml</term> of **phlegm**? Similarly, the same is true if one of the **water-drawing drugs** be given. A **bile-drawing drug**, on the other hand, clears away a great quantity of **bile**, and the skin of patients treated this way immediately becomes clear. I myself have, in many cases, first treated the condition of the liver and then removed the disease entirely with a single **purgation**; whereas, if one had used a drug for removing **phlegm**, it would have done no good at all.

And it is not as though **Hippocrates** <note>The legendary physician whom Galen considers the ultimate authority</note> alone knows that these things happen in this way, while those who rely solely on **experience** ^**1**^ <term>the Empiricists; a medical sect that believed medicine should be based on observation rather than hidden causes</term> understand them differently. On the contrary, they <margin>42</margin> and all physicians who care about the practical results of their **art** <term>original: "techne," the skilled practice of medicine</term> hold this view—everyone, that is, except for **Asclepiades**. 

For he considered it a "betrayal" of the **elements** ^**2**^ <note>original: "stoicheia"; referring to Asclepiades' theory that the body is composed of "unconnected molecules" or atoms</note> he had proposed as his foundation to admit the truth concerning these matters. For if any drug were found to possess an **attractive** power for one particular **humor** <term>one of the four vital bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</term> alone, there would be a danger that the argument would prevail—namely, that there exists in every **body** ^**3**^ a **faculty** <term>an inherent natural power or ability</term> that draws to itself its own appropriate quality. 

Because of this, he claims that **safflower** <note>original: "knekos"; used as a purgative</note>, the **Cnidian berry** <note>the fruit of the spurge flax</note>, and **hippophae** <note>a purging plant, likely a species of sea-buckthorn</note> do not draw **phlegm** <term>the cold, moist humor</term> out of the body, but rather *create* it. Furthermore, he asserts that **flowers of copper** <term>verdigris or copper oxide</term>, copper scales, burnt copper, **germander** <note>an herb often used for gout or fever</note>, and the **chameleon-plant** <note>a type of thistle</note> actually dissolve the body into water. He claims that those suffering from **dropsy** <term>edema; a condition of excess fluid in the tissues</term> are not "cleansed" by these substances but are merely emptied out, while the drugs actually *increase* the underlying disease! 

For if a drug does not empty the watery fluid already contained in the body, but instead generates more of it, it is surely adding to the patient's suffering. And indeed, according to Asclepiades' reasoning, even **scammony** <note>a potent resinous drug used to purge bile</note>—besides failing to empty the **bile** from the bodies of those with **jaundice** <term>a yellowing of the skin caused by bile entering the blood</term>—goes so far as to turn healthy blood into bile <margin>43</margin>, wasting away the body and causing such great evils while worsening the patient's condition.

Nevertheless, it is clearly visible to everyone that scammony benefits many people. "Yes," he replies, "they are benefited, but only by the very fact of..."

And **Hippocrates** <note>The famous 5th-century BCE physician whom Galen views as the ultimate medical authority</note> is not the only one who knows this to be the case, while those who take **experience** ^1^ <term>original: "empeiria"; referring to the Empiricist sect of doctors who relied on observation rather than theory</term> alone as their starting point know otherwise; rather, they, as well as all physicians who are actively engaged in the practice of medicine, are of this same opinion. 

**Asclepiades**, however, is an exception; he would consider it a "betrayal" of his foundational **elements** ^2^ <note>original: "stoicheia"; Asclepiades believed the body was composed of "unconnected molecules" or atoms, which left no room for "natural faculties" or biological attractions</note> to admit the truth about such matters. For if a single drug were discovered that **attracted** <term>the power to pull or draw a specific substance toward itself</term> only a specific **humor** <term>one of the four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</term>, there would clearly be a danger of the opinion gaining ground that there exists in every **body** ^3^ a **faculty** <term>an inherent natural power or ability</term> which attracts its own particular quality. 

He therefore claims that **safflower** ^4^ <note>original: "knekos"; Carthamus tinctorius, used as a laxative</note>, the **Cnidian berry** ^5^ <note>Daphne Gnidium; a powerful purgative</note>, and ***Hippophaes*** ^6^ <note>Euphorbia acanthothamnos; a thorny Mediterranean shrub used in ancient medicine</note> do not draw **phlegm** <term>the cold, moist humor associated with winter and the lungs</term> from the body, but actually *create* it. Furthermore, he maintains that the **flower and scales of bronze** <note>copper oxides produced by heating bronze, used as a drying agent</note>, and burnt bronze itself, as well as **germander** ^7^ <note>Teucrium chamaedrys; a medicinal herb</note> and **wild mastich** ^8^ <note>Atractylis gummifera</note>, dissolve the body into water. He argues that **dropsical** <term>suffering from dropsy or edema; an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the body</term> patients benefit from these substances not because they are **purged** by them, but because they are rid of substances that actually help to increase the disease. His reasoning is that if a medicine does not **evacuate** ^9^ <note>original: "kenōo"; to empty out or drain</note> the fluid already contained in a dropsical body, but instead generates more, it would only make the condition worse. 

Furthermore, according to the **Asclepiadean** argument, **scammony** <note>a resin from the root of Convolvulus scammonia, used as a potent laxative</note> not only fails to **evacuate** ^9^ the **bile** from the bodies of **jaundiced** subjects, but actually transforms healthy blood into bile and dissolves the body; in fact, he claims it does every kind of evil and increases the severity of the disease. 

And yet, this drug can clearly be seen to do good for a great number of people! "Yes," he says, "they derive—"

<summary>Galen critiques Asclepiades for denying that drugs have "attractive" powers. To protect his atomic theory, Asclepiades claimed that purgative drugs actually create the fluids they seem to remove, a claim Galen finds absurd and contrary to clinical success.</summary>

...by reason of the **evacuation**. Indeed, if you were to give these patients a drug that **draws phlegm** <term>original: "phlegmatos agōgon"; a phlegmagogue</term>, they will receive no benefit. This fact is so **evident** <term>original: "enarges"; a technical term in Greek philosophy for self-evident truth perceived by the senses</term> that even those who base their practice on **experience** <note>Referring to the "Empiricist" sect of physicians who rejected theoretical "reasons" in favor of what they could observe through repeated trials</note> alone recognize it. 

And yet, for these men, this is their very philosophy: to trust no logical argument, but only what is clearly perceived by the senses. They, then, are acting wisely; but **Asclepiades** <note>A famous 1st-century BCE physician who taught that the body was made of "unconnected molecules" and rejected the four humors</note> is out of his mind when he commands us to distrust our senses in cases where the **phenomena** <term>observable facts or appearances</term> clearly overturn his own hypotheses. It would have been far better for him not to challenge the evidence of his own eyes, but rather to yield everything to them.

Is it, then, only these facts that so clearly conflict with the doctrines of **Asclepiades**? Or is it also the fact that in **summer** the same drugs evacuate more **yellow bile**, while in **winter** they draw out more **phlegm**? Furthermore, in a **young man** they draw more bile, but in an **old man**, more phlegm. <margin>Kühn Edition page 44</margin> For it is clear that each drug **attracts** <term>the power of a substance to "pull" its like toward it</term> the humor that is already present; it does not "create" a humor that does not exist. 

Suppose, for example, you wished to give a **phlegm-drawing** drug to a young man—one of those lean, "warm" types—during the height of summer, provided he has not lived a sedentary life nor is suffering from a **plethora** <term>original: "plēthōra"; an over-fullness of humors or blood</term>. You will evacuate only a tiny amount of the **humor** <term>original: "chymos"; one of the four vital fluids</term>, and even then only with great **violence** <note>Galen refers to the physical strain or "wrenching" of the body when a drug tries to force out a fluid that isn't there</note> to the body, and you will harm the man excessively. On the contrary, if you give him a **bile-drawing drug** <term>original: "cholagōgon"; a cholagogue</term>, you will evacuate a great deal and cause him no harm at all.

Do we then still doubt that each drug draws to itself its own **appropriate humor**?

### XIV

Let us, then, move on to another "idle chatter" <note>original: "ἀδολεσχίαν" (*adoleschian*). Galen is being sarcastic, adopting the dismissive language his opponents use for his detailed logical proofs</note>; for these **sophists** <note>Here used as a pejorative for thinkers who use clever but fallacious arguments</note> do not allow us to take up any of the worthy questions—though there are very many of them—but instead force us to waste our time in solving the fallacies they put forward.

<margin>45</margin> What, then, is this "chatter"? It is that famous and much-talked-of **stone** <note>The lodestone or magnet</note> which draws iron || to itself. For perhaps this stone might eventually draw even their souls to believe that there exist, in each of the various bodies, certain **attractive powers** which pull in their own specific qualities.

Now **Epicurus** <note>The Greek philosopher (341–270 BCE) who taught that the universe is composed of atoms and void</note>, although he uses principles for his <term>natural philosophy</term> <note>original: "φυσιολογίαν" (*physiologian*). In antiquity, this referred to the study of all natural things, not just the functions of living organisms</note> similar to those of **Asclepiades**, nevertheless admits that iron is drawn by the "Heraclean stone" <note>An ancient name for the magnet, named after the city of Heraclea</note>, and that <term>bits of chaff</term> are drawn by amber; he even attempts to provide the cause of this phenomenon. He says that the **atoms** flowing off from the stone are similar in shape to those flowing off from the iron, so that they easily become entangled with one another. Thus, when these atoms strike against the solid masses of both the stone and the iron, and then bounce back into the space between them, they become entangled with one another and...

The followers of **Asclepiades** <note>A physician who rejected the idea of biological "powers," viewing the body instead as a system of atoms and pores</note> will perhaps agree with this—or rather, they will certainly declare that they disbelieve it, simply to avoid betraying their favorite prejudices.

## XIV

Let us move on, then, to another piece of "nonsense." These **sophists** <note>Galen's term for thinkers who prioritize clever, deceptive arguments over scientific truth</note> do not allow us to engage in any worthwhile research—though there is plenty of it to be done—but instead force us to waste our time dismantling the fallacious arguments they put forward.

What, then, is this piece of nonsense? It concerns that famous and well-known **stone** which attracts iron. <note>The lodestone or magnet</note> One might think that this stone would draw even *their* minds to the belief that all bodies possess certain **faculties** <note>Inherent natural powers or abilities</note> by which they attract their own specific qualities.

Now **Epicurus** <note>Greek philosopher (341–270 BCE) who taught that the world is made of atoms and void</note>, despite the fact that he uses elements in his **natural philosophy** <note>original: "Physics" (*Physiologia*)</note> similar to those of Asclepiades, nevertheless admits that iron is attracted by the **magnet** <note>original: "Herculean stone" (*Hērakleia lithos*)</note>, and chaff by amber. He even tries to explain the cause of this phenomenon. His view is that the **atoms** <note>original: "ἄτομος" (*atomos*), meaning "indivisible"</note> flowing out of the stone are shaped similarly to the atoms flowing out of the iron, which allows them to easily interlock with one another. He argues that after these atoms collide with the two solid masses (the stone and the iron), they bounce back into the middle and become entangled with each other.

Asclepiades adapted his atomic theory from Epicurus, who in turn took it from **Democritus**.</note>

...that the iron is drawn along with them. Now, while the implausibility of these hypotheses regarding the **causal explanation** <note>original: "aetiology" (the study of causes)</note> is perfectly clear, Epicurus nevertheless acknowledges the reality of the attraction. Indeed, he goes so far as to say that the **distribution of nutrients** <note>original: "anadosis"; the process by which food is carried from the gut to the tissues</note>, the separation of waste products, and the effects of purgative drugs in the bodies of living creatures all occur in this same way.

<margin>46</margin> **Asclepiades**, however, perceiving the implausibility of the cause mentioned above, and finding no other plausible explanation based on the **atoms** he had assumed as his basic elements, turned to a position of sheer shamelessness: he claimed that nothing is attracted by anything at all. 

What he *should* have done—if he was dissatisfied with Epicurus’ theories and had nothing better to suggest—was to abandon his starting assumptions. He should have admitted instead that **Nature** is "creative" <note>original: "technic" (*technikē*), meaning nature acts with the skill and purpose of a craftsman</note> and that the essence of all beings is fundamentally unified, constantly being altered by its own parts as they act and react upon one another. 

For if he had accepted these principles, it would not have been difficult to admit that this "creative nature" possesses specific **faculties**: one for **attracting what is appropriate** <note>original: *oikeios* (kindred or beneficial things)</note> and another for **rejecting what is foreign** <note>original: *allotrios* (alien or harmful things)</note>. Indeed, Nature's "craftsmanship," her ability to preserve the living creature, and her capacity to resolve diseases consist of nothing other than her power to accept and guard what belongs to the body while excreting what is alien to it.

<margin>47</margin> But even here, Asclepiades recognized the logical consequences of the principles he had laid down. He was not ashamed to fight against facts that are clearly visible to all; instead, he directly challenges an observation held not only by physicians but by the rest of humanity...

For if each of these particles is but a ten-thousandth part of the dust-motes floating in the air, how large must we imagine their **hooked ends** <note>original: "agkistroeides"; the atomists argued that particles had hooks to latch onto each other</note> to be, by which they are entangled with one another? For surely this hook must be the smallest part of the whole particle.

Here, he explores the logical absurdity of "effluvia"—the idea that a magnet works by constantly shedding tiny physical particles to pull iron toward it—and mocks the idea that tiny atomic "hooks" could hold such weight.</meta>

lodestone, and the power <note>original: *dynamis*; Galen uses this to describe a specific "faculty" or natural force rather than a purely mechanical action</note> ^1 being transmitted through it to the others. Moreover, it cannot be said that if you bring a second <term>stylet: a pointed iron tool used for writing on wax tablets</term> into contact with the lower end of the first, it becomes held, attached, and suspended, whereas, if you apply it to any other part of the side it does not become attached. For the power of the <term>lodestone: a naturally occurring magnetic rock, often called the "Heraclean stone" in antiquity</term> is distributed in all directions; it merely needs to be in contact with the first <term>stylet</term> at any point; from this <term>stylet</term> again the power flows, as quick as a thought <note>original: *hama noēmati*; a Greek idiom used to describe something that happens instantaneously</note>, all through the second, and from that again to the third. Now, if you imagine a small <term>lodestone</term> hanging in a house, and in contact with it all round a large number of pieces of iron, from them again others, from these others, and so on,—all these pieces of iron must surely become filled with the <term>corpuscles: the invisible, physical particles that Atomist philosophers believed made up all matter</term> which emanate from the stone; therefore, this first little stone is likely to become dissipated by disintegrating into these emanations <note>original: *aporroas*; the physical "outflows" or "effluvia" that Epicurus believed were physically shed by the magnet to create attraction</note>.^2 Further, even if there be no iron in contact with it, it still disperses into the air, particularly if this be also warm.

“Yes,” says *Epicurus*, “but these <term>corpuscles</term> must be looked on as exceedingly small, so that some of them are a ten-thousandth part of the size of the very smallest particles carried in the air.” Then do you venture to say that so great a weight of iron can be suspended by such small bodies? If each of them is a ten-thousandth part as large as the dust particles which are borne in the atmosphere, how big must we suppose the hook-like extremities by which they interlock with each other ^3 to be? <note>Atomists like Epicurus argued that atoms had physical shapes, such as hooks or loops, which allowed them to snag one another to form solid objects.</note> For of course this is quite the smallest portion of the whole particle.

Then, one small particle being entangled with another small particle, both in motion, is not immediately repelled. For by one hook they are joined to each other, while by another, they connect to either the stone <term>lodestone: a naturally magnetic rock</term> above or the iron below. Indeed, if a particle were attached to the stone at the top but failed to entwine with the iron at the bottom, it would achieve nothing. Thus, the upper part of the particle must hang from the stone, while the iron must be joined to the lower end. Then, again, when one minute particle <note>original: *smikron somaton*; Galen’s term for the atoms or corpuscles proposed by the Atomist philosophers like Epicurus</note> becomes entangled with another minute particle, or when a particle in motion becomes entangled with another that is also moving, they do not simply bounce off one another immediately. For, according to this theory, there will certainly be other particles that strike them from above and below, from the front and the rear, and from the right and the left—constantly shaking and agitating them, never allowing them to rest.

Furthermore, we must necessarily assume that each of these tiny particles possesses a vast number of these hooked ends <note>original: *ankistrode perata*; the physical "hooks" that Epicurus claimed allowed atoms to snag one another</note>. For by one hook, the particle attaches itself to its neighbors; by another—the one at the top—it attaches to the **lodestone** <term>lodestone: a naturally occurring magnetic rock, usually magnetite</term>; and by the hook at the bottom, it attaches to the iron. If it were attached only to the stone above and not interlocked with the iron below, this mechanism would be entirely useless <note>In other words, the theory fails if the chain of physical connection is broken at any point.</note>.

Thus, the upper part of the particle's highest point must hang from the **lodestone**, and the iron must be fixed to the lower part of the particle's bottom end. And since these particles also interlock with one another along their sides, they must, of course, have hooks located there as well. Keep in mind, above all, how incredibly small these bodies are supposed to be, yet they are imagined to possess all these various types of physical outgrowths <note>original: *apophyseis*; projections or extensions from the main body of the particle</note>. 

Still more, remember this: in order for a second piece of iron to become attached to the first, and a third to the second, and a fourth to that, these absurd little particles must simultaneously do two contradictory things. They must pass through the narrow channels within the first piece of iron and, at the very same time, bounce off the next piece of iron in the series—even though this second piece is naturally identical in every way to the first.

Such a hypothesis <note>original: *hypothesis*; a proposed explanation or theory</note>, once again, is certainly not lacking in audacity; in fact, to tell the truth, it is far more shameless than the theories that came before it. According to—

Thus, **Epicurus**, in his desire to stay true to the facts, cuts an awkward figure by trying to show that the facts agree with his principles. **Asclepiades**, on the other hand, protects the consistency of his principles but pays no attention to what is obvious. Whoever, therefore, wishes to reveal the absurdity of their hypotheses must—if arguing against Asclepiades—remember his conflict with observed facts; or, if answering Epicurus, his failure to be consistent with his own principles. 

Almost all other schools based on similar principles have now died out, while these two alone still maintain a following. Yet the doctrines of Asclepiades have been undeniably proven wrong by **Menodotus the Empiricist** <note>Menodotus of Nicomedia: A prominent doctor of the "Empiric" school who argued that medical knowledge should come from observation and experience, not hidden theories.</note>, who highlights how they contradict both the **phenomena** <term>phenomena: things as they appear to the senses; empirical evidence or clinical observations</term> and their own logic.

How shall we handle this argument? For I think those who refuse to admit that anything is attracted by anything will appear even more ignorant of nature than the farmers themselves. When I first heard of this phenomenon, I was amazed and wanted to see it for myself as an eyewitness. Afterward, once the evidence of experience confirmed it, I spent a long time considering the cause. I looked through all the various philosophical schools <note>original: *haireseis* — referring to the competing medical and philosophical sects of the time, such as the Stoics, Epicureans, and Peripatetics</note> and could not find any other explanation that was even plausible. In fact, all other theories were ridiculous and clearly refuted, except for the one that champions the power of attraction <note>original: *holkē* — the "drawing" or "pulling" power of a substance</note>.

The phenomenon is as follows. When our local farmers bring <margin>56</margin> wheat <note>original: *pyrous* — specifically grains of wheat</note> || from the fields into the city in wagons, and they wish to steal some of it without being caught, they fill certain ceramic jars with water and bury them in the middle of the grain. The grains then draw the moisture to themselves through the ceramic vessel, thereby increasing in volume and weight. They do not appear at all suspicious to onlookers, unless someone who is already aware of the trick examines them quite carefully. 

And yet, if you chose to place that same vessel in the very hot sun, you would find that the amount of water lost each day is absolutely minimal. Thus, it appears that wheat possesses a power to draw nearby moisture into itself that is even stronger than the intense heat of the sun. Therefore, all that talk about the "tendency toward fine-particles" <note>Galen is mocking a mechanist theory that suggested fluids move only because they break down into tiny parts and drift into empty spaces, rather than being "pulled" by a specific force</note> of the surrounding air—especially when it is sufficiently warm—is nothing but long-winded nonsense...

...illustration afforded by *grain* <note>original: *pyros* — specifically wheat grains. Galen uses this common agricultural example to ground his complex biological theories.</note>? For those who refuse to admit that anything is attracted by anything else will, I imagine, be proved here to be more ignorant regarding Nature than the very farmers. For my own part, when I first learned of what happens, I was surprised and felt anxious to see it with my own eyes. Afterwards, when experience also had confirmed its truth, I sought for a long time among the various philosophical schools <note>Galen is likely referring to the Erasistrateans and Epicureans, who sought to explain all biological functions through mechanical means rather than "faculties" or powers.</note> for an explanation. With the exception of the theory that gave the primary role to **attraction**, I could find no explanation that even approached plausibility; all the others were ridiculous and obviously quite untenable.

What happens, then, is the following. When our farmers are bringing grain from the country into the city in wagons and wish to steal <note>original: *hyphairesis* — to secretly take away or pilfer.</note> some of it without being detected, they fill ceramic jars with water and stand them in the middle of the grain. The grain then draws the moisture into itself through the jar and acquires additional bulk and weight. This fact is never detected by the onlookers unless someone who already knew about the trick makes a very careful inspection. 

Yet, if you were to set down that same vessel in the very hot sun, you would find the daily loss of water to be very little indeed <note>Galen argues that the "specific attraction" of the grain for the water is a more powerful force than the sun’s power of evaporation.</note>. <margin>57</margin> Since we have trifled enough <note>original: *ēdoleschēsamen* — to engage in idle talk or gossip. For surely, either the urine is carried to the kidneys of its own accord, because it thinks this is the better course—just as we go off to the marketplace—or, if this is impossible, some other cause for its motion must be discovered. What, then, is this cause? For if we do not grant the kidneys some **attractive faculty** <note>original: *dynamis helktikē* — a natural power to pull or draw specific substances toward itself. This is the cornerstone of Galen’s physiology.</note> for this specific quality [of urine], as Hippocrates believed, we shall find no other explanation. 

For it is clear to everyone that it is necessary either that these [the kidneys] attract it, or that the veins send it—that is, if it does not move of its own accord. If this is impossible—as we shall demonstrate—it remains that the kidneys must attract it.

# XV

Since, then, we have talked sufficient nonsense <note>original: *edoleschēsamen* — to engage in idle chatter. Galen is being self-deprecating, suggesting he only entertained these absurd arguments to show how ridiculous his opponents were.</note>—not willingly, but because we were forced, as the proverb says, **“to behave madly among madmen”**—let us return again to the subject of urinary secretion. Here let us forget the absurdities of Asclepiades <note>Asclepiades of Bithynia was a physician who denied the existence of natural "faculties," preferring to explain the body through atoms and pores.</note>, and, in company with those who are persuaded that the urine does pass through the kidneys, let us consider what is the character of this function <note>original: *energeia* — the active operation or "work" of an organ.</note>. 

For, most assuredly, either the urine is conveyed by its own motion to the kidneys, because it considers this the better course <note>Galen is using irony here to suggest the absurdity of fluids having their own free will.</note>—just as we go off to the marketplace—or, if this be impossible, then some other reason for its conveyance must be found. What, then, is this? If we are not going to grant the kidneys a **faculty for attracting** <note>original: *dynamis helktikē* — the natural power of an organ to pull specific substances to itself.</note> this particular quality <note>This refers to "specific attraction," a key Galenic concept where an organ recognizes and pulls in the specific fluid it is designed to process. See also page 87.</note>, as Hippocrates held, we shall discover no other reason. 

For, surely everyone sees that either the kidneys must attract the urine, or the veins must propel it—if, that is, it does not move of itself. But if the veins did exert a propulsive action when they contract, they would squeeze out into the kidneys not merely the urine, but along with it the whole of the blood which they contain <note>In other words, if it were just a matter of mechanical pressure, the kidneys would be full of blood, not just filtered urine, because the veins would have no way to "select" which fluid to push.</note>. And if this is impossible, as we shall show, the remaining explanation is that the kidneys do exert **traction** <note>original: *holkē* — the act of drawing or pulling.</note>.

## XVI

<term>Erasistratus: a third-century BCE Greek anatomist who often sought mechanical explanations for bodily functions</term>, however, for some reason I do not know, spoke at great length against certain other foolish opinions, but completely bypassed that of **Hippocrates**. > “My noble friend, do not run us down with rhetoric lacking proof, but state some specific charge against the doctrine, so that we may either be convinced by your successful refutation of the ancient teaching, or we may change your mind [in return]...”

Or why is it that, after stating right at the beginning of his general discourse that he would speak about the **natural activities**—first what they are, then how they occur and through which locations—on the matter of the secretion of urine, he declared that it was through the kidneys, but left out the *how*?
