# ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, Book I, Section xvii.

...they suffer and assume all sorts of guises in their attempt to find some plausible cause that does not require the faculty of **attraction** <term>attraction <gloss>original: *holke* — the magnetic-like power Galen believes organs use to "pull" what they need from the blood.</gloss></term>.

Those who lived close to the time of **Erasistratus** <note>A famous 3rd-century BCE Greek anatomist and royal physician who often sought mechanical explanations for bodily functions.</note> claim that the parts of the body located above the kidneys receive pure blood, while the **watery waste** <term>watery waste <gloss>original: *hydatodes perittoma* — the excess fluid left over after the liver has processed food into blood.</gloss></term>, because it possesses weight, sinks and flows downward. They argue that this fluid is filtered here, at the kidneys themselves, and that the blood—having thus become pure—is then sent to all the parts below the kidneys.

For a certain time, this opinion was held in high regard; it flourished and was considered true. However, after some time, it began to look suspicious even to the **Erasistrateans** <note>The followers of Erasistratus's school of medical thought.</note> themselves, and they eventually abandoned it. For they seemed to be making two assumptions that were not granted by anyone and could not be proven. First, they assumed the weight of the **serous moisture** <note>original: *orrhodous hygrotetos* — the whey-like, watery part of the blood.</note> <margin>69</margin> || was generated in the **great hollow vein** <note>original: *koile phleps* — known today as the vena cava, the largest vein in the body.</note> as if it had not existed from the very beginning, when it was being carried up from the stomach to the **liver** <note>original: *hepar*.</note>. Why, then, did it not flow downward immediately in those regions? And how could anyone think it reasonable to say that this watery moisture aids in the **distribution of nutrients** <term>distribution <gloss>original: *anadosis* — the process by which the products of digestion are delivered from the gut to the rest of the body.</gloss></term> if it is indeed so heavy?

The second absurdity is that, even if one grants that all this fluid is carried downward and through no other channel but the hollow vein, it is difficult—or rather, impossible—to say how it will fall into the kidneys. For the kidneys do not lie at the bottom of that vein, but are situated at its sides. Furthermore, the hollow vein does not grow directly into them; it only sends a certain **offshoot** <note>Galen is referring to the renal veins, which branch off the vena cava. # ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, Book I, Section xvii

...or try any shift in order to find some plausible explanation which does not demand the principle of **attraction** <term>attraction <gloss>original: *holke* — the biological power Galen believes organs possess to "pull" or "draw" specific nutrients and fluids toward themselves.</gloss></term>.

Now, those who lived near the times of **Erasistratus** <note>A prominent 3rd-century BCE Greek physician and anatomist who favored mechanical explanations for how the body works.</note> maintain that the parts of the body above the kidneys receive pure blood, while the **watery residue** <note>original: *hydatodes perittoma* — the excess fluid left over after digestion.</note>, being heavy, tends to run downwards. They claim that this fluid, after percolating through the kidneys themselves, is thus rendered serviceable, and is sent, as blood, to all the parts below the kidneys.

For a certain period at least, this view also found favor and flourished, and was held to be true; after a time, however, it became suspect to the **Erasistrateans** <note>The medical followers of Erasistratus.</note> themselves, and at last they abandoned it. For apparently the following two points were assumed, neither of which is conceded by anyone, nor is even capable of being proved. The first is the heaviness of the **serous fluid** <term>serous fluid <gloss>original: *orrhodes hygrotis* — the thin, watery, or "whey-like" part of the blood.</gloss></term>, which was said to be produced in the **vena cava** <note>original: *koile phleps* — the "hollow vein," known today as the largest vein returning blood to the heart.</note>, and which did not exist, apparently, at the beginning, when this fluid was being carried up from the stomach to the liver. Why, then, did it not at once run downwards when it was in these situations? And if the watery fluid is so heavy, what plausibility can anyone find in the statement that it assists in the process of **distribution** <term>distribution <gloss>original: *anadosis* — the movement of nutrients from the digestive tract into the veins and up to the liver.</gloss></term>?

In the second place there is this absurdity, that even if it be agreed that all the watery fluid does fall downwards, and only when it is in the vena cava <note>As opposed to an earlier stage, when it is still on its way from the alimentary canal to the liver.</note>, still it is difficult, or, rather, impossible, to say through what means it is going to fall into the kidneys, seeing that these are not situated below, but on either side of the vena cava, and that the vena cava is not inserted into them, but merely sends a branch <note>Referring to what we now call the renal vein.</note> to each.

...these people [pass urine] quickly, and in a quantity not much less than what they drink. ...son. It is well known that people who drink heavily pass urine quickly, and in a quantity nearly equal to what they have consumed. He is, as the proverb goes, like a **white crow** <note>An ancient Greek idiom describing someone who is a misfit or an oddity that doesn't belong to any known group.</note>; he cannot fit in with the real crows because of his color, nor with the pigeons because of his size. Nevertheless, we should not ignore him; he might be proposing some brilliant truth that escaped all those who came before him.

Now, everyone agrees that all parts of the body produce a certain amount of **waste** <term>waste <gloss>original: "perittoma" — often translated as residue or superfluity; the leftover material after an organ has finished absorbing nutrients from the blood.</gloss></term> while they are being nourished. However, it is neither agreed upon, nor even likely, that the kidneys—which are quite small—could produce four whole **gallons** <term>gallons <gloss>original: "congii" — plural of "congius," a Roman liquid measure roughly equal to 3 liters or 6 pints. Four "congii" would be approximately 12 quarts.</gloss></term>, or even more, of waste.

For instance, if the waste from the lung were proportional to its size, it would be many times greater than that of the kidneys. This would cause the entire **chest cavity** <term>chest cavity <gloss>original: "thorax"</gloss></term> to fill up with fluid, and the animal would immediately suffocate. 

But if one argues that the amount of waste is actually the same in every organ regardless of size, we must ask: where are the other bladders to drain it? If the kidneys of a heavy drinker produce three or four **gallons** of waste, and every other organ produces just as much, the body would need a barrel of enormous size to hold all its waste products.

...waste products. And yet, quite often, someone urinates almost as much as they have drunk, as though the entire drink were being carried straight to the **kidneys**.

It seems, then, that this third attempt at deception achieves nothing; it is immediately exposed, and the original difficulty remains for **Erasistratus** <note>A famous 3rd-century BCE physician who rejected the idea of "faculties" and tried to explain body functions through mechanical means.</note> and everyone else—except for **Hippocrates**. I am dwelling on this topic by choice, knowing full well that no one else has anything meaningful to say about the **activity** <term>activity <gloss>original: "energeia" — the specific function or "work" an organ performs.</gloss></term> of the kidneys. Furthermore, if the flow of urine is not caused by the principle of **filling a vacuum** <note>original: "tē pros to kenoumenon akolouthia" — literally "following toward that which is being emptied." More will be said on these matters in the book that follows.

Yet, we often see that a person **urinates** almost exactly the same amount they have **drunk**. This clearly shows that everything one drinks eventually makes its way to the **kidneys**.

So, the author of this third attempt at **deception** <note>Galen is mocking the convoluted theories of Erasistratus, who tried to explain bodily functions through mechanical physics rather than biological "powers."</note> seems to have achieved nothing; they have been caught in the act. We are still left with the same problem that **Erasistratus** and everyone else failed to solve—everyone, that is, except for **Hippocrates**. I am focusing on this point intentionally. I know very well that no one else has anything useful to say about the **function** <term>function <gloss>original: "energeia" — the specific "work" or active power an organ performs.</gloss></term> of the kidneys. But if blood and bile move this way, then urine must too. For all these processes must happen in the same way, as even **Erasistratus** himself would have to agree.

...speaking of the distribution of food, so that it did not even escape the notice of Asclepiades <note>Asclepiades of Bithynia (c. 124–40 BCE), a physician who rejected the theory of four humors and proposed that the body is composed of "atoms" and "pores."</note>. But Asclepiades says it is not one of two, but one of three things that must follow in the case of emptied vessels: either a vacuum is created all at once, or the contiguous fluid follows, or the vessel itself will contract. # ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, II. i

...since the bile-collecting vessels are narrower, it follows that the bile fits into these narrower vessels and openings, while the blood fits into the wider ones. ### III

The entire hypothesis of **pores** <note>original: *porōn*. These refer to the ducts, canals, or conduits through which fluids were thought to flow mechanically.</note> is therefore nothing but long-winded nonsense when it comes to explaining **natural activity** <term>natural activity (physiken energeian): the functional work performed by an organ, such as digestion or filtration</term>. For if a certain **innate faculty** <term>innate faculty (dynamis symphytos): a power or ability built into an organ by nature from the moment of its formation</term> were not granted by Nature to each of the organs right from the very beginning, animals would not be able to survive—I do not mean for such a great number of years, but not even for a few days. 

Indeed, if we were to leave them untended, destitute of both **artistry** <note>original: *technē*. Galen views the body as a work of "artistic skill" or craftsmanship by Nature.</note> and providence, navigated only by the shifting weights of their matter, and without any power anywhere—one faculty **drawing in** <gloss>attracting</gloss> what is appropriate to itself, another **pushing out** <gloss>expelling</gloss> what is foreign, and another **altering** <gloss>transforming</gloss> and attaching that which will provide nourishment—I do not know how we could avoid being made a laughingstock when we discuss **natural activities**, and even more so when we discuss <margin>81</margin> the **activities of the soul** <note>original: *psychikōn*. These refer to voluntary movements and sensory perceptions, which Galen distinguishes from "natural" autonomic functions.</note> and, indeed, the whole of life itself.

For it will be impossible for any living creature to live or endure for even the shortest time if, possessing within itself so many parts and such diverse ones, it uses neither a power for **attracting** its own proper fluids, nor one for **separating** those that are foreign, nor one for **altering** those that will provide nourishment. Truly, if we possess these faculties, we no longer have any need of **pores**—whether small or large, assumed through an unproven hypothesis—to explain the separation of urine and bile. Nor do we need to rely <insert>only</insert> on a "favorable position." In this one matter, **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus of Ceos (3rd century BCE). Galen often criticizes him for trying to explain the body as a machine made of pipes and valves rather than as a living system of powers.</note> seems to be thinking clearly: that all things were well-placed and well-formed...

## III

<margin>Is this a theory of creation?</margin>
Thus, every hypothesis involving **channels** <note>original: *porōn*. These are the microscopic "pores" or conduits that mechanical physicians used to explain the movement of fluids without invoking biological "powers."</note> as an explanation of natural functioning is perfect nonsense. For, if there were not an **inborn faculty** <term>inborn faculty: an inherent biological power (dynamis symphytos) given by Nature to an organ to perform its specific work</term> given by Nature to each one of the organs at the very beginning, then animals could not continue to live even for a few days, far less for the number of years which they actually do. 

For let us suppose they were under no guardianship, lacking in **creative artistry** <note>original: *technē*. Galen views Nature as a skilled craftsman who designs the body with "forethought" (pronoia).</note> and forethought; let us suppose they were steered only by **material forces** <note>original: *rhopai*. This refers to the mechanical momentum or "tilt" of physical matter, moving purely by weight or pressure.</note>, and not by any special faculties—the one **attracting** <gloss>drawing in</gloss> what is proper to it, another **rejecting** <gloss>expelling</gloss> what is foreign, and yet another causing **alteration** <gloss>transformation</gloss> and adhesion of the matter destined to nourish it—if we suppose this, I am sure it would be ridiculous for us to discuss natural activities, or, still more, **activities of the soul** <note>original: *psychikai energeiai*; Latin: *actio animalis*. These are the higher functions of the spirit or mind, which Galen distinguishes from the "natural" functions like digestion.</note>, or, in fact, life as a whole.

For there is not a single animal which could live or endure for the shortest time if, possessing within itself so many different parts, it did not employ faculties which were attractive of what is appropriate, eliminative of what is foreign, and alterative of what is destined for nutrition. On the other hand, if we have these faculties, we no longer need "channels," little or big, resting on an unproven hypothesis, for explaining the secretion of urine and bile. We also do not need the concept of a **favourable situation** <note>original: *eukairia*. A term used by Erasistratus to suggest that fluids go to certain organs simply because the organs are "well-placed" to receive them.</note>—which is the only point where **Erasistratus** <note>A famous Greek physician (c. 304–250 BCE) who founded a school of anatomy in Alexandria; he was Galen’s primary intellectual rival regarding the mechanical versus biological nature of the body.</note> shows some common sense, since he does regard all the parts of the body as distinct entities...

# GALEN

...believing the parts of the body to have been [formed] by Nature.

But if he were to be consistent with himself in calling **Nature artistic** <note>original: *physin techniken*. Galen views Nature as a purposive, intelligent force—like a craftsman—rather than a random mechanical process.</note>—first, from the very beginning, beautifully molding and arranging all the parts of the living creature; and after this activity, since nothing was lacking, bringing it forth into the light equipped with certain **faculties** <gloss>innate biological powers</gloss> without which it could not survive; and then gradually increasing its size until it reaches the proper proportions—if he believes all this, I do not see how he can bear <margin>82</margin> to entrust **natural activities** to the smallness or largeness of **pores** <note>original: *porōn*. These are the microscopic channels that mechanical physicians used to explain fluid movement, avoiding any mention of biological "attraction."</note> || or to any other such nonsensical hypotheses. 

For that Nature which molds the parts and increases them gradually must surely be extended throughout the whole of them; for she molds, nourishes, and increases them **through and through** <gloss>entirely from within</gloss>, not just from the outside. 

**Praxiteles** or **Phidias** <note>Two of the most celebrated sculptors of ancient Greece, famous for their lifelike statues of gods and heroes.</note>, or any other **sculptor** <term>sculptor: literally an 'image-maker' (agalmatopoios)</term>, only decorated their materials from the outside, insofar as they were able to touch them. But they left the depths of the material unadorned, idle, unskilled, and unprovided for, because they were unable to descend into it, to dive deep, and to touch all parts of the **matter** <note>original: *hyle*. Galen uses this philosophical term for the raw substance that receives a shape.</note>.

Nature, however, does not act this way. Instead, she turns every bit of bone-matter into bone, every bit of flesh into flesh, and fat into fat, and so with every other part. For there is no part of the body that she cannot touch, nor any part left unworked or unadorned. But Phidias could not turn wax into ivory and gold, nor gold into wax; for each of these materials remained as it was from the beginning, merely clothed from the outside in some **form**...

<summary>Galen argues that Nature is a superior artist to human sculptors like Phidias because she transforms and shapes every internal part of a living being, rather than just the surface. He rejects mechanical explanations of life, such as the size of pores, in favor of internal "faculties" that permeate the entire body.</summary>

(having been well and truly placed and shaped by Nature).

But let us suppose he remained true to his own statement that **Nature is “artistic”** <note>original: *physin techniken*. Galen argues that Nature is not a random force but a skilled craftsman working with purpose.</note>—this Nature which, at the beginning, well and truly shaped and disposed all the parts of the animal <note>This refers to the stage of *diaplasis* or **organogenesis**, the biological process where an embryo's organs are first formed.</note>, and, after carrying out this function (for she left nothing undone), brought it forward to the light of day, endowed with certain **faculties** <gloss>innate biological powers</gloss> necessary for its very existence, and, thereafter, gradually increased it until it reached its due size. 

If he argued consistently on this principle, I fail to see how he can continue to refer natural functions to the smallness or largeness of **canals** <note>original: *porōn*. These are the same "pores" mentioned on the previous page; Galen is mocking the idea that health is just a matter of "plumbing."</note>, or to any other similarly absurd hypothesis. For this Nature which shapes and gradually adds to the parts is most certainly extended throughout their whole substance. Yes indeed, she shapes and nourishes and increases them **through and through** <gloss>entirely from within the material</gloss>, not on the outside only. 

For **Praxiteles** and **Phidias** <note>The most famous sculptors of ancient Greece, known for creating lifelike statues of the gods.</note> and all the other **statuaries** <term>statuaries: those who craft images or statues (agalmatopoioi)</term> used merely to decorate their material on the outside, in so far as they were able to touch it; but its inner parts they left unembellished, unwrought, unaffected by art or forethought, since they were unable to penetrate therein and to reach and handle all portions of the material. 

It is not so, however, with Nature. Every part of a bone she makes bone, every part of the flesh she makes flesh, and so with fat and all the rest; there is no part which she has not touched, elaborated, and embellished. Phidias, on the other hand, could not turn wax into ivory and gold, nor yet gold into wax: for each of these remains as it was at the commencement, and becomes a perfect statue...

<margin>83</margin> ...and an artistic form, it has become a **perfect statue**. <gloss>The embryo now becomes an “organism” proper, no longer just a collection of parts.</gloss> For Nature no longer preserves the original appearance of any of the materials; if she did, all the parts of the animal would be simply **blood**—the blood which flows from the mother to the seed <note>original: *sperma*. Galen uses this term for the formative substance provided by the parents that begins the growth of the embryo.</note>, serving as a single, uniform material provided to the craftsman, much like a lump of wax. Who was it, then, that altered, solidified, and shaped these parts? I would have wanted **Erasistratus** <note>A famous 3rd-century BCE physician whom Galen often critiques for being too mechanical in his views on biology.</note> himself to answer me. Surely he would have said it was either "Nature" or "the Seed," meaning the same thing in both cases, though expressed through different concepts. For that which was previously the seed becomes a kind of **Nature** <note>original: *physis*. To Galen, "Nature" is the internal force that guides growth and function.</note> once it begins to grow and shape the animal. Just as Phidias possessed the powers of his art even before he touched his material, but only exercised them upon the material—for every power remains idle when it lacks its proper matter—so too 

<margin>84</margin> the seed possessed its **faculties** <gloss>Galen attributed to the *sperma* or seed what we should today call genetic or formative potential.</gloss> from the beginning, but it did not receive its active energies from the material; rather, it demonstrated them upon the material.

Furthermore, if the seed were to be overwhelmed by too much blood, it would be destroyed; but if it should lack it entirely...

...merely by being dressed on the outside with a particular shape and artistic form. But Nature does not keep the original character of any kind of material; if she did, then every part of the animal would be nothing but **blood**—specifically, that blood which flows toward the seed <note>original: *sperma*. Galen believes the maternal blood provides the "bricks" while the male seed provides the "architect."</note> from the mother. This blood is, so to speak, like the sculptor’s wax: a single, uniform material placed under the command of the craftsman. From this blood, none of the animal's final parts emerge as red and moist as the blood itself; for **bone, artery, vein, nerve, cartilage, fat, gland, membrane, and marrow** are not blood <gloss>they are non-sanguineous tissues</gloss>, even though they were created from it.

I would then ask **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus (c. 304–250 BCE) was a Greek anatomist and royal physician. He would undoubtedly say, "Either Nature or the seed," meaning the same thing in both cases, though describing it through different terms. For that which was previously seed becomes a kind of **special nature** <term>physis: the internal principle of growth and movement</term> once it begins to generate and shape the animal. 

Just as the great sculptor **Phidias** <note>Phidias was the most famous sculptor of Classical Greece, known for the Statue of Zeus at Olympia and the Parthenon's Athena.</note> possessed the skills of his art even before he touched his materials, and then put those skills into action when he had the material in hand (for every skill remains idle without its proper material), so it is with the seed: its **faculties** <term>dynamis: the inherent power or ability to perform a specific function</term> it possessed from the very beginning, but its activities do not come from the material itself—rather, it expresses those activities through the material.

And, of course, if the seed were to be overwhelmed by too great a quantity of blood, it would be destroyed; whereas, if it were to be entirely deprived of blood...

...if it were entirely inactive, Nature would not exist. Who then is it that measures the volume of this inflow? Who is it that prevents too much from entering? Who urges it on, so that it does not fall short? What "third overseer" of the animal's creation shall we look for here to provide the seed with the proper amount of blood? What would **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus was a famous physician who viewed the body more like a machine; Galen frequently critiques him for ignoring the "faculties" or powers of nature.</note> have said, if he had been asked these questions while he was alive? Therefore, it is not fitting for the wax to determine its own proportions, but for Phidias to do so. The craftsman will draw to himself exactly as much blood as <margin>85</margin> he needs. But at this point, we must pay close attention and consider whether we might accidentally grant the seed some form of **reasoning** <gloss>rational thought or logic</gloss> and a mind; for if we did that, we would not be making "seed" or "nature," but rather a fully-formed living creature. <note>1</note> And yet, if we are to maintain both points—the attraction of the proper amount and the absence of reasoning—we must say that a certain **power** exists in the seed that draws blood to it, just as the **magnet stone** <note>original: *lithos*; referring to the lodestone, a naturally magnetized mineral.</note> has a power that attracts iron. <note>2</note> We are forced then, here as many times before, to admit that a certain **attractive faculty** <term>helktike dynamis: the biological power of an organ or tissue to "pull" or attract the specific nutrients it needs</term> exists within the seed.

What then was the seed? It is clearly the **active principle** of the living creature; for the **material principle** is the menstrual blood <note>Galen follows the Aristotelian view that the male seed provides the "form" or "spark," while the female provides the "matter" or "fuel" for the embryo.</note>. Then, since this principle is the first to use this power so that one of its own creations may come to be, it is impossible for it to be devoid of its own specific power. How then is it that **Erasistratus** <note>A 3rd-century BC physician who often disagreed with the idea of "innate powers," preferring mechanical explanations.</note> does not know of it, if indeed this first activity of the seed is to draw a proportionate amount of blood to itself?

A "proportionate" amount would be so thin and vapor-like that, as soon as it is drawn into every part of the <margin>86</margin> seed, it would be like **dew** <note>original: *drosoeidōs*</note> and would nowhere || reveal its own appearance. For in this way the seed will easily master it, quickly assimilate it, and turn it into nourishment for itself; and then, I suppose, it will draw in a second and third amount, so as to produce a noteworthy bulk and volume for itself as it is nourished. 

And indeed, the **alterative power** <term>alterative power: the biological faculty that changes the quality or nature of a substance, such as turning blood into tissue</term> has already been discovered, though it too was not written of by Erasistratus. Third would appear the **formative power** <term>formative power: the faculty that shapes and structures the body into specific organs and membranes</term>, by which the seed first surrounds itself with a certain thin, ice-like membrane—the one mentioned by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous 5th-century BC physician whom Galen deeply revered.</note> regarding the six-day-old embryo, which he said fell out of the **dancing girl** <note>original: *mousourgos*—referring to a famous case in the Hippocratic treatise *On the Nature of the Child* where a performer miscarried a six-day-old embryo that looked like a raw egg without its shell.</note>, and which resembled the membrane of an egg. After this come all the other structures mentioned by him in his treatise *On the Nature of the Child* <note>original: *Peri physios paidiou*</note>.

But if each of these formed parts remained as small as it was at the beginning, what would be the gain? Therefore, they must **grow**. How then...

And what then is the **seed**? <note>original: *sperma*</note> It is clearly the **active principle** <note>The "active principle" is the driving force or designer of a living thing, as opposed to the "material principle" which is the raw stuff it is made of.</note> of the living creature, while the material principle is the **menstrual blood**. Next, since the active principle employs this power first and foremost, it must necessarily possess its own specific power so that any of the things it fashions can come into being. How then could **Erasistratus** <note>A 3rd-century BC physician who preferred mechanical explanations of the body and often rejected Galen’s idea of "innate powers."</note> be unaware of this, if the primary function of the seed is to draw a proportionate amount of blood to itself? 

Now, this fluid would be in the right proportion if it were so thin and vapor-like that, as soon as it were drawn like **dew** into every part of the seed, it would completely lose its own original character. In this way, the seed will easily master it and quickly **assimilate** it—essentially using it as nourishment. It will then, I imagine, draw in a second and then a third portion, and by feeding in this way, it gains significant size and volume.

In fact, we have now discovered the **alterative power** <term>alterative power: the biological faculty that changes the qualities or nature of a substance, such as turning blood into the specific tissue of an organ</term> as well, though Erasistratus did not write a single word about this either. Third, the **formative power** <term>formative power: also called the shaping faculty; the ability of the seed to "carve out" and structure the body into its proper shape</term> will become clear. By virtue of this power, the seed first wraps itself in a thin membrane, like a kind of surface hardening. This is what **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460–370 BC) whom Galen viewed as the ultimate medical authority.</note> described in the case of the "six-day birth"—which, according to his account, was expelled by a **singing-girl** and resembled the membrane of an egg. <note>Galen refers to a famous passage in the Hippocratic work *On the Nature of the Child*, describing an early miscarriage observed in a dancer/performer.</note> Following this, all the other stages of development will occur, just as he describes in his work *On the Nature of the Child*.

But if each of the formed parts were to stay as small as when they first appeared, what use would that be? They must, therefore, grow.

...how else then will it **increase**? It does so by being simultaneously **distended** <note>Distension here refers to the physical stretching or expansion of the tissues from within.</note> and **nourished** in every direction. If you recall what I said earlier regarding the **bladder** <note>original: *kystis*</note> which children blow up and rub, you will better understand this from what I am about to say.

For imagine the **heart** to be so small at the beginning that it differs not at all from a **millet seed** or, if you prefer, a **bean**. Ask yourself how it could ever become large unless it were nourished and distended in every direction throughout its whole self—just as I showed a moment ago how the seed is nourished. <margin>87</margin> But even this **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus (3rd century BC) was a pioneering anatomist who often sought mechanical explanations for bodily functions, which Galen found insufficient to explain life.</note> does not know, despite his "hymning" the artistry of **Nature** <note>original: *physis*</note>. Instead, he believes that living creatures grow like a **sieve**, a **rope**, a **sack**, or a **wicker basket**. In each of these, an "addition" <note>original: *prothesis*</note> occurs as the person who is putting them together weaves on similar parts at the ends of the original structure.

But this, O "wisest one," is not **growth** but **generation** <term>generation (genesis): for Galen, this is the initial creation or assembly of a structure, whereas "growth" is the expansion of an already formed structure</term>. For a sack, a garment, a house, a ship, or any other such thing is in the process of "being generated" as long as its proper **form** <note>original: *eidos*</note>—the very thing the craftsman is building it for—has not yet been completed. When then does it "grow"? Only when the basket is already complete—having its bottom, its mouth, its "belly," and the parts in between—and then all of these parts become larger. <margin>88</margin> "And how can this be?" someone might ask. How else, indeed, than if the basket were suddenly to become a **living animal** or a **plant**? For **growth** <term>growth (auxesis): the internal expansion and nourishment of a living thing that has already achieved its basic form</term> belongs to living things alone. But you, perhaps, think a house grows while it is being built...

Now, how will they **grow**? By becoming **extended** <note>or distended; the physical stretching of tissue from within</note> in all directions and at the same time receiving **nourishment**. And if you will recall what I previously said about the **bladder** <note>original: kystis</note> which the children blew up and rubbed, you will also understand my meaning better through what I am now about to say.

Imagine the **heart** to be, at the beginning, so small as to differ in no respect from a **millet-seed**, or, if you will, a **bean**; and consider how else it is to become large than by being extended in all directions and acquiring nourishment throughout its whole substance—in the same way that I showed a short while ago how the **semen** <note>original: sperma</note> is nourished. But this, most sapient sir, is not **growth**, but **generation**! <term>generation (genesis): for Galen, this is the initial creation or assembly of a structure, whereas "growth" is the expansion of an already formed structure.</term> For a bag, sack, garment, house, ship, or the like is said to be still coming into existence <gloss>undergoing genesis</gloss> so long as the appropriate form—for the sake of which it is being constructed by the **artificer** <note>Galen often compares Nature to a divine craftsman or artist.</note>—is still incomplete. When, then, does it grow? Only when the **basket**, being complete with a bottom, a mouth, and a belly, as it were, as well as the intermediate parts, now becomes larger in all these respects. “And how can this happen?” someone will ask. Only by our basket suddenly becoming an **animal** or a **plant**; for growth belongs to **living things** alone. Possibly you imagine that a **house** grows when it is being built, or a **basket** when being...

...long as the **basket** <note>original: talaros</note> is being woven and the **cloak** <note>original: hoimation</note> is being made. For that which **exists** grows, but that which **does not yet exist** comes into being.

### IV

And **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus (3rd century BC) was a famous Greek physician whose mechanical explanations for biology Galen frequently attacked.</note> is ignorant of these things—he, from whom nothing is supposed to escape, if indeed those of his school speak the truth when they claim he studied with the **Peripatetic** philosophers <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking in the "peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum in Athens.</note>. Now, as far as praising **Nature** <note>original: physis</note> as being full of **artistic skill** <note>original: technikē; the idea that nature works like a craftsman with a purpose</note>, I too recognize the doctrines of the Peripatetics; but in other matters, he is not even close. For if one were to consult the writings of **Aristotle** and **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus was Aristotle's successor as the head of the Peripatetic school.</note>, they would seem like commentaries on the **physiology** of **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine" (5th century BC), whom Galen considers the ultimate authority on medical science.</note>. 

<margin>89</margin> The **hot**, the **cold**, || and the **dry**, and the **wet** acting upon and being affected by one another—and of these very things, the **hot** is the most active, while the **cold** is second in its power—all these things were said first by Hippocrates, and second by Aristotle. Furthermore, that those things which are **nourished** are nourished through their whole substance, and that those which are **mixed** are mixed through their whole substance, and that those which are **altered** are altered through their whole substance—these are also doctrines held by both Hippocrates and Aristotle. And that **digestion** <note>original: pepsis; often likened to a "cooking" process in the body</note> is a kind of **alteration**...

# ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, II. III.-IV

->139<-

...plaited, or a garment when being woven? It is not so, however. **Growth** <note>original: auxēsis</note> belongs to that which has already been completed in respect to its **form** <note>original: eidos; the specific shape and structural identity of an organ</note>, whereas the process by which that which is still ***becoming*** attains its form is termed not growth but ***genesis*** <term>genesis: often translated as "generation" or "coming into being," this refers to the initial biological assembly of an organism or part.</term>. That which **exists** grows, while that which **does not yet exist** becomes.

### IV

This also was unknown to **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus (c. 304–250 BC) was a renowned Greek physician in Alexandria whom Galen frequently critiques for his "mechanical" views on the body.</note>, whom nothing escaped—if indeed his followers speak in any way truly in maintaining that he was familiar with the **Peripatetic** philosophers <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school, known for studying the natural world through observation and logic.</note>. Now, in so far as he acclaims **Nature** <note>original: physis</note> as being an artist in construction, even I recognize the Peripatetic teachings, but in other respects he does not come near them. 

For if anyone will make himself acquainted with the writings of **Aristotle** and **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus was the successor to Aristotle and a significant figure in early botanical and biological study.</note>, these will appear to him to consist of commentaries on the **Nature-lore** <term>physiology (physiologia): literally "knowledge of nature," referring to the study of how the body functions.</term> of **Hippocrates**—according to which the principles of **heat, cold, dryness and moisture** <note>The "four qualities" that formed the basis of ancient medicine; health was seen as a balance of these four.</note> act upon and are acted upon by one another, the hot principle being the most active, and the cold coming next to it in power; all this was stated in the first place by Hippocrates and secondly by Aristotle. 

Further, it is at once the Hippocratic and the Aristotelian teaching that the parts which are being nourished receive that nourishment throughout their whole substance, and that, similarly, processes of ***mingling*** and ***alteration*** involve the entire substance. <note>For definitions of *alteration* (change in quality) and *mingling* (original: *crasis*, often translated as "temperament" or "mixture"), see Book I, chapters ii and iii.</note> Moreover, that **digestion** is a species of...

# ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, BOOK II

->140<-

...there exists a transformation of the nourishing substance into the specific quality of the body being nourished; that **blood-making** <term>blood-making: Greek "exaimatōsis," the process by which food is turned into blood.</term> is an **alteration** <note>original: "alloiōsis"; a fundamental change in the properties of a substance, not just a rearrangement of parts.</note>, as is nutrition; that **growth** results from expansion in all directions combined with nutrition; and that this alteration is accomplished chiefly by **natural heat**. It is because of this heat that digestion, nutrition, and the generation of all the **humors** <note>The four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> occur. Furthermore, even the qualities found in waste products are produced by this innate heat. All these points—and many others besides—concerning the aforementioned faculties, the <margin>90</margin> || origin of diseases, and the discovery of remedies, were first stated correctly by **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BC), whom Galen considers his greatest authority.</note> and later explained correctly by **Aristotle**. 

Now, if all these principles are accepted by the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school.</note>, as indeed they are, yet none of them please **Erasistratus**, what do his followers mean by boasting of their leader’s "association" with those philosophers? For they revere Erasistratus as a god and believe everything he says is the truth. But if this is so, they must surely believe that the Peripatetic philosophers have strayed far from the truth, since nothing that Erasistratus supposed is pleasing to them. And yet, they try to secure a kind of "nobility" for his system of **physiology** <note>original: "physiologia"; the study of how nature and the body function.</note> by claiming he was a student of those very men.

Let us, then, turn the argument around in a different way than we did just a moment ago. For if the Peripatetics were correct in their physiology, then nothing could be more nonsensical than Erasistratus. I leave the choice to the followers of Erasistratus themselves:

### ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, II. iv

->141<-

**alteration** <term>alteration: Greek "alloiōsis," a qualitative change where a substance transforms into something else, like food turning into flesh.</term>—a transmutation of the nutriment into the proper quality of the thing receiving it; that **blood-production** <term>blood-production: "exaimatōsis," the specific process of turning digested food into blood.</term> also is an alteration, and nutrition as well; that **growth** results from extension in all directions, combined with nutrition; that alteration is effected mainly by the **warm principle** <note>Also known as "innate heat," this was considered the vital energy that drives all biological processes.</note>, and that therefore digestion, nutrition, and the generation of the various **humours** <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance determined health.</note>, as well as the qualities of the surplus substances <note>Waste products like urine or bile.</note>, result from the **innate heat**;¹ all these and many other points besides in regard to the aforesaid faculties, the origin of diseases, and the discovery of remedies, were correctly stated first by **Hippocrates** of all writers whom we know, and were in the second place correctly expounded by **Aristotle**. 

Now, if all these views meet with the approval of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, named for the "peripatos" or covered walkway where they studied.</note>, as they undoubtedly do, and if none of them satisfy **Erasistratus**, what can the **Erasistrateans** <note>The medical sect following Erasistratus, who often favored mechanical explanations over Galen's vitalistic ones.</note> possibly mean by claiming that their leader was associated with these philosophers? The fact is, they revere him as a god, and think that everything he says is true. If this be so, then we must suppose the Peripatetics to have strayed very far from truth, since they approve of none of the ideas of Erasistratus. And, indeed, the disciples of the latter produce his connection with the Peripatetics in order to furnish his **Nature-lore** <term>Nature-lore: Greek "physiologia," the study of the laws of the natural world.</term> with a respectable pedigree.

Now, let us reverse our argument and put it in a different way from that which we have just employed. For if the Peripatetics were correct in their teaching about Nature, there could be nothing more absurd than the contentions of Erasistratus. And, I will leave it to the Erasistrateans themselves to decide;

<margin>91</margin> Either they will accept the former argument or this one. The first suggests that the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> understood nothing correctly about nature, while the second says the same of **Erasistratus** <note>A famous 3rd-century BC physician and anatomist whom Galen frequently critiques for his mechanical views of the body.</note>. For although there are countless physical doctrines regarding the **generation and decay** <note>The natural cycle of birth and death, or the formation and breaking down of matter.</note> of living creatures, as well as health, disease, and medical treatments, only one single point will be found where Erasistratus and those men agree: the principle that **nature does everything for a purpose and nothing in vain.**

According to his account, the **spleen** was created for no purpose, as was the **epiploon** <term>epiploon: Also known as the omentum, this is a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines like an apron.</term>, and the **arteries** that branch into the **kidneys**—which are almost the largest of all the branches stemming from the **great artery** <note>The aorta, the primary artery carrying blood from the heart.</note>. If he is entirely ignorant of these parts, then his knowledge of **anatomy** <note>The study of bodily structures through dissection.</note> is barely better than a cook's. But if he knows them and yet fails to explain their **function** <note>The Greek term is "chreia," meaning the specific "use" or utility of an organ within the body's design.</note>, <margin>92</margin> it is clear he believes they were created for no reason, just like his view of the spleen. But why do I dwell on these points now? They belong to my treatise *On the Use of Parts* <note>Galen refers here to his massive work, "De Usu Partium," which argues that every part of the body is perfectly designed by a divine Creator or "Nature."</note>, which I intend to complete as a separate work.

They must choose to advance one proposition or the other. According to the first, the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, who believed nature acts with design.</note> had no accurate understanding of nature; according to the second, it was **Erasistratus** <note>A famous 3rd-century BC physician and anatomist whom Galen frequently critiques for his mechanical views of the body.</note> who lacked it. It is my task, then, to point out the conflict between these two doctrines, and it is theirs to make the choice between them.

But they certainly will not abandon their reverence for Erasistratus. Very well, then; let them stop talking about the Peripatetic philosophers. For among the numerous physical teachings regarding the **generation and decay** <note>The natural process of biological birth, growth, and the breaking down of matter.</note> of animals, their health, their diseases, and the methods of treating them, there will be found only one single view common to both Erasistratus and the Peripatetics—namely, the principle that **Nature does everything for a purpose, and nothing in vain.**

But even regarding this doctrine, their agreement is only in words; in practice, Erasistratus violates it a thousand times over. For, according to him, the **spleen** was made for no purpose, as was the **omentum** <term>omentum: Also known as the epiploon, this is a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines like an apron.</term>; similarly, too, the **arteries** which are inserted into the **kidneys** <gloss>1</gloss>—although these are practically the largest of all those that spring from the **great artery** <note>original: "aorta"</note>! 

To judge by the Erasistratean argument, there must be countless other useless structures; for, if he knows nothing at all about these structures, he has little more anatomical knowledge than a butcher, while, if he is acquainted with them and yet does not state their use, he clearly imagines that they were made for no purpose, like the spleen. Why, however, should I discuss these structures fully here, belonging as they do to my treatise ***On the Use of Parts*** <note>original: "De Usu Partium," Galen’s major work arguing that every part of the body is perfectly designed by a divine Creator or Nature.</note>, which I am personally about to complete?

Let us then take up the same argument again, and after speaking briefly to the followers of **Erasistratus** <note>A 3rd-century BC physician who viewed the body as a mechanical system, often opposing the "vitalist" views of Galen.</note>, let us keep to the sequence of our topic. For it seems to me that these men have read none of **Aristotle’s** writings; instead, they have heard from others that the man was brilliant in the study of nature and that those of the **Stoa** <note>The Stoics, a school of philosophy founded by Zeno, who believed the universe was governed by rational divine providence.</note> follow in the footsteps of his physiology. Then, finding one of the common doctrines circulating in his name which happens to match Erasistratus, they have imagined some association between him and those great men. 

But the list of previously mentioned doctrines shows that Erasistratus has no share in Aristotle’s physiology. These doctrines belonged first to **Hippocrates** <note>The famous 5th-century BC physician of Cos; Galen considers him the ultimate authority on medicine.</note>, second to Aristotle, and third to the Stoics—with only one point being changed: the idea that qualities are actually bodies <note>original: "τὰς ποιότητας εἶναι σώματα" — Galen notes that the Stoics differed from Aristotle by arguing that physical qualities like "heat" were themselves material substances.</note>.

<margin>93</margin> Perhaps they might say that Erasistratus associated with the philosophers of the **Peripatos** <note>The Peripatetic school, the followers of Aristotle, named after the "covered walkway" (peripatos) where they studied.</note> for the sake of learning logical theory. They say this not knowing that while those philosophers never wrote false or inconclusive arguments, the books of Erasistratus are full of such things.

Perhaps, then, someone might already wonder and be at a loss to know what came over Erasistratus that he turned so far away from the doctrines of Hippocrates. Why is it that—for enough has already been said about the **kidneys**—he takes away the **attractive faculty** <term>attractive faculty: The biological power of an organ to "pull" or "draw" specific fluids to itself, such as the kidneys drawing urine from the blood.</term> from the bile-collecting pores in the **liver**, and instead blames their "convenient position" and the "mouths" of the vessels?

Is it then only in these matters that the reasoning of Erasistratus is caught in inescapable difficulties because he did not wish to make any use of **attracting powers** <note>original: "ἑλκτικαῖς δυνάμεσιν" — Galen’s core theory that organs have a natural, magnetic-like power to pull in the specific fluids they require.</note>? Or are these difficulties most severe and clear here, so as not to escape even a child's notice?

->VI<-

If one were to examine it carefully, his account of **nutrition** <note>original: "θρέψεως"</note>—which he discusses in the second book of his *General Principles*—does not escape these same difficulties. For once one premise was granted—that of **following what is emptied** <term>following what is emptied: known in Latin as *horror vacui*, this is Erasistratus's mechanical theory that fluids move into empty spaces to prevent a vacuum, rather than being "pulled" by a biological force</term>, as I showed before—he reached a conclusion only regarding the veins and the blood within them. For when something flows out...

Are these, then, the only inevitable difficulties in which the argument of Erasistratus becomes involved through his disinclination to make any use of the **attractive faculty** <note>Galen's theory that organs possess a natural power to "pull" or "attract" the specific fluids they require.</note>, or is it that the difficulty is greatest here, and also so obvious that even a child could not avoid seeing it?

### VI

AND if one looks carefully into the matter one will find that even Erasistratus’s reasoning on the subject of **nutrition** <note>original: "τροφῆς"</note>, which he takes up in the second book of his *General Principles*, fails to escape this same difficulty. For, having conceded one premise to the principle that **matter flows to fill a vacuum** <note>original: "πρὸς τὸ κενούμενον ἀκολουθία" — the physical concept that nature abhors a vacuum, used by Erasistratus to explain fluid movement.</note>, as we previously showed, he was only able to draw a conclusion in the case of the veins and their contained blood. That is to say, when...

# GALEN

...shapes, increases, and nourishes the animal. But among those "unfitted" and "indivisible" bodies <note>original: "anarmōn kai amerōn." These are terms for the atoms or particles proposed by thinkers like Epicurus or Asclepiades, which Galen rejects because they cannot change or merge.</note>, none possesses within itself a **formative faculty** <term>formative faculty: The biological power to shape or "model" organs and tissues (Greek: diaplastikēn).</term>, an **augmentative faculty** <term>augmentative faculty: The power that allows an organism to grow in size (Greek: auxētikēn).</term>, a **nutritive faculty** <term>nutritive faculty: The power to convert food into the substance of the body (Greek: threptikēn).</term>, or any artistic skill at all. This is because such a body is assumed to be **impassive** and **unchangeable**. 

None of the processes I have mentioned can occur without change, alteration, and a thorough "mixing" throughout the whole <note>original: "krāseōs." In Galenic medicine, "krasis" or temperament is the blending of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) to form a unified substance.</note>, as I demonstrated earlier. Because of this necessity, those belonging to such schools of thought—being unable to preserve the logical consequences of the elements they hypothesized—were forced to declare that **Nature is without art** <note>original: "atechnon... tēn physin." This was a major point of contention; Galen believed Nature acted with purposeful, artistic skill, whereas his rivals saw the body as a mindless machine.</note>. And yet, the **Erasistrateans** <term>Erasistrateans: Followers of Erasistratus (3rd century BCE), who viewed the body's functions as primarily mechanical and hydraulic.</term> should not have to learn this from me, but rather from those philosophers who believe one must first examine the primary "elements" of all existing things.

One would not rightly believe that **Erasistratus** himself reached such a level of ignorance as to be unable to recognize this logical consequence: that he was simultaneously hypothesizing that Nature is artistic, while also breaking down substance into impassive, <margin>102</margin> unfitted, and unchangeable elements. Indeed, if he allows for some alteration, change, union, and continuity within the elements, then that **"simple vessel"** <note>Erasistratus believed the "primary" building blocks of the body were tiny "simple" versions of veins, arteries, and nerves.</note>—as he calls it—will become a single, non-composite thing. In that case, the "simple vein" will be nourished by itself, while the nerve and the artery will receive their nourishment from the vein.

### THE FAILURE OF MECHANICAL REFILLING IN RECOVERY

...nor can the principle of the **filling of a vacuum** <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "akolouthia pros to kenoumenon," literally the sequence following that which is being emptied.</note> give them any help—both because of the difficulties previously mentioned and the actual **extreme thinness** <note>original: "ischnotēta," referring to the physical wasting or emaciation seen after illness.</note> of the body, as I shall demonstrate—we must then seek another cause for **nutrition** <term>nutrition: In Galenic medicine, this is "threpsis," the process by which food is converted into the actual substance of the organs.</term>.

Because its rule is that only as much of the contiguous matter should follow as has already flowed away. Now this is sufficient for nourishment in the case of those who are in **good health** <note>original: "euektountōn," referring to a state of bodily vigor or "good habit."</note>, for, in them, the **nutriment presented** <gloss>2</gloss> <note>original: "prostithemena." It is clear, therefore, that these parts will have to exert a greater amount of *attraction*, in so far as their requirements are greater.

It refers to the absorption of nutrients from the gut and their movement through the veins.</note> of nutriment?

### VIII

**Erasistratus** <note>A famous Greek anatomist and physician who lived centuries before Galen; Galen often admires his skill but hates his mechanical theories.</note> should not have been ignorant of these things, if he had ever—even in a dream—met with the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who emphasized the importance of logic and the "natural faculties" of living things.</note>. the **lodestone** <note>original: "lithos magnetis." Galen argues his opponents use a "false dilemma" by ignoring a third possibility (C).</note> used for the purposes of demonstration is, in reality, disjunctive not of two but of three alternatives; now, if we treat the disjunction as a disjunction of two alternatives, one of the two propositions assumed in constructing our proof must be false; and if as a disjunctive of three alternatives, no conclusion will be arrived at.

### VIII

Now **Erasistratus** <note>A famous 3rd-century BCE anatomist who Galen frequently critiques for his mechanical, non-teleological view of the body.</note> ought not to have been ignorant of this if he had ever had anything to do with the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who emphasized natural philosophy and the study of causes.</note>—even in a dream. Nor, similarly, should he have been unacquainted with the genesis of the <term>humours: the four essential bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) whose balance determined health</term>, about which, not having even anything moderately plausible to say, he thinks to deceive us by the excuse that the consideration of such matters is not the least useful. Then, in Heaven’s name, is it useful to know how food is digested in the stomach, but unnecessary to know how <term>bile</term> comes into existence?

He has not even deigned to offer a counter-argument—even though **Hippocrates**, **Diocles**, **Praxagoras**, and **Philistion** <note>These were the most famous physicians of the Classical and Hellenistic periods; Galen aligns himself with this "great tradition."</note>, as well as the very best philosophers including **Plato**, **Aristotle**, and **Theophrastus**, never looked down on these matters. <margin>111</margin> Whether they were right or not, all these men say that the affairs of all living creatures are governed by the **Hot, the Cold, the Dry, and the Wet** <note>The Four Qualities; the building blocks of Galen’s physiology.</note>—some of these acting as "active" forces and others as "passive." They also claim that the **Hot** has the greatest power within the body, both for other activities and especially for the generation of the **humors** <term>humors: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determined health</term>. Now, to refuse to be persuaded by so many great men, and to think that one knows more than they do, is perhaps not a cause for resentment; however, to not even deem such a famous doctrine worthy of a counter-argument or even a mention shows a truly amazing arrogance.

...the **dropsy** <term>dropsy: historically, an accumulation of fluid (edema); Galen believes it is caused by a failure of the body's internal heat to "cook" fluids into blood</term> which begins in the flanks or in any other susceptible part; this clearly confutes **Erasistratus’s** <note>Erasistratus (3rd century BCE) was a pioneering anatomist who often sought mechanical causes for disease, which Galen—who favored functional and "vital" causes—found overly simplistic.</note> assumption, although not so obviously as does that kind of dropsy which is brought about by an excessive chilling of the whole constitution. Health was seen as a balance of these qualities, while disease was an imbalance.</note>, the one pair being active and the other passive, and that among these the **Warm** has most power in connection with all functions, but especially with the genesis of the **humours** <term>humours: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that Galen believed governed human health and temperament</term>. Now, one cannot be blamed for not agreeing with all these great men, nor for imagining that one knows more than they; but not to consider such distinguished teaching worthy either of contradiction or even mention shows an extraordinary arrogance.

<header>GALEN</header>

Indeed, he is extremely petty in his judgment and utterly mean-spirited in all his disputes. In his accounts of **digestion** <note>original: *pepsis*; often rendered as **coction**, the "cooking" of food by internal heat</note>, he ambitiously argues against those who believe that food merely rots in the stomach. In his accounts of **distribution** <note>the movement of nutrients from the gut to the rest of the body</note>, he disputes those who believe blood is transferred through the veins because of the physical juxtaposition of the arteries. In his accounts of **breathing**, he argues against those who claim air is simply pushed around <note>referring to a theory of "circular propulsion" or *antiperistasis*</note>. He did not even hesitate to argue against those who believe urine enters the bladder in the form of vapor <note>this was the view of Asclepiades of Bithynia</note>, nor against those who think drink is carried into the lungs. Thus, in every case, he picks out the worst possible opinions and prides himself on spending a great deal of time refuting them.

<margin>112</margin>

Yet regarding the **generation of blood**—the importance of which is not at all inferior to the **chylification** <note>original: *chylosis*; the process of turning food into juice/chyle; cf. p. 238, note 2</note> of food in the stomach—he did not think it worthy to argue against any of the older thinkers, nor did he dare to introduce any other opinion of his own. This, despite having promised at the start of his general accounts to explain all the **natural faculties** <term>natural faculties: the innate biological powers (like growth, nutrition, and digestion) that Galen believed governed living things</term>, how they come to be, and through which parts of the animal they operate. 

Is it that if the power whose nature is to digest food becomes weak, the animal will suffer from indigestion, but if the **blood-making power** fails, there will be no ailment at all? Is this power alone made of **adamant** <term>adamant: a legendary unbreakable material; here meaning "indestructible" or "immune to failure"</term> and incapable of being affected? Or will there be some other consequence of its weakness? <note>That is to say, the blood-making (haematopoietic) function deserves investigation as a source of disease.</note>

<page-num>174</page-num>

<summary>Galen rebukes Erasistratus for focusing his debates on easy targets and outdated theories while failing to explain the essential process of blood production. He argues that if digestion can fail and cause illness, the body's ability to create blood must also be vulnerable to impairment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Galen’s polemic against the physician Erasistratus. ### ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, II. VIII

Now, Erasistratus is thoroughly small-minded and petty to the last degree in all his disputations. For instance, in his treatise **On Digestion** <note>original: *Peri Pepseos*; Galen refers to the "cooking" or "coction" of food via internal heat</note>, he argues jealously with those who consider that this is a process of **putrefaction** <note>the theory that food simply rots in the stomach rather than being processed by heat</note> of the food. In his work **On Distribution** <note>original: *Peri Anadosis*; referring to the movement of nutrients from the stomach to the rest of the body</note>, he fights with those who think that the distribution of blood through the veins results from the mere physical contact with the arteries. Also, in his work **On Respiration**, he argues with those who maintain that the air is forced along by the body's contraction. 

Nay, he did not even hesitate to contradict those who maintain that the **urine** passes into the bladder in a vaporous state <note>a theory held by Asclepiades of Bithynia, suggesting urine was sweat/vapor that condensed</note>, as also those who say that imbibed fluids are carried into the lung. Thus he delights to choose always the most valueless doctrines, and to spend his time more and more in contradicting these; whereas on the subject of the **origin of blood**—which is in no way less important than the **chylification** <note>original: *chylosis*; the process of refining food into a milky fluid called chyle</note> of food in the stomach—he did not deign to dispute with any of the ancients, nor did he himself venture to bring forward any other opinion. 

This is despite the fact that at the beginning of his treatise on **General Principles** he undertook to say how all the various natural functions take place, and through what parts of the animal! Now, is it possible that, when the faculty which naturally digests food is weak, the animal’s digestion fails, whereas the faculty which turns the digested food into blood cannot suffer any kind of impairment? Are we to suppose this latter faculty alone to be as tough as steel and unaffected by circumstances? Or is it that weakness of this faculty will result in some failure just as much as the digestive processes which precede it?

<summary>Galen accuses Erasistratus of being an intellectual coward who refutes minor, obviously incorrect theories while failing to explain the essential process of how the body generates blood from food.</summary>

# GALEN

...and not **dropsy**? <note>original: *hyderos*; an old medical term for swelling caused by excess fluid, often linked to liver failure</note> It is perfectly clear, then, from these facts, that **Erasistratus** <note>a famous 3rd-century BCE physician often criticized by Galen for his mechanical view of the body</note> did not hesitate to argue against even the most trivial opinions in other matters; yet here, he neither dared to speak against his predecessors nor to offer any new ideas himself, for he recognized the failure of his own school of thought.

<margin>113</margin>

What is beneficial from the outside to those who are insufficiently warm becomes a source of harm and **imbalance** to the [already warm] person; because of this, it is proven that honey, when cooked, becomes **bitter** <note>original: *pikron*</note> more quickly than other substances. Some have discovered this from the nature of the substance manifesting its **power** <term>dynamis: the inherent faculty or property of a substance to act upon the body</term>, while others have found it from **experience** <note>original: *peira*; Galen is distinguishing between "Rationalist" physicians who use logic and "Empiricist" physicians who rely only on observation</note> alone. In a word: for bodies that are **hot**—whether through nature, disease, age, season, region, or occupation—it generates bile; but it produces blood in those of the opposite nature.

# ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, II. ix

Whether one says the veins, or the liver, or the arteries, or the heart, or the stomach, or any other part performs any function whatsoever, he will be forced by inescapable necessity to admit that the function belongs to it because of the specific **temperament** <note>original: *krasis*; the mixing of the four qualities—hot, cold, wet, and dry—which Galen believed determined the health and function of any body part</note> arising from the four qualities. For I would like to hear from the **Erasistrateans** <note>followers of Erasistratus of Ceos (3rd century BCE), who focused on mechanical explanations for the body, often ignoring the "qualities" Galen championed</note> why the stomach contracts around the food, and why the veins produce blood. For simply knowing that it contracts is not yet useful in itself, unless we also know the cause; for in this way, I believe, we might also treat the malfunctions <note>original: *sphalmata*; literally "slips" or failures in the body's natural operation</note>.

“This is no concern of ours,” they claim; “we do not occupy ourselves with such causes as these; they are outside the sphere of the *practitioner* <note>original: *iatros*; a clinical physician or doctor</note>, and belong instead to the *scientific investigator* <note>original: *physikos*; a natural philosopher or physiologist who studies the laws of nature</note>.”

...natural activities while claiming to investigate them for the sake of healing? Likewise, if it is parched, we must moisten it, and if it is too moist, we must dry it. <margin>128</margin> Furthermore, regarding the **pairings** <note>Galen refers to the "syzygy" or combination of qualities, such as "hot and dry" or "cold and wet"</note> of these qualities: if the stomach has become simultaneously hotter and drier than is natural, the primary goal of the healing process is to cool and moisten it at once. It seems to me that Erasistratus is even ignorant of this basic fact: that whatever condition in the body impairs a natural activity—not by some secondary accident, but primarily and in its very essence—that condition *is* the **disease** <note>original: *nosema*</note> itself. For as a general rule, whenever the spleen draws the <term>melancholic humor</term> <note>original: *melancholikos chymos*; black bile, the humor associated with earth, coldness, and dryness</note> into itself less effectively than it ought, the blood remains unpurified and the entire body takes on an unhealthy color.

And when does the spleen draw it in less effectively? Is it not clearly when the organ is in a bad state? Just as it is the function of the kidneys to draw in urine—and they perform this poorly when they are failing—so it is with the spleen. It possesses an innate, "attractive power" for the melancholic quality; if it ever becomes weakened, it must necessarily fail in this attraction, and as a result, the blood becomes thicker and darker.

All these matters, which provide the greatest utility for both the diagnosis and the cure of diseases, <margin>134</margin> **Erasistratus** has completely skipped over. He has pretended to look down upon such great men—he, who normally does not ignore even the most ordinary people, but is always ambitiously arguing against even the silliest opinions! This makes it clear: having nothing to say in opposition to the ancients regarding what they declared about the function and use of the spleen, and unable to discover anything new himself, he ended up saying nothing at all. Black bile, on the other hand, is much more malignant and...*

### ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, Book II, Chapter 9

...the primary causes—I mean the Hot, the Cold, the Dry, and the Moist—and secondly, from obvious physical evidence, that there must be a cold and dry <term>humor</term> <note>original: *chymos*; the vital fluids ancient doctors believed regulated health and temperament</note>. Having then pointed out that this humor is <term>black bile</term> <note>also called "atrabiliary" from the Latin *atra bilis*</note> and that the <term>organ</term> <note>original: *splangchnon*; a major internal organ</note> which cleanses it is the spleen—having shown this using only a few of the many proofs provided by ancient writers—I will now move on to what remains of our topic.

What is left then but to explain clearly how the humors are generated, according to the teachings and demonstrations of the Ancients? This will be easier to understand through a comparison. Imagine some <term>new wine</term> <note>original: *gleukos*; "must," or freshly pressed grape juice that has not yet finished fermenting</note> that has recently been squeezed from the grape. It is fermenting and changing because of the <term>heat</term> <note>original: *thermasia*; Galen refers here to "innate heat," the vital energy believed to drive biological processes</note> it contains. Next, imagine two leftover substances produced during this process of change: one tends to be light and like air, while the other is heavy and more like earth. Of these, one is called the *flower* <note>the foam or yeast that rises to the top during fermentation</note> and the other the *lees* <note>the sediment or dregs at the bottom of the vat</note>.

You may accurately compare yellow bile to the first of these (the flower) and black bile to the second (the lees). However, these humors do not look the same when a person is healthy as they do when they are sick. When the body is unwell, the yellow bile becomes **<term>vitelline</term>** <note>derived from the Latin *vitellus*, meaning egg yolk</note>, so named because it resembles the yolk of an egg in both its color and its thickness. Likewise, the black bile itself can become far more harmful <note>or "malignant"</note> than it is in its natural state...

<summary>Galen compares the formation of bodily humors to the fermentation of wine, where yellow bile acts like the light foam (flower) and black bile acts like the heavy sediment (lees). He notes that while these are natural products, they can change in appearance and become harmful during illness.</summary>

# ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, II. ix

...its normal condition <note>original: *kata physin*; refers to the state of a humor when it is healthy and performing its proper function</note>, but no particular name has been given to this state of the humor, except that some people have called it **corrosive** or **acidic**, because it also becomes sharp like vinegar and eats away at the animal’s body—just as it would the earth if it were poured out upon it. It produces a kind of fermentation and seething, accompanied by bubbles—a sign that an abnormal putrefaction has been added to the natural condition of the **black humor**. 

It seems to me also that most of the ancient physicians give the name **black humor** <note>original: *melas chymos*</note> and not **black bile** to the normal portion of this fluid, which is discharged from the bowel and which also frequently rises to the top of the stomach contents. They call **black bile** <note>original: *melaina chole*</note> only that part which, through a kind of combustion <note>original: *synkausis*; a metabolic "overheating" or "cooking" of the fluids</note> and putrefaction, has had its quality changed to acid. There is no need, however, to dispute about names; instead, we must realize the facts, which are as follows:

In the formation of blood, everything in the <term>nutriment</term> <note>original: *trophe*; the processed food-matter traveling through the veins</note> which belongs naturally to the thick and earth-like part of the food, and which does not easily undergo the transformation produced by our **innate heat**, is drawn into the **spleen**. 

On the other hand, that part of the nutriment which is "roasted," so to speak, or burnt (this will be the warmest and sweetest part of it, like honey and fat), becomes **yellow bile**, and is cleared away through the so-called <term>biliary vessels</term> <note>original: *choledochous*; literally "bile-receiving" vessels</note>. In its natural state, this bile is thin, moist, and fluid. It is not like the bile that has been roasted to an excessive degree, becoming yellow, fiery, and thick—similar to the yolk of an egg <note>Galen uses the word *lekythodes* to describe bile that looks like egg yolk, indicating it has been "over-cooked" by the body's heat</note>—as it is when it is conveyed to the tissues after the digestion process is complete.

<margin>140</margin> ...commentaries. Therefore, as much ***phlegm*** as is carried in the veins and is useful to living beings requires no evacuation. One must pay attention here and recognize that, just as with each of the two **biles** <note>yellow and black bile</note>, there is a portion that is useful and natural to living beings and a portion that is useless and unnatural, so it is also with **phlegm**. By "complete indigestion" <note>original: *apepsia*; the failure of the body to "cook" or transform nutrients</note> of **phlegm**, one must clearly understand that of the **second digestion** <note>Galen believed the first digestion happened in the stomach and the second in the veins and liver</note>, namely that which occurs in the veins. These notes seem to me sufficient regarding the generation and corruption of the **humors**—being reminders of what was said by **Hippocrates**, **Plato**, **Aristotle**, **Praxagoras**, **Diocles**, and many others of the ancients.
