# BOOK III

## CHAPTER I

<margin>143</margin> In the preceding book, it has already been shown that **nutrition** occurs when the nourishing substance is altered and made like the substance being nourished <note>original: "of food to feeder," referring to the process where environmental nutrients are transformed into the organism's own tissue.</note>. We also established that within every part of the living animal there exists a certain <term>faculty</term> <note>original: *dynamis*; in Galen's medicine, this refers to an innate "power" or "ability" of an organ to perform a specific natural function.</note>. We name this faculty according to its activity: in a general sense, it is **alterative**, but in a more specific sense, it is both **assimilative** and **nutritive**. 

It was further demonstrated that the nourished part obtains its supply of matter—which it transforms into its own food—through another faculty that is naturally suited to draw in the appropriate <term>humor</term> <note>original: *chymos*; here referring to the juices or fluids derived from digested food.</note>. <margin>144</margin> Each part of the body has its own specific humor which is suitable for **assimilation** <note>original: *exomoiosis*; the final stage of nutrition where the food becomes identical to the bone, flesh, or organ it is feeding.</note>. The faculty that draws this humor in is called, based on its activity, the **attractive** or **drawing-in** faculty <note>original: *helktikē* or *epispastikē*; the power of an organ to pull necessary nutrients toward itself, much like a magnet pulls iron.</note>.

It has also been shown that before assimilation can occur, there is **adhesion** <note>original: *prosphysis*; the stage where the nutrient fluid sticks to the tissue it is meant to nourish.</note>, and even before that, **addition** <note>original: *prothesis*; the initial stage where the nutrient is simply placed next to the tissue.</note> takes place. This "addition" is, so to speak, the final goal of the activity of the attractive faculty. For the actual conveying of the food from the veins into each of the parts occurs through the operation of this **attractive** faculty.

<summary>Galen summarizes the mechanics of nutrition, explaining how organs use an "attractive faculty" to pull in humors from the blood, which then undergo a three-step process: addition, adhesion, and finally assimilation into the body's tissue.</summary>

# BOOK III

## CHAPTER I

It has been made clear in the preceding discussion that **nutrition** occurs by an *alteration* or *assimilation* of that which nourishes to that which receives nourishment <note>original: "of food to feeder." This refers to the metabolic process where external nutrients are transformed to become identical to the animal's own body tissues.</note>, and that there exists in every part of the animal a <term>faculty</term> <note>original: *dynamis*; in Galenic medicine, this is an innate "power" or "ability" of an organ to perform a specific natural function.</note> which, in view of its activity, we call in general terms **alterative**, or, more specifically, **assimilative** and **nutritive**. 

It was also shown that a sufficient supply of the matter—which the part being nourished makes into nutriment for itself—is ensured by virtue of another faculty. This faculty naturally attracts its proper <term>humor</term> <note>original: *chymos*; the "juices" or fluids (like blood or bile) derived from digested food.</note>. That humor is "proper" to each part which is naturally adapted for assimilation. The faculty which attracts the humor is called, by reason of its activity, the **attractive** or **drawing-in** faculty <note>original: *epispastic*.</note>. 

It has also been shown that **assimilation** is preceded by **adhesion**, and this, again, by **presentation** <note>These terms, *prosphysis* and *prosthesis* in the original Greek, describe the physical stages of nutrient absorption. *Prosthesis* is when the nutrient is placed against the tissue, and *prosphysis* is when it begins to "grow onto" or stick to it.</note>, the latter stage being, as one might say, the end or goal of the activity corresponding to the attractive faculty. For the actual bringing up of nutriment from the veins into each of the parts takes place through the <term>activation</term> <note>original: *energeia*; the Greek distinguishes between the "faculty" (the potential power) and the "activity" (the power in actual operation).</note> of the attractive faculty, whilst to

# BOOK III

## CHAPTER I (Continued)

...the goal itself is that the nutrient has already been brought forward and **presented** <note>original: *prosthesis*; the stage where the nutrient is placed in contact with the tissue it will eventually become.</note> to the body part. This is the very reason we require such an activity <note>the attractive faculty</note>: the nutrient is drawn in specifically so that it may be presented. From this point on, the **nourishment** of the living being requires a longer period of time. While it is possible for something to be drawn in quite rapidly, it is impossible for it to immediately grow onto the part, be altered, and become perfectly identical to that which is being nourished so as to become a piece of it right away. Rather, this is a process that can only be successfully completed over a longer duration.

If this presented **humor** <note>original: *chymos*; the fluids or "juices" produced during digestion.</note> did not remain within the part, but instead shifted to another location or flowed away—constantly moving and <margin>145</margin> changing its position—then neither **adhesion** <note>original: *prosphysis*; the physical joining of the nutrient to the organ.</note> nor **assimilation** <note>original: *exomoiosis*; the metabolic process of making the nutrient "like" the body tissue.</note> could occur in any of those places. Therefore, in this instance too, **nature** <note>original: *physis*.</note> requires another specific **faculty** for the long-term retention of the humor that has been presented to the part. This power does not flow into the part from the outside, but is instead firmly established within the part itself that is to be nourished. Because of its specific activity, those who came before us were compelled to name it the **retentive faculty** <note>original: *kathektikē*.</note>.

The argument has now clearly demonstrated the necessity for the existence of such a faculty. Anyone who understands the logical sequence of things will be firmly convinced by what we have said—provided that we maintain our underlying premise and prior proof: that **Nature** is a master craftsman and acts with care for the living being. Under that premise, it is necessary that she possesses such a faculty.

<summary>Galen argues that nutrients cannot be assimilated instantly; therefore, the body must possess a "retentive faculty" to hold the humors in place long enough for them to fuse with and transform into living tissue.</summary>

# ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, III. i

...have been finally brought up and **presented** <note>original: *prosthesis*; the stage where the nutrient is placed in contact with the tissue it will eventually become.</note> to the part is the actual end for which we desired such an activity; it is attracted in order that it may be presented. After this, considerable time is needed for the **nutrition** of the animal; whilst a thing may be even rapidly attracted, on the other hand to become adherent, altered, and entirely **assimilated** <note>original: *exomoiosis*; the metabolic process of making the nutrient identical to the body tissue.</note> to the part which is being nourished and to become a part of it, cannot take place suddenly, but requires a considerable amount of time. 

But if the **nutritive juice** <note>original: *chymos*; the fluids or "juices" produced during digestion.</note>, so presented, does not remain in the part, but withdraws to another one, and keeps flowing away, and constantly changing and shifting its position, neither **adhesion** <note>original: *prosphysis*; the physical joining or "growing onto" of the nutrient to the organ.</note> nor complete assimilation will take place in any of them. Here too, then, the [animal’s] **nature** <note>original: *physis*; the innate organizing power of the body.</note> has need of some other faculty for ensuring a prolonged stay of the presented juice at the part, and this not a faculty which comes in from somewhere outside but one which is resident in the part which is to be nourished. This faculty, again, in view of its activity our predecessors were obliged to call **retentive** <note>original: *kathektike*; from the Greek verb meaning "to hold back" or "retain".</note>.

Thus our argument has clearly shown<sup>1</sup> the necessity for the genesis of such a faculty, and whoever has an appreciation of logical sequence must be firmly persuaded from what we have said that, if it be laid down and proved by previous demonstration that Nature is artistic and solicitous for the animal’s welfare, it necessarily follows that she must also possess a faculty of this kind.

GALEN

## II

<margin>146</margin> But we are not accustomed to using this type of proof¹ alone; rather, by adding to it the compelling and forceful evidence from clearly visible phenomena, we shall now proceed to these matters. We will show that in certain parts of the body the **retentive faculty** <note>original: *kathektike dynamis*; the innate power of an organ to hold onto its contents.</note> is so manifest that its activity can be recognized by the **senses** <note>original: *aisthesis*; physical observation rather than abstract reasoning.</note> themselves. In other parts, it may be less obvious to the senses, but even there it can be detected by **reason** <note>original: *logos*; the logical conclusion or theory derived from evidence.</note>².

Let us therefore begin our instruction by first selecting, through a systematic method, certain parts of the body in which it is possible to accurately test and investigate the nature of this retentive faculty.

Could one start the investigation from a better place than from the largest and hollowest organs? To me, at least, it does not seem possible to find a better starting point. It is likely that in these organs the activities will appear clearly because of their size; whereas in small things, even if they possess such a faculty in a powerful way, their activity might not be easily recognized by the senses.

Now, among the most hollow and largest parts of the living creature are the **stomach** <note>original: *gaster*.</note> and what are called the **womb** or **uterus** <note>original: *metrai* and *hysterae*.</note>. What, then, prevents us from first setting these before us and examining their activities—at least as many as can be seen even before **dissection** <note>original: *anatomes*; the physical opening of the body for study.</note>?

## II

Since, however, it is not our habit to employ this kind of **demonstration** <note>original: *apodeixis*; a formal logical proof.</note> alone, but to add to it the compelling and forceful evidence drawn from obvious facts, we will also proceed to the latter kind in the present instance. We will demonstrate that in certain parts of the body the **retentive faculty** <note>original: *kathektike dynamis*; the natural power of an organ to hold onto its contents (like food or a fetus) until the proper time for release.</note> is so obvious that its operation can be actually recognized by the **senses** <note>original: *aisthesis*; physical observation or perception.</note>, while in other parts it is less obvious to the senses, but is capable even here of being detected by **logical reasoning** <note>original: *logikē theōria*; often translated as 'theorizing' or 'rational investigation,' this refers to the intellectual process of understanding truths that are not immediately visible.</note>.

Let us begin our exposition, then, by first dealing systematically for a while with certain definite parts of the body, in reference to which we may accurately test and inquire into the nature of the retentive faculty.

Now, could one begin the inquiry in any better way than with the largest and hollowest organs? Personally, I do not think one could. It is to be expected that in these, owing to their size, the activities will show quite clearly, whereas with respect to the small organs—even if they possess a strong faculty of this kind—its activation will not be immediately recognizable to the senses.

Now, those parts of the animal which are especially hollow and large are the **stomach** <note>original: *gastēr*.</note> and the organ which is called the **womb** or **uterus** <note>original: *mētrai* or *hysterai*. Ancient Greek writers often used these plural forms because they believed the human uterus was 'bicornuate'—meaning it had two distinct 'horns' or chambers—a feature common in many other mammals but not typically present in humans.</note>. What prevents us, then, from taking up these first and considering their activities, conducting the inquiry on our own...

# GALEN

It is not unreasonable to accept this teaching as a universal principle. The work of the **retentive faculty** <note>original: *kathektikē dynamis*; the biological power to grip and hold contents.</note> is to wrap the womb around the fetus from every side. Consequently, it is logical that to midwives who touch them, the **mouth of the womb** <note>The cervix.</note> appears closed. Furthermore, the pregnant women themselves—during the first few days and especially on that very day when the **conception of the seed** <note>original: *gonēs syllēpsis*; the moment the male "seed" is caught and held by the womb.</note> occurs—experience a sensation of the womb moving and contracting in upon itself. If both these things occur—the closing of the mouth without **inflammation** <note>original: *phlegmonē*; Galen distinguishes between a natural closing for pregnancy and a pathological closing due to swelling.</note> or any other ailment, and the subsequent sensation of movement within the uterus—then women believe they have already received and are now retaining the seed from the man.

<margin>150</margin> We are not merely inventing these details ourselves now; rather, they have been recorded by almost everyone who has treated these matters, having been proven through long experience. **Herophilus** <note>An early Greek physician (c. 335–280 BCE) known as the "Father of Anatomy," who performed early dissections in Alexandria.</note>, for instance, did not hesitate to write that the mouth of the womb would not even admit the tip of a **probe** <note>original: *mēlē*; a common medical instrument used for examination.</note> before a woman gives birth, and that it does not stand open even the slightest bit once pregnancy has begun. He also noted how it opens more widely during the flow of the **menses** <note>Monthly menstruation.</note>. All others who have studied these topics agree with him, and first of all physicians and philosophers, **Hippocrates** <note>The famous 5th-century BCE physician often credited with the origins of Western medicine.</note> declared that the mouth of the womb closes during both pregnancy and inflammation; however, in pregnancy it does not depart from its natural state, whereas in inflammation it becomes hard.

However, Hippocrates noted a distinction: in pregnancy, the womb does not depart from its own natural state, while in a state of inflammation, it becomes hard and rigid.

When the opening is sufficient for the passage of the fetus, they then raise the women up and seat them on the stool.

### IV

<margin>153</margin> Thus, in the case of the mothers, these two powers are clearly visible; in the case of the **stomach** <gloss>Greek: *gaster*</gloss>, it is as follows. First, consider the **fluctuations** <term>fluctuations: audible sloshing sounds (Greek: *kludones*) produced by liquid moving in a hollow organ</term>, which physicians have come to believe—and quite rightly so—are symptoms of a weak stomach. At other times, however, the stomach is full, yet the <column-break/> fluctuations are heard as if it were empty. 

When the stomach is in its natural state and making proper use of its **peristaltic power**, even if the contained material is small, it encompasses the whole of it and leaves no empty space. But when it is weak, and to the extent that it is unable to encompass the contents accurately, it creates a certain **roominess** <gloss>Greek: *eurychoria*</gloss> there. This allows the contained liquids to flow to different parts as the body changes posture, thereby producing the sloshing fluctuations.

It is reasonable, then, for those experiencing this symptom to expect that they will not digest their food sufficiently; for it is impossible for a weak stomach to digest well. In such people, the food remains in the stomach for a longer time...

## IV

Thus, the two faculties <note>Galen is referring to the 'attractive' and 'expulsive' faculties</note> are clearly seen in the case of the womb; in the case of the **stomach** <gloss>original Greek: *gaster*</gloss>, they appear as follows. 

First, consider the condition of **gurgling** <term>fluctuations: audible sloshing or splashing sounds within the body, which Galen calls *kludones*</term>, which physicians are convinced—and with good reason—is a symptom of a weak stomach. For sometimes, even when the very smallest quantity of food has been consumed, this does not occur, because the stomach is **contracting** <term>peristalsis: the involuntary, wave-like constriction of the muscles of a canal or organ that pushes contents forward</term> precisely upon the food and squeezing it at every point. At other times, however, even when the stomach is full, the gurglings are heard as though it were empty. 

For if the stomach is in its natural state, employing its **contractile power** in the ordinary way, then even if its contents are very small, it grasps all of them and does not leave any empty space. When it is weak, however, being unable to lay hold of its contents accurately, it produces a certain amount of vacant space. This allows the liquid contents to flow about in different directions as the stomach changes shape, and so produces these gurglings.

Thus, those who are troubled with this symptom expect, with good reason, that they will also be unable to digest adequately; for proper digestion cannot take place in a weak stomach. In such people also, the mass of food may be plainly seen to remain...

### ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, III. iv
->241<-

It is not only because the stomach is swollen and burdened, or because fluid sloshes from one part of the organ to another accompanied by gurgling noises—it is not only for these reasons that we can conclude food stays too long in the bodies of people with certain constitutions. We can also judge this from the nature of their *vomiting*. For instance, there are some people who vomit up every single bit of what they have eaten, not merely three or four hours after the meal, but actually in the middle of the night, long after a significant amount of time has passed.

Suppose you fill any animal whatsoever with liquid food—an experiment I have often performed on pigs, giving them a kind of gruel made of wheat flour and water, and then dissecting them three or four hours later. If you perform this yourself, you will find the food is still in the stomach. This is because it is not **chylification** <term>original: *chylōsis*. The mechanical and chemical breakdown of food into a milky fluid called chyle.</term> <note>Galen notes that this is not just mechanical breaking down, but a vital "alteration" of the food's nature.</note> which determines how long food stays in the stomach—since that breakdown can happen even outside the body. Rather, the deciding factor is **digestion** <term>original: *pepsis*. Often called "concoction," this is the process where the body's internal heat "cooks" and transforms food into a substance the body can actually use.</term>, which is something quite different from chylification, just as the production of blood and the act of nutrition are distinct processes.

For, just as it has been shown <note>Referring to Book I, chapters 10 and 11.</note> that these two processes depend upon a change in the qualities of the matter, similarly, the digestion of food in the stomach involves a **transmutation** <note>original: *metabolē*. A fundamental change in the substance's essence.</note> of that food into the specific quality of the body that is being nourished. <note>This relates back to Galen's earlier point on page 222 regarding how food becomes "like" the body.</note> Then, when it is completely digested, the lower outlet <note>The pylorus, or the "gatekeeper" of the stomach.</note> opens and the food is quickly pushed out through it, even if the meal included many stones, bones, grape seeds, or other things that cannot be turned into chyle. And you may observe this...

<summary>Galen argues that the stomach is an active organ that retains food until "digestion" (a vital transformation) is complete, using evidence from late-night vomiting and animal dissections. He distinguishes between simple liquefaction (chylification) and the vital "cooking" of food (digestion) that prepares it for the body's use.</summary>

...you can observe this for yourself in an animal, if you try to catch the exact moment when the food begins to descend from the stomach. But even if you fail to find that specific time—perhaps because nothing has passed down yet and the food is still undergoing **digestion** in the stomach—you will still find that dissection is not without its uses. You will observe, as I have just described, that the **pylorus** <term>original: *pylōros*. Literally "the gatekeeper"; the muscular valve at the base of the stomach.</term> is tightly closed. You will also see that the entire stomach is in a state of contraction, wrapped around the food much like the womb contracts around a fetus. It is impossible to ever find a vacant space in the uterus, the stomach, or in either of the two **bladders** <note>The urinary bladder and the gall-bladder.</note>—that is, the one called the **bile-receiving** vessel <margin>1</margin> <term>original: *cholēdochos*. The gall-bladder.</term> or the other. Whether their contents are plentiful or scarce, their cavities always appear completely full because their walls contract constantly upon whatever they contain—at least as long as the animal is in its natural, healthy condition.

Now **Erasistratus** <note>A famous Greek physician (c. 304–250 BCE) who favored mechanical explanations for biology, often clashing with Galen’s "vitalist" views.</note> for some reason claims that the **contractions** <margin>2</margin> <term>original: *peristolē*. The way an organ's walls "enfold" or "wrap" around their contents.</term> of the stomach are the cause of every part of the process—that is to say, the softening of the **food** <margin>3</margin>, the removal of waste matter, and the absorption of the food once it has been **chylified** <term>original: *chylōsis*. The process of turning food into "chyle," a milky fluid of emulsified fats.</term>.

I have personally, on countless occasions, opened the **peritoneum** <term>The thin membrane that lines the abdominal cavity and covers the organs.</term> of a still-living animal and have always found all the **intestines** contracting **peristaltically** <margin>4</margin> <term>original: *peristaltikōs*. A wave-like motion where the organ contracts and dilates to move contents along.</term> upon their contents. The condition of the stomach, however, is less simple to observe. In the case of substances that have been recently swallowed, the stomach grasps them accurately at both the top and bottom—in fact, at every single point. In this state, the stomach appears to be without movement <note>Galen is arguing that while the intestines move in waves, the stomach holds still while tightly gripping the food to digest it.</note>.

### V

<margin>158</margin> All these facts, then, agree with one another: the stomach, the womb, and the **bladders** <note>Galen refers to both the urinary bladder and the gallbladder as "cysts" or bladders.</note> possess certain **innate powers** <term>original: *dynameis*. ### VI

One can also often see this clearly in those who have **lost their appetite** <term>original: *apositōn*. ## VI

This can often be clearly observed in people who have an aversion to food. When they are forced to eat, they do not even have the strength to swallow. The stage of nutrition where the food-substance is brought into direct contact with the organ's tissues to prepare for assimilation.</term> it to them. For it is impossible for two bodies that are naturally suited to act upon one another to come together without both either acting and being acted upon, or one acting and the other being acted upon. 

If their powers are equal, they will affect each other equally. However, if one is much stronger, it will exert its activity upon its passive neighbor. In this case, while it produces a significant and visible effect, it will itself be changed very little or not at all. This is also where the main difference lies between nourishing food and a **harmful drug**; a drug masters the forces of the body, whereas food is mastered by them <margin>This describes the mutual influence between a living organism and its environment.</margin>.

There cannot, then, be any food suited for an animal that is not also "subdued" by the qualities existing within that animal. To be "subdued" in this context means to undergo an **alteration** <term>original: *alloiōsis*. A qualitative change where the food loses its original properties and takes on the properties of the body.</term>. Now, some parts of the body are stronger in power and others are weaker; therefore, while every part will subdue the nourishment proper to the animal, they will not all do so to the same degree. Thus, the stomach will subdue and alter its food, but not to the same extent as the liver, veins, arteries, and heart.

We must therefore observe exactly how much the stomach does alter it. This alteration is more significant than that which...

Indeed, the magnitude of this transformation is perhaps incomparable, if we consider the **phlegm**, **bile**, **vital spirit** <term>original: *pneuma*. In Galenic physiology, a subtle, air-like substance that carries life-force and heat throughout the body.</term>, and **heat** within the stomach, as well as the entire substance of the belly itself. What is there in the intestines that has a more powerful capacity for transformation than what is found in the stomach? Is it the thickness of the membranes, the arrangement of the neighboring organs, the length of time the food stays there, or some **innate heat** <note>original: *symphytos thermasia*. **Erasistratus** <note>Erasistratus of Ceos (c. 304–250 BCE) was a Greek anatomist and royal physician. Galen frequently targets him for his "mechanical" view of the body, which Galen believed ignored the vital "faculties" of Nature.</note> is much more simple-minded and ridiculous—either because he does not understand how the ancients meant that ***digestion is similar to boiling*** <note>original: *pepsis hepsei paraplēsios hyparchein*. He claims that it is unlikely that digestion—which involves such a mild heat—could be similar to boiling; as if it were necessary to assume that **Mount Etna** <note>A famous active volcano in Sicily, used here to represent intense, destructive heat.</note> was placed under the stomach, or as if the stomach were otherwise unable to **alter** <term>original: *alloiōsai*. To change the essential quality of a substance, not just its shape.</term> the food. Or, perhaps, [he thinks] that while it is able to alter it, it does not do so by means of the **innate heat** <term>original: *emphyton thermasian*. The vital internal warmth that ancient doctors believed was essential for life and digestion.</term>, which is clearly moist in nature and for this reason was described as *boiling* <note>original: *hepsein*. This refers specifically to cooking in liquid.</note> rather than *roasting* <note>original: *optan*. This refers to dry heat, like grilling or baking.</note>.

He ought, if he truly wished to dispute the facts, to have attempted to show—ideally and first of all—that the food is not changed in principle nor qualitatively altered by the stomach. Secondly, if he were unable to prove this, he should have shown that this alteration is useless to the animal.

And if he could not attack even this, he should have refuted the assumption regarding the **active principles** <note>original: *drastikas archas*. The four qualities—hot, cold, dry, and moist—that were thought to drive all biological processes.</note> and demonstrated that the **activities** <term>original: *energeias*. The specific functions or operations of an organ.</term> within the parts of the body do not exist because of a specific **temperament** <term>original: *krasin*. The unique "blend" of the four primary qualities in an individual or organ.</term> of hot, cold, dry, and moist, but because of something else entirely. Or, if he did not dare attack that, he should have shown that heat is not the most active of all qualities in things governed by **Nature** <term>original: *Physis*. The creative and organizing force that Galen believed directed all bodily functions with purpose.</term>. But if he could demonstrate none of these points, nor any of the others mentioned before, he should not talk nonsense by wrestling with a mere word! <note>Galen accuses Erasistratus of "word-wrestling"—attacking the metaphor of "boiling" rather than addressing the physiological reality of heat-driven transformation.</note>

But, as has been frequently said already,^1 the one starting-point of all this is a thoroughgoing enquiry into the question of the **Warm, Cold, Dry and Moist** <note>The four primary qualities or "humors" that Galen believed governed all biological change.</note>; this Aristotle carried out in the second of his books ***On Generation and Corruption*** <note>original: *De Generatione et Corruptione*</note>, where he shows that all the transmutations and **alterations** <term>original: *alloiōseis*. ### VIII

Thus, as regards digestion, even though he neglected everything else, he did at least attempt to prove his point—namely, that digestion in animals differs from boiling carried on outside; in regard to the question of **swallowing** <note>original: *kataposis*. The act of moving food from the mouth to the stomach.</note>, however, he did not go even so far as this. What are his words?

> "The stomach does not appear to exercise any **traction** <term>original: *holkē*. A "drawing" or "magnetic" force Galen believes organs use to pull in what they need.</term>." ^2

Now the fact is that the stomach possesses two **coats** <note>Layers of tissue or membranes.</note>, which certainly exist for some purpose; they extend as far as the mouth, the internal one remaining throughout similar to what it is in the stomach, and the other one tending to become of a more fleshy

...becoming more fleshy in the **gullet** <note>original: *stomachō*. The inner coat has **straight fibers** <note>original: *eutheias inas*. Galen identifies these as longitudinal fibers responsible for "attraction."</note>, for it was created for the sake of **attraction** <note>original: *holkēs*. The power of an organ to pull substances (like food) toward itself.</note>. The outer coat has **transverse fibers** <note>original: *egkarsias*. These are circular fibers responsible for squeezing or peristalsis.</note> for the sake of **contracting** <note>original: *peristellesthai*. The root of the modern term "peristalsis," referring to the way an organ wraps around and moves its contents.</note> in a circle. For in every moving organ in the body, the movements occur according to the positioning of its fibers. 

If you wish, first test this reasoning on the **muscles** themselves; in these, the fibers are most distinct, and their movements are clearly seen because of their intensity. After the muscles, proceed to the **natural organs** <note>This refers to the involuntary organs like the stomach and intestines, which Galen believed were governed by "Nature" rather than the conscious will.</note> and you will see that everything moves according to its fibers. This is why, in each of the **intestines**, the fibers are circular in both coats; they only **contract** <note>original: *peristellontai*</note>, they do not **attract** <note>original: *helkousi*</note>. 

The **stomach**, however, possesses straight fibers for the purpose of attraction and transverse ones for the purpose of contraction. Just as in the muscles, movement occurs when each fiber is tensed and drawn toward its origin, the same principle applies to the stomach. # GALEN

This phenomenon follows the passage of a mass; indeed, it would be a wonder if a volume passing through an organ did not cause it to dilate. Thus, the fact that the parts below dilate while the parts above contract is a feature common to dead bodies <note>original: *nekrois somasi*. Galen argues that simple expansion and contraction due to a physical mass is a purely mechanical process that can be observed even in non-living tissue.</note>—through which any object might pass—as well as to living ones, whether the organ wraps itself around the contents or exerts a pull upon them.

But the **shortening of length** is a property unique to those organs possessing **straight fibers** <note>original: *eutheias inas*. These are longitudinal fibers that, when contracted, shorten the organ and pull contents toward the source of the contraction.</note>, enabling them to perform traction <note>The act of drawing or pulling something toward oneself.</note>. Now, it has been demonstrated that the **gullet** <note>original: *stomachus*. In this context, it refers to the esophagus.</note> is drawn downwards, for otherwise it would not pull upon the larynx; it is therefore clear that the **stomach** <note>original: *gaster*. The organ we today call the stomach.</note> pulls the food through the gullet.

Likewise, during the act of **vomiting** <note>original: *emeton*.</note>, as the vomited matter is carried up to the mouth, those parts of the gullet distended by the rising material are certainly dilated. As each successive part is reached, it begins to expand, leaving the part <margin>172</margin> behind it <column-break/> clearly contracted. In this respect, the condition of the gullet is entirely similar to that of people who are swallowing; however, because the "pulling" action is absent, the total length of the organ remains the same during such occurrences.

For this reason, it is easier to swallow than to vomit. Swallowing is accomplished by the action of both coats of the stomach: the inner coat pulls the food down, while the outer coat wraps around it and helps push it along. Vomiting, however, is performed by the action of only one of the two—the outer coat.

<summary>Galen explains that swallowing is an active "pulling" process involving two muscle layers, whereas vomiting is a more difficult, one-layered mechanical push. He uses the movement of the esophagus and larynx as evidence for the stomach's active "traction" of food.</summary>

Rather, these are two opposite states of the stomach itself: it yearns after and tends towards what is advantageous and **familiar** <note>original: *oikeia* — things that are natural or "at home" in the body</note> to it, but it loathes and rids itself of what is **foreign**. 

Thus, the actual process of swallowing occurs very quickly in those who have a strong appetite for such foods as are proper to the stomach; the organ clearly **attracts** <note>original: *epispatai* — to draw towards oneself</note> and pulls them down before they are even fully chewed. Consequently, it is active only during **deglutition** <term>deglutition|the act of swallowing</term>. The **external coat**, however—which contains **transverse fibers** <note>Fibers running across or around the organ.</note>—was designed so that it may **contract** <note>original: *peristellesthai*; the root of the modern term "peristalsis."</note> upon its contents and propel them forward. ... [Aristotle] wrote in his *History of Animals* <note>original: *historiais*</note> and adds the reason, stating that this happens to them because of **gluttony** <note>original: *laimargia*</note>.

For the matter stands thus: during the most intense cravings, the **stomach** <note>original: *gaster*</note> runs upward in all animals, so that some people, having a vivid perception of this occurrence, say that their stomach "creeps out" of them. In others, while they are still chewing and before the food has been properly processed in the mouth, the stomach clearly snatches the food away against their will. 

<margin>174</margin> Consequently, in those animals which are naturally gluttonous, and where the mouth has ample space and the stomach is positioned nearby—as is the case with the **sea-bream** <note>original: *synodontos*</note> and the **comber** <note>original: *channes* — varieties of fish noted in ancient biology for their large mouths</note>—it is not at all surprising that when they are very hungry and pursuing one of the smaller creatures, and are just about to catch it, the stomach runs up into the mouth, driven by the urgency of desire. Indeed, this would be impossible if the stomach did not pull the food toward itself through the **esophagus** <term>esophagus|Galen uses the term *stomachos* here to refer to the gullet or "neck" of the stomach</term> as if using a hand. For just as we ourselves, out of eagerness, sometimes stretch our whole bodies along with our hand in order to more quickly grasp the object before us, so too the stomach stretches out along with the esophagus as if with a hand. For this reason, in animals where these three things coincide—a violent longing for food, a short esophagus, and a wide mouth—a slight impulse of extension brings the whole stomach up into the mouth.

It would perhaps be enough for a **natural philosopher** <note>original: *physiko* — a student of nature or a "physicist" in the Aristotelian sense</note> to take the evidence of this function from the construction of the organs alone.

And thus, in these animals in whom those three factors co-exist—an excessive propensity for food, a small gullet, and ample mouth proportions—in these, any slight tendency to movement forwards brings the whole stomach into the mouth.

## IX

We shall, therefore, no longer have any doubt even regarding the **spleen**, whether it **attracts** <note>original: *helkei* — the power of drawing in necessary substances</note> what is appropriate to it and **excretes** <note>original: *apokrinei* — the power of expelling waste</note> what is foreign, or whether it is its nature to **alter** and **retain** as much as it has drawn to itself. For these **four powers** <note>The four "natural faculties" are attraction, retention, alteration (assimilation), and excretion</note> have been shown to be necessary for every part that is intended to be nourished, and for this reason we stated that they are the **servants of nutrition**. For just as human excrement is most pleasant to dogs, so too the waste-products of the **liver** are appropriate—one to the **spleen**, another to the **gall-bladder**, and another to the **kidneys** <note>Galen believed that the spleen "feeds" on the thick, dark waste of the liver (black bile), while the gall-bladder takes the yellow bile</note>.

-># GALEN: ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES<-

## IX

Regarding the **spleen**, we shall no longer have any reason to doubt <note>Galen is responding to rival medical sects, like the Erasistrateans, who questioned the active powers of organs.</note> whether it **attracts** what is appropriate to it, **excretes** what is foreign, and possesses a natural power to **alter** and **retain** everything it draws in. Similarly, we should have no doubt concerning the **liver**, the **veins**, the **arteries**, the **heart**, or any other organ. 

It has been demonstrated that these **four faculties**—attraction, retention, alteration, and excretion—are necessary for every part of the body that requires nourishment. For this reason, we have called these powers the **handmaids of nutrition** <note>The "servants" or "assistants" that perform the work of processing food into living tissue.</note>. 

Nature operates with such efficiency that what one organ discards, another utilizes. For just as human excrement is most pleasing to dogs, so the waste-products remaining from the **liver** are appropriate for other organs: some are drawn to the **spleen**, others to the **gall-bladder**, and others to the **kidneys**. <note>Galen believed the liver "refined" blood, leaving behind "residues": yellow bile (for the gall-bladder), black bile (for the spleen), and watery waste (for the kidneys).</note>

However, while the conclusions the Ancients reached on these matters were correct, they did not always support their arguments with formal logical proofs. They likely never suspected that there could be **sophists** <note>Here, Galen uses "sophist" as an insult for contemporary doctors who used clever but (in his view) deceptive language to deny obvious biological facts.</note> so shameless that they would attempt to contradict the plain evidence of nature. Unfortunately, more recent physicians have been—

## Chapter XI

We must, therefore, bring our discussion to a conclusion for the sake of those who desire the **truth**, by adding what is still missing from the argument. For just as the **stomach** <note>original: "γαστὴρ" (*gastēr*). While often meaning 'belly,' Galen here refers specifically to the stomach's role in digestion.</note> clearly draws and pulls down food in those who are very hungry, even before it has been thoroughly softened in the mouth, yet feels disgust and rejects food in those who have no appetite and are eating by force, so also each of the other organs possesses both powers: the **attractive** <term>attractive power: the natural ability of an organ to draw in what is beneficial or necessary for its function</term> of what is appropriate, and the **expulsive** <term>expulsive power: the natural ability to reject or push out what is foreign, redundant, or harmful</term> of what is foreign. 

And for this reason, even if an organ is composed of only one **tunic** <note>original: "χιτῶνος" (*chitōnos*). In ancient anatomy, this refers to the 'coats' or layers of tissue that form the walls of internal organs.</note>—such as both the bladders <note>Galen refers to the urinary bladder and the gall bladder.</note>, the uterus, and the veins—it possesses both types of **fibers** <note>Galen identified different directions of fibers (longitudinal, transverse, and oblique) and assigned a specific physiological function to each.</note>, the straight and the transverse.

## XI

For the sake, then, of those who are aiming at **truth**, we must complete this treatise by adding what is still wanting in it. Let us recall what has already been established and provide the finishing touch to the entire subject by adding what is still required. It has been demonstrated that every part of a living creature draws into itself the **appropriate juice** <note>original: "οἰκεῖον χυμὸν" (*oikeion chymon*). In Galen’s system, each organ has a natural affinity for specific fluids that nourish it.</note>. This is essentially the *primary natural faculty*. 

The next point to understand is that an organ does not get rid of this attracted **nourishment** <insert>nutriments</insert>—neither in its entirety nor even the leftover portions—until either the organ itself or the majority of its contents undergoes a change in condition. For example, when the **stomach** <note>original: "γαστήρ" (*gastēr*).</note> has been sufficiently filled with food and has absorbed and stored the most useful parts within its own tissue layers, it then rejects the remainder as if it were a foreign burden. The same process occurs in the **bladders** <note>Galen typically refers to both the urinary bladder and the gall bladder in this context.</note>; when the matter drawn into them begins to cause distress—either because the volume stretches them too much or the quality of the fluid causes irritation—they seek to expel it.

The same logic applies to the **uterus** <note>The womb.</note>. It strives to relieve itself of annoyance either because it can no longer endure being stretched, or because it is irritated by the quality of the fluids being poured into it. Both of these conditions can sometimes occur with actual violence, resulting in a **miscarriage** <note>original: "ἔκτρωσις" (*ektrosis*).</note>. However, for the most part, these events happen in a natural and normal way; in those cases, it is not called a miscarriage, but rather **delivery** or **parturition** <note>The act of giving birth.</note>. 

Certain conditions, such as the use of **abortifacient drugs** <term>abortifacient: substances used to induce an abortion</term>, the death of the embryo, or the rupture of its protective membranes, are followed by an abortion. This also happens when the uterus is in pain due to an unhealthy state of tension. Furthermore, as has been wisely noted by **Hippocrates** <note>The most famous physician of Antiquity, whom Galen considered the ultimate authority.</note>, excessive movement by the embryo itself can also bring on the labor of birth. The situation is much the same regarding the **bladder situated upon the liver** <note>the gallbladder</note>; from which it is clear that it possesses very few nerves. Here too, the natural philosopher must seek out the corresponding principle. Similarly, the **neck of the uterus** <note>the cervix; Galen uses "stomachus" here to mean a narrow neck or throat of an organ</note> is the way inward for the seed and the way outward for the fetus.

But here again, while the **expulsive faculty** <term>expulsive faculty: the natural power of an organ to push out what is burdensome or waste</term> is evident, the **attractive faculty** <term>attractive faculty: the natural power of an organ to draw in what is useful or necessary</term> is not equally clear to the common person. However, **Hippocrates** <note>the "Father of Medicine," whom Galen considered the ultimate authority</note>, when blaming a weak uterus, says: "For its neck is not able to **draw in** the seed." <note>original: "Οὐ γὰρ δύναται αὐτέης ὁ στόμαχος εἰρύσαι τὴν γονήν."</note>

But **Erasistratus** and **Asclepiades** <note>two famous rival physicians/theorists who often disagreed with Galen’s "faculties" in favor of mechanical explanations</note> reached such a height of "wisdom" that they deprive not only the stomach and the uterus of such a power, but also the gallbladder and the **kidneys**. And yet, it has been demonstrated in the first book of this treatise that it is impossible to name any other cause for the secretion of **urine** or **bile**.

<margin>188</margin> Therefore, finding that the uterus, the stomach, and the gallbladder perform both **attraction** and **secretion** through one and the same neck, let us no longer wonder if Nature often excretes **waste products** <note>original: "περιττώματα" (*perittōmata*); the leftovers of digestion</note> into the stomach through the veins. Still less should we wonder if food can be drawn back again from the liver into the stomach during prolonged periods of **fasting**, through the very same veins by which it was originally delivered to the liver from the stomach. For to disbelieve such things...

He criticizes rivals like Erasistratus for denying these natural powers, which Galen believes also allow veins to move nutrients in reverse during hunger.</summary>

Still less need we be astonished if a certain amount of the food should, during long fasts, be drawn back from the liver into the stomach through the same veins by which it was yielded up to the liver during **absorption of nutriment** <term>anadosis: the "up-yield" or delivery of nutrients from the digestive tract into the veins and liver</term>. # GALEN

It is surely like no longer believing that **purgative drugs** draw their specific **humors** <note>original: "χυμούς" (*chymous*); the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that Galen believed governed health and disease</note> from the whole body into the stomach through the same openings through which **distribution** <term>distribution: original "ἀνάδοσις" (*anadosis*), the physiological process by which digested food is carried from the gut to the liver and then to the rest of the body</term> previously occurred. Instead, it would be like searching for one set of openings for distribution and another set for **purgation** <note>the process of cleansing the body of excess or harmful humors</note>.

And indeed, if one and the same opening serves two distinct **faculties** <term>faculties: natural powers or functions inherent to an organ, such as the power to attract, retain, or expel substances</term>, which at different times perform their **attraction** in opposite directions—at first by the power of the **liver**, and then, at the time of purgation, by the power of the drug—what is so strange about there being a double service and utility for those **veins** stationed in the middle between the liver and the parts of the belly? <margin>189</margin> Thus, when there is plenty of food contained in these <column-break/> parts, it is carried up into the **liver** through the aforementioned veins <note>the mesenteric veins</note>; but whenever the stomach and intestines are empty and in need of nourishment, it is drawn back again from the liver through these very same veins.

For every part appears to draw from every other part and to share with every other, and there is "one conflux and one conspiracy of all things," <note>Galen is quoting a famous aphorism attributed to Hippocrates, meaning the whole body breathes together in harmony and is interconnected.</note> just as the most divine **Hippocrates** <note>the 5th-century BCE physician whom Galen considered the ultimate authority on medicine</note> said. Therefore, the stronger part draws, and the weaker part is emptied.

One part is stronger or weaker than another either simply by nature and in common to everyone, or it occurs specifically in a certain individual. By nature and in common to all humans and animals alike, the **heart** is stronger than the **liver**, the liver is stronger than the **intestines** and the **stomach**, and the **arteries** are stronger than the **veins**, both to draw what is useful to themselves and to separate out what is not.

As a matter of fact, one and the same opening serves two distinct **faculties** <term>faculties: the natural "powers" or functions inherent to an organ, such as the power to attract or to expel</term>, and these exercise their pull at different times in opposite directions—first, it serves the pull of the **liver** and, during **catharsis** <note>the process of medicinal purging or cleansing</note>, it serves that of the drug. Thus, when there is an abundance of **nutriment** <note>nourishment or food-matter</note> contained in the food-canal, it is carried up to the liver by the veins mentioned; and when the canal is empty and in need of nutriment, this is again attracted from the liver by the same veins.

For everything appears to attract from and to go shares with everything else, and, as the most divine **Hippocrates** <note>the famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE, whom Galen viewed as the ultimate medical authority</note> has said, there would seem to be a **confluence** <note>original: "con-sensus," implying a "breathing together" or harmony</note> in the movements of fluids and vapors.² Thus the stronger draws and the weaker is evacuated.

Now, one part is weaker or stronger than another either absolutely, by nature, and in all cases, or else it becomes so in such and such a particular instance. Thus, by nature and in all men alike, the **heart** is stronger than the liver at attracting what is serviceable to it and rejecting what is not so; similarly the liver is stronger than the intestines and stomach, and

294

...are stronger. Specifically, within each of us, at one particular time the **liver** exerts a stronger pull, while the **stomach** does so at another. For when there is a great deal of **nutriment** <note>nourishment or food-matter</note> contained in the abdominal cavity and the liver is intensely desiring and in need of it, then that **viscus** <term>viscus: a large internal organ; here referring specifically to the liver</term> exerts a much stronger pull. 

Conversely, when the liver <margin>190</margin> is full and distended, while the stomach is hungry and empty, the power of **attraction** <term>attraction: the natural power (holke) of an organ to draw what it needs toward itself</term> shifts to the latter.

Consider an analogy: if we were holding food in our hands and trying to snatch it from one another—if we both had an equal need, the stronger person would likely prevail. But if the stronger person were already full and therefore held the leftovers carelessly, or perhaps even wished to share them with someone else, while the weaker person were desperately hungry, there would be nothing to prevent the weaker one from taking it all. 

In the same way, the stomach easily draws from the liver when the stomach itself is sufficiently in need of food and the liver is full. Indeed, the reason an animal sometimes does not feel hunger is due to the abundance of nourishment stored in the liver; for since the stomach has a better and more ready supply of nourishment available from there, it has no need for food from the outside world. 

But if the stomach should ever be in need and yet lack a supply, it becomes filled with **residues**. These are certain **ichors** <note>original: "ἰχῶρες"; here meaning thin, watery, or serous fluids rather than the "blood of the gods" in mythology</note> that are bilious, phlegmatic, or serous; these are the only things the liver releases to the stomach when the stomach itself is pulling for nourishment but the liver has nothing better to give.

Just as the parts of the body draw nourishment from one another, <margin>191</margin> so also do they at times deposit it into one another...

For each of the body’s parts possesses a certain innate **tension** <note>original: "tonos"</note> by which it pushes away its surplus. 

When, therefore, one of these parts becomes weaker due to some specific condition, the waste products must, of necessity, flow from all the other parts into that one. The strongest part deposits its waste into all its neighbors; each of those, in turn, passes it on to other parts that are weaker; and then each of those passes it again to others. This process continues until the waste matter, driven out of all the stronger areas, settles in one of the weakest parts of all. From there, it can no longer flow into anything else, because no stronger part will receive it, and the affected part itself lacks the strength to push it away.

But regarding the origin and cure of diseases, when we demonstrate these matters elsewhere, we will find sufficient evidence there for everything that has been correctly shown in this entire discourse. ...in each other, and just as the stronger part prevailed when the two were pulling against one another, so it is also when they are depositing waste. The strongest part deposits its surplus matter into all the parts near it; these, in turn, pass it into other parts that are weaker; these then pass it into yet others. This process continues for a long time, until the waste, being driven from one part into another, finally comes to rest in one of the weakest parts of all. It cannot flow from this weak part into any other because none of the stronger parts will accept it, while the affected part itself is too weak to drive it away.

When, however, we come to deal again with the origin and cure of disease, it will be possible to find there even more proofs of everything we have correctly pointed out in this book. For now, let us resume the task we have before us—that is, to show that there is nothing surprising in **nutriment** <note>nourishment or food energy</note> moving from the liver back to the intestines and stomach by way of the very same veins through which it had previously been delivered from those organs into the liver. 

Indeed, in many people who have suddenly and completely given up active exercise, or who have had a limb cut off, there occurs at certain times an evacuation of blood by way of the intestines—as **Hippocrates** <note>A famous Greek physician (c. 460–370 BCE) often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> has also pointed out in his writings. This causes no further trouble, but instead sharply purges the entire body and clears out **plethoras** <term>plethora: a medical state of "over-fullness," particularly an excess of blood in the system</term>.

For each part of the body, once it has **attracted** its proper humor and has then retained and enjoyed it, hastens to get rid of all the surplus. It does this as best, as quickly, and as effectively as possible, following the natural inclination of that surplus.

Hence the stomach clears away by vomiting those **superfluities** which come to the surface of its contents,² whilst the sediment it clears away by **diarrhoea**. And when the animal becomes sick, this means that the stomach is striving to be evacuated by vomiting. ...movements of substances. This can be clearly seen in the heart, the various arteries, the chest, and the lungs. Why, then, do you feel such a difficulty in the case of the veins which pass down from the liver into the stomach and intestines? Do you think it is strange that nourishment should be yielded up to the liver and then drawn back from the liver into the stomach by these same veins? 

You must define what you mean by this expression "at once." If you mean "at the same time," this is not what we ourselves are saying; for just as we take in a breath at one moment and give it out again at another, so at one time the liver draws nourishment from the stomach, and at another, the stomach draws from the liver. 

But if your expression "at once" means that within one and the same animal, a single organ serves to transport matter in opposite directions, and if it is this which disturbs you, consider **inspiration** and **expiration**. For of course these also take place through the same organs, even though they differ in their manner of movement and in the way in which the matter is conveyed through them.

Now the lungs, the chest, the **rough and smooth arteries** <term>rough arteries: "tracheiai arteriai" or windpipes; "smooth" arteries refer to the standard blood vessels.</term>, the heart, the mouth, and the nostrils reverse their movements at very short intervals and change the direction of the substances they contain. If it did so, it would no longer be a **physiological organ** <note>original: "organon physikon." Galen argues that these are "instruments of Nature" (Physis) acting through biological necessity, rather than "instruments of the Soul" (Psyche) acting through conscious reason or choice.</note>, but an animal possessing reason.

...[let us assume that] the stomach has by now completely **assimilated** <term>assimilated: "homoiosis," the final stage of nutrition where the food becomes identical to the substance of the organ.</term> to itself those materials which had adhered to it; that **adhesion** <note>original: "prosphysis"</note> to the intestines and the liver is now occurring for the materials that were previously **presented**; <margin>201</margin> and that **distribution** <note>original: "anadosis," the movement of nutrients from the digestive tract into the veins.</note> and **presentation** <note>original: "prosthesis"</note> are occurring throughout the whole body.

### XV

Therefore, one should not wonder if an altogether small amount of blood from the stomach—only as much as has been accurately refined—reaches the **arteries**, which are filled beforehand by lighter substances. Instead, one must recognize that there are two distinct kinds of **attraction** <term>traction: or *holke*, the power of an organ to pull matter to itself</term>. The first occurs through the sequence of filling a **vacuum** <note>original: *pros to kenoumenon akolouthia*, nature’s tendency to fill empty space</note>, while the second occurs through an **affinity of quality** <note>original: *oikeiotēti poiotētos*. This is the "magnetic" or "biological" attraction where like draws like.</note>.

For air is drawn into bellows in one way, whereas iron is drawn by the **Heraclean stone** <note>Heraclean stone: the ancient term for a magnet or lodestone.</note> in another. And while the sequence of filling a **vacuum** <margin>207</margin> draws the lighter substance first, the attraction based on the **affinity of quality** often draws the heavier substance, if it should happen to be more naturally akin. 

Consequently, for the **arteries** and the **heart**, insofar as they are hollow organs capable of dilating, the lighter substance always follows first; but insofar as they require nourishment, the appropriate matter is drawn into the **walls** <note>original: *chitones*, literally "tunics," referring to the structural layers of the organ's tissue</note> themselves, which constitute the actual bodies of the organs. Thus, of whatever blood is taken up into their cavities as they dilate, that which is most appropriate...

### XV

It is no wonder, therefore, that only a very small amount of nutrient matter—specifically, that which has been highly refined—moves from the stomach into the **arteries**, since these are filled beforehand with lighter substances. We must understand that *there are two kinds of attraction*: the first is that by which a **vacuum** becomes refilled, and the second is that caused by an **affinity of quality** <note>original: *oikeiotēti poiotētos*. This refers to a "magnetic" or biological pull where an organ identifies and attracts substances that are naturally suited to its needs.</note>. 

Air is drawn into bellows in one way, and iron is drawn by the **lodestone** <note>lodestone: a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite, used by the Greeks to illustrate "affinity."</note> in another. We must also understand that the suction resulting from evacuation acts primarily on what is light, whereas the attraction from **affinity of quality** frequently acts on what is heavier (provided it is naturally more **akin** <note>original: *oikeioteron*. Galen uses this to describe a "family-like" relationship between the organ and the substance it attracts.</note>). 

Therefore, in the case of the heart and the arteries, they attract lighter matter first insofar as they are hollow organs capable of **diastole** <term>diastole: the expansion of the heart or arteries, which creates suction</term>. However, insofar as they require nourishment, it is actually into their **walls** <note>The original term "coats" refers to the physical tissues or layers that form the bodies of these organs. Galen distinguishes between the mechanical filling of the heart's chambers and the biological feeding of the heart's own flesh.</note> that the appropriate matter is drawn.

That something is transferred from the **veins** into the **arteries**, in addition to what has already been said, there is also this sufficient evidence: if you wished to kill an animal by cutting through many large arteries, you would find its veins emptied just like the arteries. This would never have happened without the existence of mutual **anastomoses** <term>anastomoses: small openings or "mouth-to-mouth" connections where two vessels meet, allowing fluid to pass between them</term> between them. Similarly, in the heart itself, the thinnest part of the blood is drawn from the right ventricle into the left, as there are certain pores in the **middle septum** <note>septum: the muscular wall dividing the right and left sides of the heart</note> between them.

<margin>208</margin> These pores can be seen to a great extent; they are like certain **pits** <note>original: *bothynoi*. It is not possible, however, to see their actual terminal ends, both because of their extreme smallness and because, once the animal is dead, everything has become cooled and condensed. 

But **reason** <note>original: *logos* — Galen refers here to the use of scientific deduction and logical inference to understand physiological processes that cannot be directly observed. See also p. 226, note 2.</note> even here, starting first from the premise that *nothing is created by Nature in vain*, discovers these connections between the ventricles of the heart; for these pits, which terminate in such a narrow way, were certainly not created by chance or at random.

Secondly, this is also evident from the fact that of the two openings in the right ventricle of the heart—one for bringing blood in and one for taking it out—the one bringing it in is much larger. This implies that not all of the blood provided to the heart by the **vena cava** <term>vena cava: the large vein that Galen identifies as the primary source of blood for the heart</term> is sent back out from it...

Now, apart from what has already been said, the following is sufficient proof that something is taken over from the veins into the arteries. If you kill an animal by cutting through several of its large arteries, you will find the veins becoming empty along with the arteries; now, this could never occur if there were not **anastomoses** <term>anastomoses: small, invisible connections or "mouth-to-mouth" openings where veins and arteries meet, allowing fluid to pass between the two systems</term> between them. 

Similarly, also, in the **heart** itself, the thinnest portion of the blood is drawn from the **right ventricle** into the **left**, owing to there being perforations in the **septum** <note>the muscular wall dividing the right and left sides of the heart</note> between them. These can be seen for a great part of their length; they are like a kind of **pits** <note>original: *fossae*. Galen likely observed the deep recesses between the muscular columns of the heart wall and assumed they were the entries to tunnels.</note> with wide mouths, and they get constantly narrower. It is not possible, however, actually to observe their extreme terminations, owing both to the smallness of these and to the fact that when the animal is dead all the parts are chilled and shrunken. 

Here, too, however, our reasoning—starting from the principle that *nothing is done by Nature in vain*—discovers these connections between the **ventricles** <note>the lower chambers</note> of the heart; for it could not be at random and by chance that there occurred pits ending thus in narrow terminations.

And secondly, the presence of these connections has been assumed from the fact that, of the two orifices in the right ventricle—the one conducting blood in and the other out—the former <note>the tricuspid orifice, where blood enters the heart from the body</note> is much the larger. <meta>This page continues Galen's argument regarding the movement of fluids in the body. <page-num>324</page-num>
<header>GALEN</header>

But first, let us remind ourselves that there are two types of **attraction** <note>original: *holkē*; Galen uses this term to describe how organs "pull" nutrients toward themselves.</note>. The first occurs through wide passages, where a vacuum is created during expansion, and the substance follows to fill the emptied space. The second occurs through an **affinity of quality** <note>a natural "liking" or magnetic-like pull between the organ and the specific nutrient it needs</note>. In this second case, we must state that while the former type can draw substances even from a distance, the latter type can only draw from its immediate surroundings. For instance, if one places a very long tube into water, it is easy to draw the liquid up into the mouth through it. However, if you move iron too far from a **magnet** <term>magnet: literally the "Heraclean stone"</term>—or, as in the example we used previously, if you move chaff too far from a piece of amber—no attraction can take place.

<margin>211</margin> You can see this most clearly in the **irrigation channels** <note>original: *ochetoi*</note> found in gardens. From these channels, a certain amount of **moisture** <note>original: *ikmas*</note> is distributed to all the parts immediately adjacent and nearby, but it cannot reach the parts further away. For this reason, gardeners are forced to craft many small channels, cut from the main one, leading to every part of the garden to manage the inflow of water. They set the distances between these small channels at a width they believe is sufficient to allow the plants to enjoy and **draw** <note>original: *helkonta*</note> enough of the moisture flowing past them on either side. This is exactly how it is in the bodies of living creatures. Many channels, scattered throughout all the limbs, carry blood to them just like the waterworks in gardens. The distances between these channels were marvelously arranged by **Nature** <note>original: *physis*</note> from the very beginning, so that the parts lying between them are neither left in want of blood as they draw it into themselves, nor are they overwhelmed by a flood of it.

The spaces between these small channels are made of a size that presumably best allows the soil to satisfy its needs by drawing from the liquid flowing toward it from every side.

Furthermore, the intervals between these conduits have been wonderfully arranged by **Nature** <note>Galen frequently describes Nature as a wise, purposeful artisan who designs the body perfectly</note> from the very beginning. # GALEN

...immediately following these, the vessels themselves seize the fluid for themselves, and then those next in order take it from them in turn, until it reaches the **vena cava** <note>original: *koilēn phleba*; literally the "hollow vein," which Galen identifies as the primary vessel carrying blood from the liver to the heart</note>. Thus, when the arteries expand, they draw in **vapor**, **pneuma** <term>pneuma: the "vital spirit" or "breath of life" that Galen believed was carried by the arteries to animate the body</term>, and thin **blood**. ->### ON THE NATURAL FACULTIES, III. xv<-

...in their turn snatch it away, then those next again take it from these, until it reaches the **vena cava** <note>original: *koilēn phleba*; the "hollow vein," which Galen views as the central vessel for distributing blood from the liver</note>, whence finally the **kidneys** <note>original: *nephroi*</note> attract that part of it which is proper to them. Thus it is in no way surprising that **wine** <note>original: *oinos*</note> is taken up more rapidly than water, owing to its **appropriateness of quality** <note>original: *oikeiotēs*; the principle that an organ attracts substances that share its own "affinity" or nature</note>, and, further, that the **white clear** kind of wine is absorbed more rapidly owing to its **thinness** <term>thinness: *leptotēs*; a refined, subtle consistency that allows for easy movement through narrow vessels</term>, while **black turbid** wine is checked on the way and retarded because of its **thickness** <note>original: *pachos*; a dense or viscous quality that hinders flow</note>.

These facts, also, will afford abundant proof of what has already been said about the **arteries**; everywhere, in fact, such blood as is both specifically appropriate and at the same time thin in consistency answers more readily to their **traction** <note>The drawing or "pulling" force exerted by an organ</note> than does blood which is not so; this is why the arteries which, in their **diastole** <term>diastole: the expansion phase of the heart or arteries, which Galen believed acted like a bellows to draw in fluid and spirit</term>, absorb **vapour**, **pneuma** <term>pneuma: the "vital spirit" or "breath" thought to be carried in the arteries to animate the body</term>, and thin blood attract either none at all or very little of the juices contained in the stomach and intestines.

->N 2<-

<summary>Galen explains how the kidneys and arteries use selective attraction to draw in specific fluids, such as wine or pneuma, based on their consistency and quality. He distinguishes between the rapid absorption of "thin" white wine compared to the slower movement of "thick" dark wine.</summary>

<keywords>vena cava, kidneys, wine, arteries, diastole, pneuma, traction, thinness, thickness, attractive faculty</keywords>

These facts, also, will afford abundant proof of what has already been said about the **arteries**; everywhere, in fact, such blood as is both specifically appropriate and at the same time thin in consistency answers more readily to their **traction** <note>The drawing or "pulling" force exerted by an organ</note> than does blood which is not so; this is why the arteries which, in their **diastole** <term>diastole: the expansion phase of the heart or arteries, which Galen believed acted like a bellows to draw in fluid and spirit</term>, absorb **vapour**, **vital spirit** <note>original: *pneuma*; the life-breath or refined substance carried by arteries</note>, and thin, refined blood, but do not draw in that which is thick and heavy.

<summary>Galen explains how the kidneys and arteries selectively attract fluids and spirits based on their consistency and natural affinity, using the rapid absorption of thin wine as a primary example. This passage reinforces his theory that biological movement is driven by specific organ faculties rather than simple mechanical pressure.</summary>

# THE LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY

**HORACE: ODES AND EPODES.** <note>original: "Carmina" and "Epodi"; the lyrical poems of Quintus Horatius Flaccus, covering themes of love, friendship, and philosophy.</note> C. E. Bennett. (13th *Imp. revised.*)
**HORACE: SATIRES, EPISTLES, THE ART OF POETRY.** <note>original: "Sermones," "Epistulae," and "Ars Poetica." These works showcase Horace's wit, social commentary, and influential advice on writing poetry.</note> H. R. Fairclough. (8th *Imp. revised.*)
**JEROME: SELECT LETTERS.** <note>Saint Jerome was a key figure in early Christianity, famous for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> F. A. Wright.
**JUVENAL AND PERSIUS.** <note>Two of Rome’s most famous satirists who wrote biting critiques of the corruption and decadence of Roman society.</note> G. G. Ramsay. (7th *Imp.*)
**LIVY.** <note>Titus Livius, the historian who wrote a comprehensive history of Rome from its founding until his own time.</note> B. O. Foster, F. G. Moore, Evan T. Sage and A. C. Schlesinger. 13 Vols. Vols. I-XII. (Vol. I 3rd *Imp.*, Vols. II-VII, IX-XII 2nd *Imp. revised.*)
**LUCAN.** <note>Known for his epic poem on the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey the Great.</note> J. D. Duff. (3rd *Imp.*)
**LUCRETIUS.** <note>A poet and philosopher who explained the Epicurean view of the universe, arguing that the world is made of atoms.</note> W. H. D. Rouse. (6th *Imp. revised.*)
**MARTIAL.** <note>A master of the short, witty poem known as the epigram, often used to lampoon Roman social life.</note> W. C. A. Ker. 2 Vols. (Vol. I 5th *Imp.*, Vol. II 4th *Imp. revised.*)
**MINOR LATIN POETS:** from PUBLILIUS SYRUS TO RUTILIUS NAMATIANUS, including GRATTIUS, CALPURNIUS SICULUS, NEMESIANUS, AVIANUS, with "**Etna**," "**Phoenix**" and other poems. <note>A diverse collection of shorter or less-famous works covering nature, fables, and travel.</note> J. Wight Duff and Arnold M. Duff. (2nd *Imp.*)
**OVID: THE ART OF LOVE AND OTHER POEMS.** <note>original: "Ars Amatoria"; a playful and controversial series of poems on the techniques of romance.</note> J. H. Mozley. (3rd *Imp.*)
**OVID: THE CALENDAR.** <note>original: "Fasti"; an unfinished poem explaining the origins of Roman holidays and myths associated with the calendar.</note> Sir James G. Frazer. (2nd *Imp.*)
**OVID: HEROINES AND LOVE AFFAIRS.** <note>original: "Heroides" and "Amores"; the former features fictional letters from mythological women to their lovers, while the latter focuses on the poet's own romantic adventures.</note> Grant Showerman. (4th *Imp.*)
**OVID: TRANSFORMATIONS.** <note>original: "Metamorphoses"; Ovid's most famous work, a narrative poem weaving together myths of people changing into new forms.</note> F. J. Miller. 2 Vols. (Vol. I 10th *Imp.*, Vol. II 8th *Imp.*)
**OVID: SORROWS AND LETTERS FROM THE BLACK SEA.** <note>original: "Tristia" and "Ex Ponto"; mournful poems written by Ovid during his lonely exile on the edge of the Roman Empire.</note> A. L. Wheeler. (2nd *Imp.*)
**PETRONIUS.** <note>Likely the author of the "Satyricon," a bawdy comic novel.</note> M. Heseltine; **SENECA: THE PUMPKINIFICATION.** <note>original: "Apocolocyntosis"; a rare example of "Menippean satire" mocking the late Emperor Claudius's transition to a god.</note> W. H. D. Rouse. (8th *Imp. revised.*)
**PLAUTUS.** <note>Rome's most successful comic playwright, whose boisterous plays influenced modern sitcoms and musical theater.</note> Paul Nixon. 5 Vols. (Vols. I and II 5th *Imp.*, Vol. III 4th *Imp.*, Vols. IV and V 2nd *Imp.*)
**PLINY: LETTERS.** <note>Pliny the Younger's letters describe everything from the eruption of Mount Vesuvius to his daily life as a Roman official.</note> Melmoth's translation revised by W. M. L. Hutchinson. 2 Vols. (Vol. I 5th *Imp.*, Vol. II 4th *Imp.*)
**PLINY: NATURAL HISTORY.** <note>Pliny the Elder's massive encyclopedia of the ancient world's knowledge of science, geography, and art.</note> H. Rackham and W. H. S. Jones. 10 Vols. Vols. I-V. (Vols. I-IV 2nd *Imp.*)
**PROPERTIUS.** <note>A Roman poet of "elegy," primarily focused on his intense and often troubled love for a woman named Cynthia.</note> H. E. Butler. (5th *Imp.*)
**PRUDENTIUS.** <note>The most significant Christian poet of Late Antiquity.</note> H. J. Thomson. 2 Vols. Vol. I.
**QUINTILIAN.** <note>A celebrated teacher of rhetoric whose work outlines the ideal education for a Roman citizen.</note> H. E. Butler. 4 Vols. (2nd *Imp.*)
**REMAINS OF OLD LATIN.** <note>A collection of surviving fragments from the very earliest period of Roman literature.</note> E. H. Warmington. 4 Vols. Vol. I (Ennius and Caecilius). Vol. II (Livius, Naevius, Pacuvius, Accius). Vol. III (Lucilius, Laws of the XII Tables). Vol. IV (Archaic Inscriptions). (Vol. IV 2nd *Imp.*)
**SALLUST.** <note>A historian who focused on the moral decline of the Roman Republic through his accounts of political conspiracies and wars.</note> J. C. Rolfe. (3rd *Imp. revised.*)
